question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. The app is run by a payments company my agent uses, and it's that company that charges the card fee. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the retrieved documents, the card fee is very likely unlawful under the current Act, and it does not matter whether the fee goes to the app company or the agent. The documents don't cover refunds or complaint steps, though.

**Version used:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 115, in force from 13 October 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This is the version in force today. The regulations document I retrieved (Version 005) shows an end date of 9 February 2026 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf), so I could not confirm the current regulations.

### What the law says

- **Charges for electronic payment are prohibited.** A person must not demand or receive a charge in relation to "the establishment or use of direct debit facilities or any other electronic payment facility for payment of rent." The penalty is 60 penalty units [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A card payment through an app is likely an "electronic payment facility," though a tribunal would have the final say.
- **Fees for paying rent are prohibited.** A person other than an ADI must not demand or receive a fee for any prescribed matter in relation to the payment of rent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Version 115 removed the exemption for providers and agents that appeared in the earlier version, which named them as exempt [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The regulations list the prescribed matters, including "rent payment (other than payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act)" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). That regulation is in the version that ended on 9 February 2026, so I can't confirm it applies today.
- **A free method must be available.** The provider or agent must ensure that a payment method incurring no additional costs (other than the renter's own bank or account fees) is reasonably available. The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person or 400 for a body corporate [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Costs must be disclosed.** Before the renter agrees to a payment method, the provider or agent must give information about any costs, including third-party transaction fees [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### Does it matter who gets the fee?

Not under the text I found. The prohibitions apply to "a person," with no exception for who receives the money [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The agent is not exempt in Version 115 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents do not say whether a third-party payments company is caught directly. The agent's duties to offer a free method and disclose costs apply regardless, and the bank transfer option suggests the agent can meet them [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do

1. **Ask the agent in writing** which fee-free methods are available and what fees apply to card payment. The agent must give you this information before you choose a method [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Pay by bank transfer** (or Centrepay, if you use it). The agent must permit Centrepay [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether slower processing is a problem, and nothing I found suggests that speed affects your rights.
3. **Question the card fee** in writing, citing the sections above.

The documents do not set out how to get a refund of a card fee already paid, or which body handles complaints about it. For that, you would need to check other sources, such as Consumer Affairs Victoria or VCAT.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. (1) The answer says the agent 'must ensure that a payment method incurring no additional costs (other than the renter's own bank or account fees) is reasonably available.' (2) The hardest point, the fee ban, is covered by 'A person other than an ADI must not demand or receive a fee for any prescribed matter in relation to the payment of rent', together with the regulation's 'other than payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act' and the short answer that 'it does not matter whether the fee goes to the app company or the agent.' The caveats about the regulation version and about third-party companies do not hide which way the point falls. (3) It gives next steps, such as paying by bank transfer and questioning the fee in writing.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: neither failure statement is asserted, because the answer says "the card fee is very likely unlawful under the current Act" rather than allowing it because a free option exists, and it mentions the old exemption only to reject it ("Version 115 removed the exemption for providers and agents" and "The agent is not exempt in Version 115").

version-cited.reason: No — the answer correctly names the Act as "Authorised Version No. 115", but it never names the Regulations' in-force Version 009. Instead it applies the prescribed-matters rule ("rent payment (other than payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act)") from "Version 005" (21-3sra005), which was not in force on that date, and this counts as relying on it even with a caveat.

question: My lease is on the standard form and started in 2024. It has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. I cleaned them myself and they're back to how they were when I moved in, but the agent wants a receipt from a professional cleaner. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?
answer:
**What the law says**

- The Act bans terms requiring professional cleaning at the end of a tenancy unless the term is in the standard form [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). A standard-form term may require professional cleaning, or payment for it, only if professional cleaning "becomes required to restore the premises to the condition they were in immediately before the start of the tenancy, taking into account fair wear and tear" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The Regulations add that the provider "must not require the renter to arrange professional cleaning or cleaning to a professional standard at the end of the tenancy" unless either the premises were professionally cleaned before the tenancy started and the renter was told so, or professional cleaning "is required to restore the rented premises to the same condition they were in immediately before the start of the tenancy, having regard to the condition report and taking into account fair wear and tear" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- If that second condition is met, the renter "must have all or part of the rented premises professionally cleaned, or pay the cost" of it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

So the key question is whether professional cleaning is actually *required* to restore the carpets. If your own cleaning restored them to their starting condition, the documents suggest professional cleaning may not be required.

**What the renter can do or ask**

- **Check the condition report.** The renter must fill in their part within 5 business days after moving in, and the report "may help the renter verify the condition of the rented premises, if there is a later dispute about the renter's responsibility for damage or cleaning" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Gather photos.** The form advises taking photos "at the beginning and at the end of the tenancy," dated and labelled by location [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Photos are useful in a dispute about condition [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Check the end-of-tenancy inspection.** The provider must complete the final inspection and condition report "within 10 days after the end date of the agreement," give the renter an opportunity to attend if possible, and "allow for fair wear and tear" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Dispute the requirement.** A renter can apply to VCAT for an order declaring a term invalid or varying it if it is "harsh or unconscionable" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The Act also lets VCAT declare a term invalid where it is a prohibited term [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**What the documents do not cover**

- They do not say whether a renter must provide a receipt from a professional cleaner, or whether a self-cleaned carpet can be treated as meeting the clause.
- They do not say what happens if you refuse to pay for professional cleaning.

**Version note**

I cannot confirm which version applies today (9 November 2026). The most recent Act I retrieved is Authorised Version No. 110, in force from 6 August 2025 to 24 November 2025 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), so it does not show the law in force today. The Regulations I retrieved are Authorised Version No. 002, in force until 30 November 2024 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Neither covers the period after those dates, so you should check the current versions on the Victorian legislation website or with Consumer Affairs Victoria or Victoria Legal Aid before relying on this.

must-mention.reason: No. The answer covers the reg 12 conditions and the role of the condition report and photos as evidence. It omits the s 63 point: it never states the renter's general duty to leave the premises reasonably clean and in the same condition as at the start, fair wear and tear excepted. The pre-tenancy condition appears only as a trigger for professional cleaning, not as the renter's own obligation.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer never says the renter must pay simply because of the clause or the pet, and instead makes it conditional, stating 'the key question is whether professional cleaning is actually *required* to restore the carpets. If your own cleaning restored them to their starting condition, the documents suggest professional cleaning may not be required.'

version-cited.reason: No. The answer relies on versions that were not in force on the date: 'Authorised Version No. 110' of the Act (97-109aa110), version 101 (97-109aa101), and 'Authorised Version No. 002' of the Regulations (21-3sra002). It never names the in-force Act Version No. 115 or Regulations Version No. 009. The rules it applies on professional cleaning and VCAT would be lost if those outdated sources were deleted.

question: When I moved out I agreed the agent could take an amount for cleaning out of my bond, but I never signed a bond claim form for it. Then my full bond came back to me, and a month later the agent sent a separate invoice for the cleaning. Do I have to pay it? Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved law does not say you must pay a separate invoice after your full bond has been refunded, and it does not address whether agreeing verbally to a deduction is the same as agreeing to pay an invoice. The Act does set out how a cleaning cost can be taken from a bond, and that process points away from a separate invoice.

**Version used:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 115 (in force from 13 October 2026, no end date shown) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- A landlord can claim from a bond for "the reasonable cost of cleaning any part of the premises, if the premises were not left reasonably clean by the renter, having regard to the condition of the premises at the commencement of the residential rental agreement" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- A claim must be made to the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority, "in a form approved by the Authority" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Before a landlord-side claim is made, the provider "must give each renter bond claim evidence that supports the claim" at least 3 days before the claim is made. That evidence "must not conflict with a statement in a condition report" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- A provider "must not request or obtain a renter's signature to a claim form" unless the form specifies "the amount of bond to be refunded" and any apportionment. The penalty is 60 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- If a claim is made without the consent of all parties, the Authority must notify the other parties. The notice must state that the Authority will pay the claim unless, "within 14 days after receiving notice," a party gives written notice that the claim is subject to a Tribunal application [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The Authority must repay the bond where no party has notified an application within 14 days after that notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask the agent for the claim form and the cleaning evidence.** Under the current law, a cleaning deduction has to go through a claim, and the claim must be supported by bond claim evidence given to you at least 3 days before it is made [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Check the condition report.** The evidence must not conflict with the condition report from the start of the tenancy, and the cleaning cost is only claimable if the premises were not left reasonably clean, judged against their condition when you moved in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Check whether you received a notice of claim.** If a claim was made without your consent, the Authority had to notify you, and you had 14 days to say it was subject to a Tribunal application [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Your full refund suggests no claim was paid out from the bond, but I can't confirm this from the documents.
4. **Ask the agent what legal basis they rely on for the invoice.** The retrieved provisions cover claims against the bond. They don't address a separate invoice sent after the bond has been refunded.

## What the documents don't cover

- Whether an oral or informal agreement to a bond deduction is binding, or whether it counts as agreeing to pay an invoice. The Act's claim-form requirements are relevant here, but the retrieved excerpts don't say how an informal agreement is treated.
- Whether the agent can recover cleaning costs directly from you after the bond has been fully refunded. The retrieved section of the current version does not cover this. An older version (No. 111) refers to a bar on further claims against the Authority once it has paid out a bond in good faith [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), but that version is no longer in force and doesn't settle the question.
- Whether you must pay the invoice as a matter of contract. That is outside the retrieved documents.

If the invoice is for a real amount and you dispute it, the documents don't say what the agent's next step would be. A tenancy dispute body or a legal adviser could confirm that.

---

[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf (Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, in force from 13 October 2026)
[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) rta-1997-v111-2025-11-25.pdf (Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 111, in force from 25 November 2025 to 29 June 2026)

must-mention.reason: No. The first point is missing. The answer never states that agreeing to a bond deduction is agreement to a claim on the bond rather than agreement to pay a separate invoice. Instead it says the law "does not address whether agreeing verbally to a deduction is the same as agreeing to pay an invoice" and lists this under "What the documents don't cover." That hedges the point so far that a reader cannot tell which way it falls, even though it adds that the process "points away from a separate invoice." The second point is covered: the answer says cleaning is claimable only "if the premises were not left reasonably clean by the renter, having regard to the condition of the premises at the commencement."

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the renter must pay because they agreed to a deduction, and it never says full repayment bars any further claim; it says "The retrieved law does not say you must pay a separate invoice" and that the older version's bar on further claims "is no longer in force and doesn't settle the question."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115' and draws every rule it applies from that version. Its mention of Version No. 111 is explicitly flagged as 'no longer in force' and 'doesn't settle the question'. It is not presented as the law or as a step the user can take, so deleting it would not change the answer's substance.

question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. I've called them twice today. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
**Short answer:** You don't have to wait indefinitely, but the law doesn't let you do the repair yourself. You can arrange for a suitably qualified person to do it if the owner can't, under the conditions below.

**What the law says**

- Only a suitably qualified person may carry out repairs, both urgent and non-urgent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). A DIY repair isn't what the law allows.
- A burst water service is given as an example of an urgent repair [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Urgent repairs also include failure or breakdown of an essential service or appliance for hot water, cooking, heating or laundering supplied by the rental provider [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether a whole-house water shut-off is covered, so check this with Consumer Affairs Victoria (consumer.vic.gov.au/urgentrepairs), which the regulations reference [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- The rental provider must carry out urgent repairs after being notified [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- A renter may arrange urgent repairs if they have taken reasonable steps to get the provider to do them immediately and the provider has not done them [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The Act frames this as the renter being unable to get the provider or agent to carry out the repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do**

1. **Notify the owner in writing.** The form advises that if an urgent repair is needed, the renter should notify the rental provider in writing [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Put it in writing now, referring to the two calls you made today, and state that it is urgent. The documents don't say how many calls or how much time counts as "reasonable steps," so a written record is your best protection.
2. **Arrange a suitably qualified person** (such as a licensed plumber) to fix it. The renter may be reimbursed directly by the rental provider for the reasonable cost of repairs up to $2500 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Give written notice of the repairs and cost.** The renter must give 7 days' written notice of the repairs carried out and the cost, and the provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days after receiving that notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
4. **If the owner refuses to pay, or the cost is more than $2500, apply to VCAT.** A renter can apply for an order requiring the provider to carry out urgent repairs if they cannot meet the cost, the cost is more than $2500, or the provider refuses to pay for repairs the renter arranged [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The Act says VCAT must hear such an application within 2 business days of it being made [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**Important caveats**

- The Act document I found (Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110) shows an in-force end date of 24 November 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). That means it is not the version in force today (9 November 2026), and I could not find the current Act in the documents. The 7-day notice and 2-business-day hearing rules above come from that superseded version and should be checked against the current Act.
- The Regulations I relied on are the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, S.R. No. 3/2021, Authorised Version **rt-regs-2021 v009**, in force from 30 June 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Their urgent repair provisions are the current ones I could find.
- The documents don't say how long you must wait before acting, or whether two phone calls meet the "reasonable steps" test.

must-mention.reason: No. The answer covers the first two points: it names a burst water service as an urgent repair, and it says the renter can arrange the repair after reasonable steps and be reimbursed up to $2500 within 7 days of written notice. It misses the third point. It never says that a term requiring the owner's nominated tradespeople is prohibited (reg 11(e)), and it never says the owner's preferred-tradesperson policy cannot stop an urgent repair.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer asserts neither failure condition, saying "You don't have to wait indefinitely... You can arrange for a suitably qualified person to do it" and that "The renter may be reimbursed directly by the rental provider for the reasonable cost of repairs up to $2500."

version-cited.reason: No: the answer names the Act only as "Authorised Version No. 110" (link 97-109aa110) and not the in-force Version No. 115. It also applies rules from that superseded version, the 7-day written notice and the 2-business-day VCAT hearing, as steps the user can take, despite its caveat. It does correctly name the Regulations as "Authorised Version rt-regs-2021 v009".

question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. I haven't moved any of my things in or stayed there yet. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
**Short answer:** Under the current Act, you may be able to refuse to move in and avoid rent for the period before you actually move in. The documents I found do not clearly give you a right to cancel the lease, and they do not provide a general right to a rent reduction for disrepair.

## What the law says

- **Premises must be ready on the move-in day.** The provider must ensure the premises are vacant and reasonably clean on the day you are due to move in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Rental minimum standards.** The provider must ensure the premises comply with the prescribed rental minimum standards on or before the day you enter occupation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Standards that may apply here.** The Regulations require the premises to be "structurally sound and weatherproof," and that "each room... must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Ongoing repair duty.** The provider must keep the premises "in good repair" and "in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation." This applies whether or not you knew of the disrepair before moving in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs.** The Act's definition of urgent repairs includes "any fault or damage that makes rented premises... unsafe or insecure, including... the presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

Your situation matters here. The Act uses "entering into occupation," so whether you have already entered occupation (having keys alone may not be enough) is a question the documents do not answer. Get advice on that point.

## Your options

**1. Refuse to move in and avoid rent (the closest answer to "cancel").**
- You are "not required to enter into occupation of premises which do not comply" with the vacant and reasonably clean requirement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- You are "not required to pay rent" for the period from the agreed move-in day until you actually move in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The documents do not say that this ends the lease. They also refer to a notice to vacate under section 91ZD of the Act where premises are "destroyed or unfit for habitation" [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). That section's text is not in the documents I retrieved, so I cannot tell you how it works or whether it applies.

**2. Ask for repairs.**
- Give the provider written notice. A renter must give written notice "as soon as practicable" after becoming aware of damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Because mould and damp are urgent repairs, you may issue a request for urgent repairs when the premises do not meet the minimum standards on or just after you enter occupation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- If the provider does not act, you may arrange the urgent repairs yourself after taking "reasonable steps" to get the provider to act immediately. The provider must reimburse "the reasonable cost of the repairs," and the Regulations' summary says reimbursement is available "up to $2500" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- You may apply to VCAT for an order requiring urgent repairs if you cannot meet the cost, the cost is more than $2,500, or the provider refuses to pay [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The Act says VCAT must hear such an application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- For non-urgent repairs, you may apply to the Director for an investigation, and then to VCAT [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**3. Ask for a lower rent.**
The documents I found do not provide a rent reduction for disrepair. The only rent relief they describe is the rent-free period before you move in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I can't tell you whether you could seek a rent reduction through other routes, such as a VCAT order.

## Next steps

- Put your complaint in writing now, describing the damp, mould and rotting timber, and keep copies.

question: Our rental was broken into several times while we were moving out, and there are about three weeks left on our fixed-term lease. The burglars damaged the plumbing and wiring, so we can't even clean properly. What are our options before the lease ends?
answer:
**Short answer:** The current Act gives you a few routes. You should report the damage in writing now, ask the landlord to repair, and arrange urgent repairs yourself if they don't act. If the premises are unfit or unsafe, you may be able to end the tenancy on short notice. The general notice route won't help you break the lease early. The documents don't cover burglary-specific issues, insurance, or police reporting.

**Which law applies:** The Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115 (file rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf), in force from 13 October 2026. It is the latest version in the retrieved set and has no end date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

---

### What the law says

- **Duty to report:** You must give the landlord written notice as soon as practicable after you become aware of damage to the premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 72AA). The notice must state the fact that the damage occurred and its nature [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 62).
- **Duty not to damage:** You and your visitors must not intentionally or negligently cause damage, but fair wear and tear is excluded [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 61). The documents don't say whether burglars count as "visitors" or how liability applies to a break-in. A repair notice can be issued where damage results from your failure to take care [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 78).
- **Condition at the end:** You must leave the premises, "as far as practicable," reasonably clean and in the same condition as when you moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 63(2)). The documents don't say how this applies when damage prevents cleaning.
- **Urgent repairs:** You may arrange urgent repairs if you have taken reasonable steps to have the landlord do them immediately and they haven't. You must give 7 days' written notice of the repairs and their cost. The landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days of that notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 72). The Act caps reimbursement at the lesser of the reasonable cost or a prescribed amount. An expired regulations version stated $2,500 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf), so check the current figure. The documents don't include the s 3(1) definition of "urgent repairs," so I can't confirm that plumbing or wiring damage qualifies.
- **VCAT:** If you can't pay for urgent repairs, or the landlord refuses to reimburse you, you can apply to VCAT. It must hear the application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 73).
- **Non-urgent repairs:** If the landlord doesn't act within 14 days of written notice, you can apply to VCAT [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (ss 75, 74).

### Ending the lease early

- **General notice:** A notice of intention to vacate must give at least 28 days' notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 91Z). With about three weeks left, that period would run past the end of the lease. A notice that sets a termination date earlier than the end of the fixed term has no effect in any other case [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 91ZA(1)(b)).
- **Unfit or unsafe premises:** You may give a notice of intention to vacate if the premises are unfit for human habitation or have been destroyed to an extent that makes them unsafe. The termination date can be the date the notice is given or a later date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 91ZD). This is the most relevant route if the wiring is unsafe.
- **Lease-break fees:** The text I retrieved says no lease-break fee applies to terminations under s 91ZB or s 91ZC [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). It doesn't say whether that applies under s 91ZD, so I can't confirm it.
- **Reduced notice (14 days):** The categories in s 91ZB don't include damage from a break-in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

---

### What you can do now

1. **Notify in writing today.** List each damaged item, when you found it, and what it is. Keep copies and photos.
2. **Get a professional assessment** of the plumbing and wiring. This supports both an urgent-repair request and any claim that the premises are unsafe.
3. **Ask the landlord in writing** to carry out urgent repairs, and give a reasonable deadline.
4. **If they don't act,** arrange urgent repairs yourself and send the 7-day written notice with the cost. An expired regulations version states that only a suitably qualified person may carry out repairs [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf), so use a licensed tradesperson.
5. **If the wiring or plumbing makes the home unsafe,** consider a s 91ZD notice of intention to vacate.
6. **Clean what you can** and keep records showing what you couldn't do because of the damage.
7. **If there's a dispute,** apply to VCAT for urgent repairs or reimbursement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't cover insurance claims, police reports, or how a burglary affects liability. The regulations summary refers to consumer.vic.gov.au/renting for more information [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf), but that regulations version has expired, so please check it before relying on it.

question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. The app is run by a payments company my agent uses, and it's that company that charges the card fee. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
**Short answer:** On the current text, the card fee is likely prohibited if it is a charge for using an electronic payment facility for rent. The documents don't settle whether it is, and they don't say whether it matters who keeps the fee.

**Which law applies today:** The *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Vic), Authorised Version (version) 115, is in force from 13 October 2026 and is the version I've relied on [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What the law says**

- **Charges for electronic payment:** A person must not demand or receive from a renter a charge or indemnity for a charge relating to "the establishment or use of direct debit facilities or any other electronic payment facility for payment of rent." The penalty is 60 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A card fee charged for paying rent looks like it fits this wording.
- **Other rent payment fees:** A person other than an ADI (authorised deposit-taking institution) must not demand or receive a fee for any "prescribed matter" relating to the payment of rent. The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person and 400 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't define "prescribed matter," so I can't confirm whether a card fee falls within it.
- **Free payment method:** The provider or agent must ensure that a rent payment method incurring no additional costs (other than bank or account fees on the renter's account) is reasonably available to the renter [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Your bank transfer option appears to meet this. The text doesn't say anything about speed, so slowness doesn't break this rule on its face.
- **Cost disclosure:** The provider or agent must tell the renter about costs of a payment method, including third-party transaction fees and electronic payment facility fees, before the renter consents to using that method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**Does it matter who gets the fee?**

The prohibitions apply to "a person" who demands or receives a charge from the renter. Nothing in the current text limits them to the provider or agent, so routing the fee through a payments company doesn't obviously avoid them. The documents don't address this directly.

The current s 51A wording shown only excludes ADIs. The earlier version (version 111, in force from 25 November 2025 to 29 June 2026) also excluded residential rental providers and agents [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). So the agent's exposure under s 51A is different under the current version, though the question of whether a card fee is a "prescribed matter" remains open.

**What you can do or ask**

- Ask your agent in writing what costs apply to each payment method, since the agent must give this information before you consent to a method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Ask the agent to confirm that bank transfer is available at no extra cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Pay by bank transfer, which the documents say must be reasonably available at no additional cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover**

- Whether a card fee is a "prescribed matter" under s 51A.
- Whether a renter can get a refund of a card fee already paid, or how to complain or apply to the Tribunal.
- The terms of your app's contract or the payments company's arrangements.
- The dollar value of a penalty unit.

For a definite answer on your situation, consider Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy lawyer.

question: My lease is on the standard form and started in 2024. It has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?

**Short answer:** Probably not, if the carpets are back to their move-in condition. The law requires a professional clean only when one is *needed* to restore the premises to their condition at the start of the tenancy. Your evidence is the key question. The documents don't say whether a self-clean can satisfy the clause.

**Which version I used:** The current Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 file is version 009, in force from 30 June 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The page text doesn't show the Authorised Version number, so I'm relying on the version label in the file's metadata. The professional cleaning wording is the same in earlier versions, including the 2022 version, which lists "Authorised Version No. 002" [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf), and the 2025 version [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). So the wording your 2024 lease would have used is consistent with the current text.

**What the law says**

- The standard form allows a clause requiring professional cleaning at the end of a tenancy only if it is needed to restore the premises to their condition before the tenancy started, taking into account fair wear and tear [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- Under regulation 12, the provider must not require you to arrange professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy unless either:
  - (a) professional cleaning was done before the tenancy started and you were told so; or
  - (b) professional cleaning is required to restore the premises to the same condition they were in immediately before the tenancy started, having regard to the condition report and taking into account fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- The clause you describe (you must pay for or arrange professional cleaning) is valid only in that situation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- Note that you described this as a "pet clause," but the text you quote is a professional cleaning clause. I've treated it as the cleaning clause.

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Check the move-in paperwork.** Look for (a) whether professional cleaning was done before you moved in and (b) whether you were told that. Those are the only exceptions under regulation 12(1)(a) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
2. **Find your condition report.** You should have received 2 copies (or one emailed copy) on or before move-in [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The provider must give a signed condition report specifying the state of repair and general condition of the premises [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Regulation 12 requires the cleaning question to be judged against it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Gather evidence of the carpets' condition.** The documents don't list specific evidence types. Useful practical steps include:
   - move-in and move-out photos or video with dates;
   - receipts for your cleaning products or equipment;
   - a written statement of what you did and the carpets' condition.
4. **Respond to the agent in writing.** Say that professional cleaning isn't required because the carpets were restored to move-in condition, and attach your evidence. The documents don't set a specific deadline for this.
5. **If the agent claims cleaning costs from your bond,** the provider can claim the reasonable cost of cleaning only if the premises were not left reasonably clean, having regard to their condition at the start of the agreement [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). If you disagree, you must notify the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority in writing within 14 days after it notifies you of the claim that the claim is subject to a Tribunal application [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. I've called them twice today. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
**Short answer:** You probably don't have to wait indefinitely. Under the current Act, you may be able to arrange the repair yourself, but only if the conditions below are met and you follow the notice steps. The documents don't say whether two phone calls on one day count as "reasonable steps," so act carefully.

**Document and version:** The *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version **No. 115**, in force from 13 October 2026 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The regulations that apply are the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised Version **No. 009**, in force from 30 June 2026 [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Your right to arrange urgent repairs:** You may arrange urgent repairs if you have taken reasonable steps to get the owner or their agent to carry out the repairs immediately, and you are unable to get them to do it [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Notice of the breakdown:** You must give the owner written notice as soon as practicable after becoming aware of the breakdown of a facility or fixture they provide [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Who can do the work:** Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, both urgent and non-urgent [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). So a licensed plumber, not you, should do the work.
- **Notice of the repair and cost:** After the repair, you must give the owner 7 days' written notice of the repairs and their cost [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Reimbursement:** The owner must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days after receiving that written notice. The amount is capped at the reasonable cost or the prescribed amount, whichever is less [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The regulations state the prescribed amount is up to $2,500 [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs list:** Urgent repairs include failure or breakdown of an essential service or appliance for hot water, cooking, heating or laundering supplied by the owner [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The documents don't confirm that a water shut-off from a broken tap is on the urgent list. The regulations refer to the Consumer Affairs Victoria website for the full list, which isn't in these documents [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do

1. **Keep a record of your attempts.** Note the time, date and method of each call. Also send the owner or agent a written message (email, if your agreement allows it) saying the tap has broken, water is off, and you need an immediate repair. The documents say the emergency contact should be notified in writing [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
2. **Check your agreement's emergency contact.** Your agreement should list an emergency contact for urgent repairs [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Use that contact and record the response.
3. **Hire a suitably qualified person** (such as a licensed plumber) only if the owner or agent still can't or won't act. Keep the invoice and receipts.
4. **Give written notice within 7 days** of the repair, stating what was done and what it cost [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The owner must then reimburse you within 7 days of that notice [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. **If the owner refuses to pay or you can't afford the repair,** you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring the owner to carry out the urgent repairs. The grounds are that you cannot meet the cost, the cost is more than the prescribed amount, or the owner refuses to pay for the repairs if you carry them out [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). VCAT must hear the application within 2 business days [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't cover

- Whether two phone calls on the same day satisfy "reasonable steps" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Whether a tap or whole-house water shut-off is an urgent repair under the official list [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- Whether the owner can legally restrict repairs to their own tradespeople. The documents don't address this, and the Act's rule above depends on whether the owner or agent can actually carry out the repair.

This is general information, not legal advice. If the owner keeps refusing, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria or VCAT.

question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. I haven't moved any of my things in or stayed there yet. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
**Short answer:** Under the current law, you can refuse to move in, you can require repairs, and you may be able to recover rent for the period before you move in. The documents I found don't clearly support cancelling the lease or getting a rent reduction, and they don't include the text of the provision that would allow ending the lease.

**Which law applies:** Today (9 November 2026), the current Act is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version **No. 115** (in force from 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The current Regulations are the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised Version **No. 009** (in force from 30 June 2026) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Earlier versions are superseded, so I have relied on these.

---

### What the law says about your situation

- **Premises must meet the standards on move-in day.** The provider must ensure the rented premises comply with the prescribed rental minimum standards on or before the day you enter occupation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Mould and damp.** Each room must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Structure.** The premises must be structurally sound and weatherproof [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Rotting timber may fall under this standard, though the documents don't say so expressly.
- **Repairs duty.** The provider must keep the premises in good repair and reasonably fit and suitable for occupation. This applies even if you were aware of the disrepair before moving in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **You can refuse to move in.** You are not required to enter occupation of premises that don't comply with the clean and vacant requirement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents also say you can't be required to enter occupation of premises that don't comply with the rental minimum standards, but the exact wording is in s 65(2), which covers the "vacant and reasonably clean" duty [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **No rent before you move in.** If the premises don't comply, you are not required to pay rent for the period from the agreed move-in day until you actually move in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

---

### What you can do or ask for

**1. Ask for repairs**
- **Urgent repairs:** Damp or mould caused by the building structure counts as an urgent repair, as does a failure to comply with the rental minimum standards [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You can issue a request for urgent repairs if the premises don't comply on or just after the move-in day [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The provider must carry out urgent repairs after being notified. If you have taken reasonable steps to get them done immediately and the provider hasn't, you may arrange them yourself and be reimbursed directly for the reasonable cost up to **$2,500**. You can apply to VCAT if you can't meet the cost, the cost is over $2,500, or the provider refuses to reimburse you [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Non-urgent repairs:** Notify the provider in writing as soon as practicable. The provider must carry out the work in a reasonable time. You can apply to VCAT if the repairs are not done within **14 days** of notice [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**2. Cancel or end the arrangement**
- The documents refer to a notice to vacate on the basis that premises are "destroyed or unfit for habitation" under **s 91ZD** of the Act [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). However, the text of s 91ZD is not in the documents I retrieved, so I can't confirm its conditions or the notice period.
- The documents also refer to an application to VCAT to reduce the term of the agreement on grounds of severe hardship, under s 91U [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Again, the provision itself is not in the retrieved text.

**3. Ask for lower rent**
- The documents I retrieved do **not** contain a provision allowing a rent reduction for disrepair. The only rent-related protection is that you pay no rent before you actually move in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). For any other rent reduction, the documents don't say.

---

### Practical next steps
- Notify the provider **in writing** about the damp, mould and rotting timber, and keep copies and photos.
- Make your urgent repair request in writing as well.
- Check the Consumer Affairs Victoria guidance and consider speaking to VCAT or a tenancy advocate about cancelling or any rent claim, since those points depend on provisions the documents don't include.

*This is general information based on the documents I found, not legal advice.*

question: Our rental was broken into several times while we were moving out, and there are about three weeks left on our fixed-term lease. The burglars damaged the plumbing and wiring, so we can't even clean properly. What are our options before the lease ends?
answer:
**Applicable version:** The Residential Tenancies Act 1997 in force today is **Authorised Version No. 115**, which took effect on 13 October 2026 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The current Regulations are the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, version 009, in force from 30 June 2026 [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The excerpts I retrieved from the current versions don't cover every provision, so where I rely on an earlier version I say so.

## What the law says

- **Notify the landlord in writing.** A renter must give written notice to the rental provider "as soon as practicable" after becoming aware of damage to the premises or a breakdown of facilities [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations say the same [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs.** A renter may arrange urgent repairs if they have taken reasonable steps to get the provider to do them immediately and the provider is unable to do so. The renter must give the provider 7 days' written notice of the repairs and the cost. The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days of that notice [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations give a burst water service as an example of an urgent repair [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Non-urgent repairs.** If repairs aren't urgent, the renter must give written notice. If the provider hasn't carried out the repairs within 14 days, the renter can apply to the Tribunal, which must hear the application within 7 days [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Rent into the Rent Special Account.** After giving a repair notice, the renter may apply to the Tribunal to pay rent into the Rent Special Account if the provider has failed to carry out the repairs [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Ending the lease early.** A notice to vacate given under s 91Z has no effect in a fixed-term agreement if its termination date is earlier than the end of the term [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A renter may give notice to vacate if the premises are unfit for human habitation or have been destroyed to an extent that makes them unsafe. The notice may take effect on the date it is given or a later date [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Cleaning.** The provider can't require professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy unless it was done before the tenancy started, or it is needed to restore the premises to their original condition, allowing for fair wear and tear [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Damage by others.** The renter's duty not to damage premises applies to the renter and their visitors [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The current excerpts don't address damage caused by burglars. When the Tribunal decides a repair claim, it must consider whether the repairs were needed because of an act or omission of the renter [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Your options before the lease ends

1. **Give written notice now.** Describe the break-ins and the damage to the plumbing and wiring, and send it as soon as practicable [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Keep a copy and any proof of delivery.
2. **Arrange urgent repairs if the landlord doesn't act.** If the damage is urgent, such as a water leak or electrical hazard, and the landlord doesn't respond immediately, you may arrange repairs yourself. Give 7 days' written notice of the repairs and the cost [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Act says the landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations note that the reimbursement cap was $2,500 in an earlier version [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf), but the current text I retrieved doesn't state a figure. Please check the current amount.
3. **Apply to the Tribunal for urgent repairs.** If you can't pay for the repairs, the landlord refuses to pay, or the cost is above the prescribed amount, you can apply to the Tribunal. It must hear the application within 2 business days [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Change the locks.** You need the landlord's consent. If consent is withheld and you believe that is unreasonable, you can apply to the Tribunal for a determination that consent isn't required [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations say the landlord must not unreasonably refuse consent to change a lock in a master key system [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
5. **Leave early, if the premises are unsafe.** A standard 28-day notice won't help, because a notice ending before the fixed term ends has no effect [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If the damage leaves the premises unfit for habitation or unsafe, a notice under s 91ZD may be available [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Whether the damage meets that test is a factual question the documents don't answer.
6. **Cleaning.** Tell the landlord in writing that you can't clean the premises because of the damage. The provider can't require professional cleaning unless it is needed to restore the original condition, allowing for fair wear and tear [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The renter's general duty to leave the premises reasonably clean appears in an earlier version of the Act [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The current excerpts I retrieved don't show that provision, so please check it.

## What the documents don't cover

- Whether your damage is "unsafe" for the purposes of s 91ZD.
- Your lease's own terms, including any early-termination clause.
- Insurance claims and police reporting.
- The current reimbursement cap for urgent repairs.

Because these depend on your facts, consider a free check with Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenants' legal service before you give any notice to leave.

(3) The hardest point is met by the statement that a renter may give notice to vacate if the premises are 'unfit for human habitation or... unsafe', taking effect 'on the date it is given'. question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. The app is run by a payments company my agent uses, and it's that company that charges the card fee. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
**Short answer:** Under the current Act, the card fee is very likely not allowed, but the documents don't settle every point. Whether the fee goes to the app company or the agent doesn't change the answer, because the Act's main fee prohibition applies to "a person."

**Version relied on:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Version 115, in force from 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Version 009, in force from 30 June 2026, also applies [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### What the law says

- **Fee-free method must be available:** The agent must ensure that a rent payment method incurring no additional costs (other than the renter's own bank or account fees) is reasonably available to the renter [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A bank transfer with no fee may meet this, but the documents don't define "reasonably available," so being slower may or may not matter [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Cost disclosure:** The provider or agent must tell the renter about any costs, including third-party transaction fees and electronic payment facility fees, before the renter consents to a payment method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Charges for electronic payment:** A person must not demand or receive a charge, or an indemnity for a charge, for the establishment or use of direct debit or "any other electronic payment facility for payment of rent." The penalty is 60 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Fee for payment of rent:** A person other than an ADI must not demand or receive a fee for any prescribed matter in relation to the payment of rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't list the prescribed matters, so I can't confirm whether card fees fall within this.
- **Regulations:** The rental provider must permit at least one fee-free payment method (other than the renter's own bank fees) and must allow Centrepay or another form of electronic funds transfer [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### Does it matter who receives the fee?

Not under the current text I could see. The charge prohibition applies to "a person" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), so it covers the app company as well as the agent. The earlier version of section 51A exempted providers and agents from the business-person fee rule [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), but that version is no longer in force.

### What you can do or ask

- Ask the agent in writing which payment methods are available, and whether the card fee applies, before you choose a method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Ask the agent to confirm that a fee-free method (such as bank transfer) is available to you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- If the agent or app wants to pass the card fee to you, point out the charge prohibition in section 51(3)(b) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What the documents don't cover

- What "prescribed matters" are under section 51A, so I can't confirm whether card fees are caught by that section [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- How "reasonably available" is interpreted, including whether a slower method counts [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- How the disclosure duty in section 42(7) fits with the charge prohibition in section 51(3)(b). Section 42(7) refers to third-party fees a renter "may incur," which could be read as allowing some fees, but the documents don't resolve this [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The complaint or enforcement process. Please check with Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy advisor before relying on this.

This conclusion is clear, though the answer hedges on whether card fees are a prescribed matter under s 51A, relies on s 51(3)(b) instead, and omits the exception for surcharges permitted under another law. question: My lease is on the standard form and started in 2024. It has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. I cleaned them myself and they're back to how they were when I moved in, but the agent wants a receipt from a professional cleaner. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?
answer:
**Short answer:** Probably not, if your DIY clean actually restored the carpets to their move-in condition. The law requires professional cleaning only where it is *required* to restore the premises, and the documents don't say who decides that or what evidence is needed.

**What the law says**

- A standard-form lease may include a term requiring professional cleaning only if professional cleaning becomes required to restore the premises to their pre-tenancy condition, taking into account fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The prescribed standard term says the provider must not require the renter to arrange professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy unless either (a) professional cleaning was carried out before the tenancy started and the renter was told so, or (b) professional cleaning is required to restore the premises to the same condition they were in immediately before the tenancy, having regard to the condition report and taking into account fair wear and tear [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- The renter must have the premises professionally cleaned, or pay for it, only "if professional cleaning becomes required" to restore the premises to that condition, again having regard to the condition report and fair wear and tear [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- A term requiring professional cleaning that isn't in the standard form is a prohibited term [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Check the condition report.** The standard form ties the cleaning obligation to the condition report [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Compare the carpets with what that report recorded at the start. If it records them as clean, that supports your position.
2. **Ask the agent in writing what makes professional cleaning "required"**, and whether they are relying on paragraph (a) or (b) above. Ask them to identify the specific carpet problem that DIY cleaning did not fix.
3. **Keep evidence of the carpets' condition.** The documents don't list what evidence is acceptable. Dated photos, your cleaning receipts (for supplies or equipment), and any move-out inspection notes would help show the condition, but I can't confirm from these sources that they will be accepted.
4. **Seek the Tribunal's view if it stays disputed.** A renter may apply to the Tribunal to declare invalid or vary a term that is harsh or unconscionable [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The documents don't say how the Tribunal would treat this particular dispute.

**Version and coverage notes**

- **Regulations:** The cleaning wording above comes from the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised Version No. 009 (metadata version "009", in force from 30 June 2026, with no end date listed) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). That is the version in force today. The same wording appeared in Authorised Version No. 002, which covered your 2024 start date [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Act:** The section 27C text I cite comes from the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* Authorised Version No. 110, which ran only until 24 November 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The latest Act version in my results (No. 111) ended on 29 June 2026, so I could not confirm the Act version in force today.
- **Pet clause:** The documents don't address pet clauses. The cleaning obligation is the relevant rule here, so check that your clause matches the standard-form wording.
- **Not covered:** The documents don't say whether the agent can require a receipt specifically, or what evidence a Tribunal would accept on carpet condition.
