question: When I moved out I agreed the agent could take an amount for cleaning out of my bond, but I never signed a bond claim form for it. Then my full bond came back to me, and a month later the agent sent a separate invoice for the cleaning. Do I have to pay it? Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents don't say whether you must pay a separate cleaning invoice sent after your bond was refunded. They also don't say whether agreeing verbally to a bond deduction is the same as agreeing to pay an invoice.

**Which law applies:** The current version is Authorised Version No. 115 of the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (in force from 13 October 2026, the latest version retrieved) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Its bond provisions are in Part 10, and I've relied on that version.

## What the law says about cleaning and bonds

- A landlord (called a "residential rental provider") can claim from the bond "the reasonable cost of cleaning any part of the premises, if the premises were not left reasonably clean by the renter, having regard to the condition of the premises at the commencement of the residential rental agreement" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Bond claims are made to the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority, and "a claim must be in a form approved by the Authority" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Before a landlord claims bond money for the renter to be repaid to the landlord, the landlord "must give each renter bond claim evidence that supports the claim" at least 3 days before the claim is made. That evidence "must not conflict with a statement in a condition report" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- A landlord "must not request or obtain a renter's signature to a claim form" unless the form specifies the amount of bond to be refunded and any apportionment. The penalty is 60 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Your situation

- **Verbal or informal agreement to a deduction:** The documents set out a formal claim process, with an approved form and evidence. They don't say whether an informal agreement you gave, without signing a claim form, binds you to a deduction or to a later invoice. I can't determine that from these documents.
- **Invoice after the full bond was refunded:** The documents don't address whether a landlord can invoice a renter separately for cleaning after the bond has been returned in full. If the full bond came back, that suggests no cleaning claim was paid out of it, but the documents don't say what happened in your case.

## What you can ask or do

1. **Ask for the bond claim evidence.** Under the rules above, a landlord claiming cleaning costs from the bond must provide supporting evidence [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Ask the agent for that evidence and for the condition report.
2. **Check the cleaning cost against the law.** The cost must be reasonable, and cleaning is claimable only if the premises were not left reasonably clean, judged against their condition at the start of the tenancy [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Consider the Tribunal.** A renter or other person with an interest in a bond claim may apply to the Tribunal for a bond repayment order. That application "must be made within 14 days after the residential rental agreement has terminated" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Given the timing you describe, check whether that window has already passed.
4. **Seek advice on the invoice.** The contents page of the Act lists sections on applications for loss or damage (s 213B) and compensation (s 209) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). However, the retrieved material does not include the text of those sections, so I can't say how they apply to an invoice sent after bond refund. You may want advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy service.

## What the documents don't cover

- Whether an informal or verbal agreement to a bond deduction is binding.
- Whether a landlord can issue a separate invoice for cleaning after returning the full bond.
- The full text of the Tribunal and compensation provisions (ss 209, 213B), which appear only in the table of contents.

question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. I've called them twice today. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
**Short answer:** You don't have to wait indefinitely. Under the current Act, you may be able to arrange the urgent repair yourself, but only through a suitably qualified person, and you must follow the notice steps below. The documents don't say whether an owner's "only our tradespeople" rule changes this.

**What the law says**

- A renter may arrange urgent repairs if they have taken reasonable steps to get the landlord or agent to immediately carry out the repairs, and they are unable to get the landlord or agent to do them [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Urgent repairs include failure or breakdown of an essential service or appliance for hot water, cooking, heating or laundering supplied by the rental provider [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The regulations' sample agreement also gives "a burst water service" as an example of an urgent repair [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The full statutory definition is not in the documents I retrieved, so I can't confirm whether a whole-house water shut-off is covered.
- "Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs—both urgent and non-urgent" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). So doing it yourself, without a qualified person, is not what the law allows.
- The renter must give written notice of the damage or breakdown as soon as practicable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Put it in writing now.** Notice must be given as soon as practicable, and the sample agreement says the renter should notify the provider in writing for an urgent repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Send the email or letter to the owner and agent, not just phone calls, and keep records of your two calls.
2. **Arrange a suitably qualified person** (e.g., a licensed plumber) if the owner and agent still cannot get the repair done. The documents don't define "reasonable steps," so whether two calls today is enough is not something I can confirm.
3. **Give the provider 7 days' written notice** of the repairs and the cost after the work is done. The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days of receiving that notice, up to the lesser of the reasonable cost or the prescribed amount [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Know the cap:** the regulations say the provider may reimburse "up to $2500" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Costs above that amount are a problem.
5. **If the owner refuses to pay or you can't afford the repair,** you may apply to VCAT for an order requiring the provider to carry out the urgent repairs. VCAT must hear the application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The regulations also list these grounds: the renter cannot meet the cost, the cost is more than $2500, or the provider refuses to pay [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
6. **Get help if needed:** Consumer Affairs Victoria is listed as 1300 558 181 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover**

- Whether an owner can lawfully require you to use only their own tradespeople, and whether that overrides your right to arrange urgent repairs.
- What counts as "reasonable steps" in practice.
- Whether a whole-house water shut-off falls within the statutory definition of urgent repairs.

**Sources and versions**

- Residential Tenancies Act 1997, version 115, in force from 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This is the current version in the documents.
- Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, version 009, in force from 30 June 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

This is general information based on the retrieved documents, not legal advice. If the owner keeps refusing, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria or VCAT promptly.

The first two points are adequately covered.

question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. I haven't moved any of my things in or stayed there yet. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents support a repair claim, and they point to a possible exit route. They do not contain a rent-reduction remedy.

## What the law says

- **Damp and mould are defined as urgent repairs.** The Act's definition includes "any fault or damage that makes rented premises ... unsafe or insecure, including ... the presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). It also includes "a failure to comply with any rental minimum standards" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **The minimum standards are specific.** The premises must be "structurally sound and weatherproof" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). "Each room in the rented premises must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- **The landlord must meet these standards before you move in.** The rental provider "must ensure that the premises comply with the rental minimum standards, and is vacant and reasonably clean when the renter moves in" and must "maintain the premises in good repair and in a fit condition for occupation" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

## What you can ask for

**Repairs:**
- **Notify in writing.** Non-urgent damage must be notified "in writing, as soon as practicable" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). For urgent repairs, the provider "must carry out urgent repairs after being notified" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Put your notice in writing.
- **Urgent repairs:** If you take reasonable steps to get the provider to act immediately and they don't, you may arrange the repairs. The provider may reimburse "the reasonable cost of repairs up to $2500" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). You can apply to VCAT if you cannot meet the cost, the cost is over $2500, or the provider refuses to pay [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- **Non-urgent repairs:** The provider "must carry out non-urgent repairs in a reasonable time." You may apply to VCAT if they have not done the repairs "within 14 days of receiving notice" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- **Who does the work:** "Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

**Cancelling:**
- The regulations refer to a renter giving notice to vacate "under section 91ZD of the Act on the basis the premises are destroyed or unfit for habitation," and state that the provider is then not entitled to rent-foregone compensation [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The retrieved documents do not contain the text of section 91ZD, so I cannot confirm the test for "unfit for habitation" or the notice steps. Get advice before relying on this.

**Lower rent:**
- The documents do not cover a rent reduction for disrepair. The only reduction mechanism I found is a VCAT order reducing the term of the agreement for severe hardship under section 91U [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). That is not a rent cut, so I cannot say whether you can get lower rent.

## Your situation

You have not moved in, which matters for the move-in obligation above. The documents do not say how that affects your options beyond the points already covered.

## Sources

- [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) Residential Tenancies Act 1997, version 115 (in force from 13 October 2026).
- [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, version 009 (in force from 30 June 2026).

For the current rules and urgent repair list, see consumer.vic.gov.au/urgentrepairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). This is general information, not legal advice. Consider speaking to Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy lawyer before taking action.

question: Our rental was broken into several times while we were moving out, and there are about three weeks left on our fixed-term lease. The burglars damaged the plumbing and wiring, so we can't even clean properly. What are our options before the lease ends?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents I retrieved give you several repair and notice options, but they don't cover how to end a fixed-term lease early under the current law, so I can't confirm that part.

**Sources used:** The current Act is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 115, in force from 13 October 2026 [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The current regulations are the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised Version No. 009, in force from 30 June 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Reporting damage:** A renter must give written notice to the landlord as soon as practicable after becoming aware of damage to the rented premises [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The regulations say the same thing [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs:** Urgent repairs include failure or breakdown of an essential service or appliance for hot water, cooking, heating or laundering [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The full list is in the Act's definition, which the documents don't reproduce, so you'd need to check whether your plumbing or wiring damage qualifies [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Who can do repairs:** Only a suitably qualified person may do urgent or non-urgent repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Locks:** The landlord must ensure the premises have locks to secure all windows capable of having one, and deadlocks for external doors where a functioning deadlock is possible [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). A renter must get consent to change a lock in a master key system, and the landlord must not unreasonably refuse it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Keeping the premises clean and undamaged:** A renter must avoid damaging the premises and must keep them reasonably clean. The landlord must keep the premises in good repair and in a fit condition for occupation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

1. **Notify the landlord in writing now.** Describe the break-in damage to the plumbing and wiring, and send the notice as soon as practicable [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask for urgent repairs.** The landlord must carry out urgent repairs after being notified [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). If you've taken reasonable steps to get them done immediately and the landlord hasn't done them, you may arrange the repairs yourself [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **If you arrange repairs yourself:**
   - You must give the landlord 7 days' written notice of the repairs and their cost [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
   - The landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days of that notice [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
   - The regulations say you may be reimbursed directly for up to $2,500 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
4. **Apply to VCAT if needed.** You may apply for an order requiring urgent repairs if you cannot meet the cost, the cost is more than $2,500, or the landlord refuses to pay for repairs you arrange [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Tribunal must hear an urgent repairs application within 2 business days [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. **Ask about locks.** If the landlord won't consent to changing locks after the break-ins, you can apply to VCAT for a determination that consent isn't required [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). - **Whether the damage counts as an urgent repair:** The full definition isn't in the retrieved text.

Given the damage to wiring, prioritise the safety point: the landlord should arrange a suitably qualified person to make the electrical repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Before ending the lease, I'd recommend confirming the early-termination rules with Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy advisory service.

question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. The app is run by a payments company my agent uses, and it's that company that charges the card fee. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
## What the law says

The current document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115, in force from 13 October 2026**, authored by **Barbara Hargreaves**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

- The rental provider or agent must ensure that the renter has a rent-payment method with **no additional cost**, apart from bank or account fees payable on the renter’s own bank account. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- The rental provider or agent must tell the renter about costs—including **third-party transaction fees** and electronic-payment-facility fees—before the renter agrees to use a particular payment method. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- The Act also says that **a person other than an ADI** must not demand or receive a fee for any **prescribed matter** relating to the payment of rent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The retrieved documents do not state whether this particular card fee is a “prescribed matter” or whether the payments company is an ADI, so they do not establish conclusively whether that prohibition applies.
- The prescribed rental-agreement form confirms that at least one payment method must be fee-free, apart from the renter’s own bank fees, and that the renter must be allowed to use Centrepay or another electronic-funds-transfer method. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

**Does it matter who receives the fee?** The retrieved provision applies to “a person,” not only to the rental provider or agent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) However, the documents do not say whether a fee charged directly by a payments company is lawful in these circumstances. They do show that a third-party fee must be disclosed and that a genuinely fee-free method must reasonably be available. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What the renter can do or ask

Ask the agent, in writing:

1. Which payment method is the required **fee-free** option, and how can you use it? [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
2. What the card fee is, who receives it, and whether the payments company is an **ADI**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
3. For the legal basis for charging the fee and whether the fee is a “prescribed matter” under section 51A. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
4. For confirmation that the no-fee bank-transfer option is reasonably available—not merely technically available but unreasonably slow or impractical. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The documents do not provide a rule saying that a slower fee-free bank transfer automatically fails the “reasonably available” requirement, so they do not allow a definite conclusion on that point. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: No. The answer hedges too much on the second point: it says 'the documents do not establish conclusively whether that prohibition applies' and 'do not say whether a fee charged directly by a payments company is lawful'. It therefore never clearly states that rent-payment fees are banned for anyone other than an ADI (s 51A with reg 21C), or that it does not matter whether the app company or the agent collects the fee. A reader could not tell which way that point falls.

question: My lease is on the standard form and started in 2024. It has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. I cleaned them myself and they're back to how they were when I moved in, but the agent wants a receipt from a professional cleaner. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?
answer:
## What the retrieved law says

The retrieved document is **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version v002**—in force from **1 June 2022 to 30 November 2024**—and lists **Lavina Mandy** as Author. It does **not** establish the law in force today. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

Under that version, a rental provider could not require professional cleaning merely because the lease contained a pet or cleaning clause. Professional cleaning could be required only if:

- professional cleaning was done immediately before the tenancy and you were told this; or
- professional cleaning was needed to restore the premises to their pre-tenancy condition, considering the condition report and fair wear and tear. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

If professional cleaning genuinely became necessary for that restoration, the renter had to arrange it or pay its cost. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf) The retrieved provisions do **not** say that a renter must always provide a professional cleaner’s receipt. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

Therefore, if the carpets are truly restored to their starting condition, allowing for fair wear and tear, the retrieved document does not support requiring you to pay for professional cleaning solely to obtain a receipt. However, because the retrieved document expired on 30 November 2024, it cannot confirm your legal position today.

## What you can do or ask

- Send the agent the original condition report and explain that the carpets are in the same condition as at the start, taking fair wear and tear into account. The condition report is specifically relevant to whether professional cleaning is required. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
- Ask the agent to identify the particular carpet condition they say has not been restored and to explain why professional cleaning—not ordinary cleaning—is required under the applicable current law.
- Keep dated photographs or video of every carpet, together with the condition report and your written communications. **The retrieved documents do not prescribe these forms of evidence**, so they cannot confirm that photographs or video will be sufficient.
- Do not assume that the lease clause alone settles the issue: the standard-form professional-cleaning term itself limits when professional cleaning can be required. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The retrieved documents do not contain the **current Authorised Version** applicable today, so I cannot definitively say whether the same rule remains in force or whether any current procedure applies.

It mentions pre-tenancy condition only as part of the professional-cleaning test, not as a standalone duty to leave the premises reasonably clean. The reg 12 point and the condition-report evidence point are covered.

question: When I moved out I agreed the agent could take an amount for cleaning out of my bond, but I never signed a bond claim form for it. Then my full bond came back to me, and a month later the agent sent a separate invoice for the cleaning. Do I have to pay it? Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?
answer:
## What the law says

The current document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997**, **Authorised Version No. 115**, incorporating amendments as at **13 October 2026**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Cleaning can be a legitimate bond claim if the premises were not left reasonably clean, having regard to their condition when the tenancy began; the provider may claim the **reasonable cost** of that cleaning. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

However, the Act requires a bond claim to be made in an Authority-approved form. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) If the provider claims bond repayment without the renter’s consent, the Authority must notify the renter, who has **14 days** to notify the Authority that the claim is subject to a Tribunal application. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) A provider’s Tribunal application for an order requiring bond repayment must be made within **14 days after the residential rental agreement ended**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved provisions do **not** say that:

- an informal agreement that cleaning may be deducted from the bond is automatically an agreement to pay a separate invoice;
- repayment of the full bond permanently prevents the provider from pursuing a separate cleaning claim; or
- the provider is automatically entitled to payment merely because the renter once agreed to a bond deduction.

Therefore, from these documents alone, **it cannot be concluded that you must pay the invoice**. The documents also do not determine whether your particular agreement created a separate debt.

## What you can do or ask

Ask the agent to identify the legal basis for the invoice and provide evidence of the claimed cleaning cost. Under the Act, “bond claim evidence” includes an **invoice, receipt, quote, photograph or other prescribed evidence**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Ask the agent to explain whether they rely on:

1. a claim against the bond; or  
2. a separate agreement or claim for payment.

You can point out that the full bond was repaid and that you did not sign a bond claim form, but the retrieved provisions do not state the legal effect of those facts on a later invoice. If the dispute concerns the bond itself, the Act allows a renter or provider to apply to the Tribunal for a bond-repayment order, but the provider’s application must be made within **14 days after termination**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: No. The first point is missing because it is hedged too far. The answer never states that agreeing to a deduction is agreement to a claim on the bond rather than to a separate invoice. It only says the provisions do not say the two are 'automatically' the same, and then adds that 'the documents also do not determine whether your particular agreement created a separate debt', so a reader cannot tell which way the point falls. The reasonably-clean test judged against the start condition is covered.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer asserts neither forbidden claim: it states 'it cannot be concluded that you must pay the invoice' and that the provisions do not say 'repayment of the full bond permanently prevents the provider from pursuing a separate cleaning claim,' raising both points only to say the retrieved documents do not establish them.

question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. I've called them twice today. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
## What the law says

The current retrieved document is **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009**, in force from **30 June 2026**, authored by **Lavina Mandy**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

It says the rental provider must carry out urgent repairs after being notified. A renter may arrange the repair themselves if they have taken **reasonable steps** to arrange for the rental provider or agent to do it immediately, but have been unable to get them to do so. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) The regulations do not say that the owner’s preference for particular tradespeople requires you to wait when those tradespeople cannot attend. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

Only a **suitably qualified person** may perform the repair. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) If you arrange it, the rental provider may be required to reimburse the **reasonable cost up to $2,500**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved documents do **not expressly classify a broken tap that requires shutting off the whole house’s water as an “urgent repair.”** They state that urgent repairs include failure or breakdown of an essential service or appliance supplied by the rental provider for hot water, cooking, heating or laundering. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) Therefore, the documents do not conclusively answer whether this particular tap qualifies.

## What you can do or ask

You have called twice today, which may support that you took reasonable steps, but the documents do not specify how many calls are required. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) You can:

- tell the emergency contact in writing that the water is shut off to the whole house, that the owner’s tradespeople are unavailable, and that you will arrange a suitably qualified plumber unless they arrange the repair immediately; [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- obtain a suitably qualified plumber and keep the invoice, photographs and records of your calls and messages; [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- ask the rental provider to reimburse the reasonable cost, up to **$2,500**; [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- if you cannot pay, the cost exceeds **$2,500**, or the provider refuses to pay, apply to VCAT for an order requiring the urgent repair. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 111** is dated **25 November 2025–29 June 2026**, so it is not the version in force today and cannot establish the current Act’s exact requirements. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: No. The answer is missing the point that no water supply or a burst water service is an urgent repair; it instead says the documents 'do not conclusively answer whether this particular tap qualifies.' It also omits the s 72 duty to reimburse within 7 days of written notice, saying only that the provider 'may be required to reimburse'. It never states that a nominated-tradesperson term is prohibited (reg 11(e)); it says only that the regulations 'do not say' the owner's preference requires waiting.

The answer never says the renter must wait or cannot recover costs; it states "The regulations do not say that the owner's preference for particular tradespeople requires you to wait when those tradespeople cannot attend" and "the rental provider may be required to reimburse the reasonable cost up to $2,500."

question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. I haven't moved any of my things in or stayed there yet. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
## What the law says

The current documents are:

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115**, in force from **13 October 2026**, authored by **Barbara Hargreaves**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009**, in force from **30 June 2026**, authored by **Lavina Mandy**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The premises must be **structurally sound and weatherproof**, and each room must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) The rental provider must also provide premises that meet the minimum standards, are reasonably clean, in good repair and fit for occupation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

Structural mould or damp is expressly an **urgent repair**, as is any fault or damage making the premises unsafe or insecure; the Act specifically includes mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

### 1. Cancel the agreement

Because you have not moved in or stayed there, you may be able to give a **written notice of termination before entering into possession**. Section 91L allows this where the premises:

- are not in good repair;
- are unfit for human habitation;
- do not meet a rental minimum standard; or
- are otherwise unavailable for occupation. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Damp, mould and rotting timber may engage those grounds, but whether the condition is sufficiently serious—particularly whether the premises are “unfit for human habitation”—would depend on the evidence. The documents do not define that threshold. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The prescribed agreement says the rental provider cannot claim rent foregone for early termination where the renter terminates under section 91ZD because the premises are unfit for habitation or destroyed/unsafe. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) However, that clause refers to section 91ZD, while your situation before possession is addressed by section 91L; the documents do not expressly state whether the same protection applies to a section 91L termination. **Do not simply stop paying without giving a formal written notice or obtaining agreement.**

### 2. Ask for repairs

You can notify the rental provider or agent **in writing**, describing each defect and attaching dated photographs or reports. The provider must carry out urgent repairs after being notified. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

If the provider does not act, the documents say that a renter may arrange urgent repairs after taking reasonable steps to have the provider do them immediately, and may seek reimbursement of reasonable costs up to **$2,500**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) The documents do not explain whether arranging repairs yourself before entering possession would be appropriate, so do not authorise substantial structural work without written agreement or advice.

For non-urgent repairs, the provider must act within a reasonable time; a renter may apply to VCAT if repairs have not been completed within **14 days** after written notice. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) Because structural mould/damp is expressly classified as urgent, the urgent-repair pathway is the more relevant one here. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

### 3. Ask for lower rent

You may ask the rental provider to agree in writing to a lower rent while repairs are completed. The documents do not provide an automatic right to unilaterally reduce the rent simply because the premises are defective.

You may instead seek compensation for loss or damage caused by the provider’s failure to comply with the agreement or the Act. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) VCAT may order compensation, and that compensation may take the form of a **refund or reduction of rent**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

### Practical next step

Send a written notice immediately stating that you have not entered into possession, identifying the mould, damp and rotting timber, attaching evidence, and either:

1. **terminating under section 91L**, if you do not want the property; or  
2. requiring urgent repairs and asking for a written timetable and an agreed rent reduction while the premises are unavailable.

Do not sign a condition report describing the defects as acceptable, and do not move belongings in before deciding which option you will pursue.

It says only generally that the provider 'must also provide premises that meet the minimum standards', with no timing and no s 65A. The s 91L termination and urgent-repair points are covered.

question: Our rental was broken into several times while we were moving out, and there are about three weeks left on our fixed-term lease. The burglars damaged the plumbing and wiring, so we can't even clean properly. What are our options before the lease ends?
answer:
## What the law says

The current **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115 (incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026)** applies. The supporting **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, version 009, dated 30 June 2026** also applies. [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

Damage that makes rented premises **“unsafe or insecure”** is an urgent repair. The Act’s urgent-repair definition includes a dangerous electrical fault, failure of electricity or water, and any fault or damage making the premises unsafe or insecure. [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The rental provider must maintain the premises in good repair and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation, and repairs must be done by a suitably qualified person. [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

If the premises are **unfit for human habitation**, or have been destroyed totally or enough to be unsafe, you may give the rental provider a written notice of intention to vacate. The termination date can be **the date the notice is given or a later date**. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) The notice must be in writing and signed. [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

For the prescribed fixed-term agreement, the rental provider is not entitled to rent foregone when the agreement ends because the renter gives notice under section 91ZD on the basis that the premises are destroyed or unfit for habitation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

1. **Immediately notify the rental provider or agent in writing** of the burglary damage, especially the plumbing and wiring damage, and state that the premises may be unsafe or unfit for habitation. Renters must report damage and breakdowns as soon as practicable. [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

2. **Request urgent repairs immediately.** If you have taken reasonable steps to arrange them but the rental provider or agent does not do them, you may arrange urgent repairs yourself. The rental provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days after receiving written notice of the repairs and their cost, subject to the prescribed limit. [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The retrieved documents do not state the current prescribed dollar limit in the Act text, although the agreement form refers to reimbursement up to **$2,500**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

3. If you cannot pay, the repairs cost more than the prescribed amount, or the rental provider refuses to pay, **apply to VCAT for an urgent-repairs order**; the Tribunal must hear that application within **2 business days**. [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

4. If the premises are genuinely unfit or unsafe, **give a section 91ZD notice of intention to vacate** and specify an immediate termination date or a later date. On the documents available, this is the clearest way to end the fixed term without liability for rent foregone under the agreement form. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

5. Alternatively, you and the rental provider can agree in writing to end the fixed term early. The documents also allow either party to apply to VCAT to reduce or terminate a fixed-term agreement for **severe hardship**, but compensation may be ordered. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

6. **Do not attempt electrical or plumbing repairs yourselves.** The documents say only a suitably qualified person may perform repairs. Preserve photographs, police reports, invoices and messages, and ask the agent to record the burglary damage in the final condition report. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[10]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

7. Regarding cleaning, you must ordinarily leave the premises reasonably clean, but professional cleaning can only be required in the circumstances stated in the prescribed agreement—generally, where professional cleaning was done immediately before the tenancy or is needed to restore the premises to their prior condition, allowing for fair wear and tear. The retrieved documents do not state a specific exemption for cleaning that is impossible because of burglary damage. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) You should therefore ask the rental provider in writing to confirm that cleaning affected by the unrepaired plumbing and wiring damage will not be treated as renter-caused damage, or seek a VCAT order if they refuse. [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The documents do **not** state that rent automatically stops merely because the premises are damaged or cannot be cleaned, so do not stop paying rent without an agreement or Tribunal order. [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The rental provider must reimburse the reasonable cost'), and the hardest one, the s 91ZD notice to vacate with an immediate date ending the fixed term ('give a section 91ZD notice of intention to vacate and specify an immediate termination date... the clearest way to end the fixed term').

question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. The app is run by a payments company my agent uses, and it's that company that charges the card fee. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
## What the law says

The current document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, in force from 13 October 2026**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

- The rental provider or agent must ensure that a rent-payment method with **no additional costs**—apart from bank or account fees payable on the renter’s own bank account—is **reasonably available**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) Therefore, if the manual bank-transfer option is genuinely available and has no fee, the documents indicate that the app may charge a card fee **only if that fee-free option is reasonably available**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- Before you consent to use a particular payment method, the rental provider or agent must tell you about costs you may incur, expressly including **“third party transaction fees”** and other electronic-payment-facility fees. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- The Act also says that a person must not demand or receive a charge or indemnity for a charge relating to the **establishment or use of any electronic payment facility for rent**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) On the wording supplied, this may apply to a card fee for using the app, but the retrieved documents do not explain how that provision interacts with the newer section 51A.
- Section 51A says that a person **other than an ADI** must not demand or receive a fee for any **prescribed matter** relating to payment of rent. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) The retrieved documents do not state what the relevant prescribed matter is or whether the payments company is an ADI.

**Does it matter who receives the fee?** The documents do not say that the fee becomes lawful merely because it is collected by the payments company rather than the agent. They expressly contemplate **third-party transaction fees**, while separately requiring a fee-free method to be reasonably available. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) However, the documents do not provide enough information to give a definite answer about the payments company’s liability under section 51A, particularly whether it is an ADI. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

Ask the agent, in writing:

1. To confirm the fee-free bank-transfer method and why it is reasonably available despite being slower. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
2. To disclose the card fee and any other payment costs before you use or consent to that method. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
3. Who receives the card fee, whether the payments company is an **ADI**, and the legal basis for charging it under sections 51(3) and 51A. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)
4. To confirm that you may pay rent by the fee-free method without disadvantage or additional charge. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved documents do **not** state whether “slower” by itself makes the fee-free bank-transfer option unreasonable, so that cannot be determined from these documents.

must-mention.reason: No. Point 2 is missing: the output never states that rent-payment fees are banned for anyone other than a bank under s 51A and reg 21C, so it does not matter who collects the fee. It instead says the documents 'do not provide enough information to give a definite answer' and suggests the app 'may charge a card fee only if that fee-free option is reasonably available'. Points 1 and 3 are covered: the output says a fee-free method must be reasonably available and suggests written requests to the agent.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer treats the fee-free option as a necessary condition, not a sufficient one: it says the app 'may charge a card fee **only if that fee-free option is reasonably available**'. It then raises section 51(3) ('a person must not demand or receive a charge... relating to the establishment or use of any electronic payment facility for rent') and section 51A as possibly barring the fee, so it never concludes the fee is allowed simply because a fee-free option exists. It also never says the landlord or agent is exempt from the fee ban; the only exemption it mentions is for 'a person other than an ADI', which does not exempt agents.

version-cited.reason: No. The answer names the Act as "Authorised Version No. 115", but it never names the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 Version No. 009 (reg 21C). It also relies on the link "21-3sra005", which is Regulations version 005 and was not in force on that date. Its Act link "97-109aa111" points to version 111, not 115.

question: My lease is on the standard form and started in 2024. It has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. I cleaned them myself and they're back to how they were when I moved in, but the agent wants a receipt from a professional cleaner. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?
answer:
## What the law says

The current retrieved document is **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009**, authorised by **Lavina Mandy**, in force from **30 June 2026**. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The standard-form cleaning term does **not** automatically require a professional cleaner merely because the lease contains a pet clause. Professional cleaning may be required only if:

- professional cleaning was done immediately before the tenancy began and you were told this; or
- professional cleaning is necessary to restore the premises to their starting condition, having regard to the condition report and **fair wear and tear**. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

Therefore, if you cleaned the carpets yourself and they are restored to the condition they were in when you moved in, the retrieved documents do **not** establish that you must pay for professional cleaning or provide a professional cleaner’s receipt. The documents also do not state that a receipt may be demanded as proof. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

Send the agent:

- the signed starting condition report;
- dated, labelled photographs or video of the carpets from before and after, including close-up views and wider room views; and
- any written messages, cleaning records, or other evidence showing what you did.

The prescribed condition-report form says that photos should be taken at the beginning and end of the tenancy, dated, labelled, and identified by room or location; it also says close-up and distance photos may help in a dispute. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

Ask the agent to identify **具体** differences between the carpets’ current condition and the starting condition, allowing for fair wear and tear, rather than simply requesting a receipt. The form says the final inspection must allow for fair wear and tear and must be completed within 10 days after the agreement ends, with an opportunity for the renter to attend if possible. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved Act document—**Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 111**, authorised by **Barbara Hargreaves**—was in force only until **29 June 2026**, so it is not the version in force today and I have not relied on it for today’s Act position. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: No: the answer omits the s 63 point that the renter must leave the premises reasonably clean and in the same condition as at the start, fair wear and tear excepted; it explicitly declines to rely on the Act and mentions starting condition only in the context of the reg 12 professional-cleaning term.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer does not say the renter must pay simply because of the clause or the pet; it says the cleaning term 'does not automatically require a professional cleaner merely because the lease contains a pet clause' and that the documents 'do not establish that you must pay for professional cleaning'.

question: When I moved out I agreed the agent could take an amount for cleaning out of my bond, but I never signed a bond claim form for it. Then my full bond came back to me, and a month later the agent sent a separate invoice for the cleaning. Do I have to pay it? Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?
answer:
## What the law says

The current retrieved document is **_Residential Tenancies Act 1997_, Authorised Version 115** (in force from 13 October 2026). [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

A rental provider may claim from a bond the **reasonable cost of cleaning** if the premises were not left reasonably clean, having regard to their condition at the start of the tenancy. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

However, a bond claim must be made in an **Authority-approved form**. A renter’s signature is specifically required where the claim is a joint claim by the renter and provider directing payment to the provider; that signature must be obtained no earlier than 14 days before the tenancy ends. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The Act also says the provider must give the renter supporting **bond claim evidence at least three days before** making a claim for repayment to the provider. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved provisions do **not** say that:

- agreeing that cleaning may be deducted from the bond is automatically an agreement to pay a later, separate invoice;
- failing to sign a bond claim form automatically cancels any separate agreement;
- receiving the whole bond automatically extinguishes, or confirms, a separate cleaning debt; or
- a separate invoice is enforceable in these circumstances.

So, **the documents do not establish that you must pay the invoice**. They also do not establish that you definitely do not have to pay it. Whether your agreement created a separate obligation would depend on the terms and evidence of that agreement, which the retrieved documents do not address.

## What you can do or ask

You can ask the agent to identify:

1. the legal or contractual basis for the invoice;
2. whether they are relying on your agreement to a **bond deduction** or claiming a separate debt; and
3. the evidence supporting the claimed cleaning cost.

You can state that you did not sign a bond claim form, that the full bond was repaid, and that you do not accept that an agreement about a bond deduction was necessarily an agreement to pay a separate invoice. The Act permits a provider to claim cleaning costs from the bond, but the retrieved provisions do not explain how that bond process determines liability for a later invoice. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

For a disputed bond claim, the Authority’s notice must say that it will pay the claim unless the renter gives written notice within **14 days** that the claim is subject to a Tribunal application. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The Act also provides for an application to the Tribunal concerning repayment of bond, generally within **14 days after the tenancy ended**, but the documents do not say that this procedure determines liability for a separate invoice after the bond has already been repaid. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: No. The first point is missing because it is hedged too far: the answer says the documents do not say a bond-deduction agreement is 'automatically an agreement to pay a later, separate invoice', but then says 'Whether your agreement created a separate obligation would depend on the terms and evidence of that agreement', so it never states that agreeing to a deduction is agreement to a bond claim rather than to a separate invoice. The second point is covered ('reasonable cost of cleaning if the premises were not left reasonably clean, having regard to their condition at the start of the tenancy').

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer asserts neither failing claim: it says "the documents do not establish that you must pay the invoice," and it lists "receiving the whole bond automatically extinguishes, or confirms, a separate cleaning debt" only as something the provisions do not say.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the required document with its version, "Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115" (in force from 13 October 2026), and cites the link 97-109aa115; every rule it applies comes from that in-force version, and it does not rely on any other version.

question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. I've called them twice today. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
## What the law says

The retrieved **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009**, in force from **30 June 2026**, says that only a suitably qualified person may carry out urgent or non-urgent repairs. It also says a renter may arrange urgent repairs if they have taken reasonable steps to get the rental provider to arrange them immediately, but the provider has not done so. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The regulations state that urgent repairs include the failure or breakdown of certain essential services or appliances supplied by the rental provider, including hot water, cooking, heating or laundering services. However, the retrieved documents do **not** state whether a broken tap that requires the water to be turned off to the whole house is an urgent repair under the version in force today. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The current retrieved regulations state that the renter may be reimbursed directly by the rental provider for the reasonable cost of urgent repairs, up to **$2,500**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The latest retrieved **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 111**, is only identified as in force until **29 June 2026**, so it does not establish the Act’s wording for today, **9 November 2026**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) The documents therefore do not contain enough information to give a conclusive current-law classification of this particular tap failure.

## What you can do or ask

You do **not necessarily have to wait** for the owner’s preferred tradespeople: if this is an urgent repair, the current regulations allow you to arrange it yourself after taking reasonable steps to have the rental provider or agent arrange it immediately, which your two calls may support. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

Ask the repairer to:

- be suitably qualified; and
- provide an itemised invoice and evidence of the work and cost. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

You can then seek reimbursement of the reasonable cost, up to **$2,500** under the current retrieved regulations. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) If the repair will cost more than $2,500, or the provider refuses to pay, the documents say you may apply to VCAT for an order requiring the provider to carry out the urgent repairs. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

Because the documents do not clearly say that this particular broken tap is an urgent repair under today’s law, I cannot confirm from them alone that reimbursement is guaranteed.

It also omits the 7-day reimbursement after written notice (s 72), saying only that the renter 'may be reimbursed' and that reimbursement cannot be confirmed. It does not say that a preferred-tradesperson requirement is a prohibited term or cannot block an urgent repair.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer asserts neither failure condition, saying "You do **not necessarily have to wait** for the owner's preferred tradespeople" and "You can then seek reimbursement of the reasonable cost, up to **$2,500**"; its caveat that it "cannot confirm... that reimbursement is guaranteed" is a hedge, not a statement that the cost cannot be recovered.

question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. I haven't moved any of my things in or stayed there yet. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
## What the law says

The current documents are:

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, in force from 13 October 2026** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 009, in force from 30 June 2026** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The premises must comply with rental minimum standards. They must be **structurally sound and weatherproof**, and each room must be free from **mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) The rental provider must also maintain the premises in good repair and in a fit condition for occupation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The standard agreement states that the agreement’s start date is the date from which the renter may move in. It also says the rental provider must provide premises complying with the minimum standards, vacant and reasonably clean, when the renter moves in. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) The documents do **not** say that collecting the keys or not yet moving in automatically cancels the agreement.

## What you can do or ask

1. **Notify the rental provider in writing immediately.** Describe the damp, mould and rotting timber, attach dated photographs or other evidence, and state that the defects appear inconsistent with the structural-soundness, weatherproofing and mould/damp standards. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) The renter must give written notice as soon as practicable after becoming aware of damage or a breakdown of supplied facilities, fixtures, furniture or equipment. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

2. **Ask for the defects to be repaired before you move in**, and ask for written confirmation of the repair scope and completion date. Non-urgent repairs must be carried out in a reasonable time; after written notice, you may apply to VCAT if they have not been done within **14 days**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) VCAT can order specified repairs, require a suitably qualified person to do them, and order compensation. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

3. **If the condition makes the premises unsafe or uninhabitable, ask urgently for action.** The retrieved documents do not provide enough information to classify damp, mould and rotting timber in a residential house as an “urgent repair” on those facts alone. They do state that urgent repairs must be carried out after notice, and that VCAT applications for urgent repairs may be made where the renter cannot meet the cost, the cost exceeds the prescribed amount, or the provider refuses to pay. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

4. **You can ask the provider to agree to cancel the lease without penalty**, or to agree in writing to a reduced rent while specified repairs are outstanding. However, the retrieved documents do not state a general right to cancel in this situation, nor do they state a specific statutory right to a rent reduction merely because the renter has not yet moved in. Do not simply stop paying rent or treat the lease as cancelled without an agreement or an order.

5. **If repairs are not done, consider the formal repair remedies.** You may apply to the Director to investigate after giving written notice and waiting 14 days; the Director may negotiate repairs or issue a report directing the provider to comply. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) You may also apply to VCAT for non-urgent repairs after the 14-day period. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The Act also allows a renter who has given a repair notice to seek an order permitting rent to be paid into the **Rent Special Account** if the provider has failed to repair, subject to the statutory conditions; this is not the same as an automatic rent reduction. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Preserve the keys, lease, inspection records, photographs, messages and any reports. The retrieved documents do not contain a specific cancellation procedure for your precise pre-move-in situation, so they do not establish that you can unilaterally terminate without possible liability.

must-mention.reason: No. The answer misses the s 91L point: a renter who has not taken possession can end the agreement by notice if the premises do not meet the minimum standards, are not in good repair or are unfit for habitation. Instead it says 'the retrieved documents do not state a general right to cancel in this situation' and warns against treating the lease as cancelled, which contradicts that right.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer never says the renter must move in or pay rent before acting; it says to "Ask for the defects to be repaired before you move in". It also denies any statutory right to lower rent, stating the documents do not show "a specific statutory right to a rent reduction" and that a reduction would need the provider to "agree in writing".
