question: Our rental was broken into several times while we were moving out, and there are about three weeks left on our fixed-term lease. The burglars damaged the plumbing and wiring, so we can't even clean properly. What are our options before the lease ends?
answer:
## What the law says

The current document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115**, in force from **13 October 2026**, authored by **Barbara Hargreaves**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

A renter may give the rental provider a **written notice of intention to vacate** if the premises are **unfit for human habitation** or have been destroyed to an extent that makes them **unsafe**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The notice may make the agreement end **on the day the notice is given or a later date**, even though the fixed term has three weeks remaining. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The renter must report damage to the rental provider **in writing as soon as practicable**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Plumbing or wiring damage may require urgent repairs; the current prescribed reimbursement limit shown in the retrieved regulations is **$2,500**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) Only a suitably qualified person may carry out repairs. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The renter’s obligation at the end of the agreement is to leave the premises reasonably clean **“as far as practicable”**, and the renter is not responsible for cleaning to the extent the rental provider is responsible under the Act. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

1. **Immediately send written notice** to the rental provider or agent describing the break-ins, plumbing and wiring damage, and why the premises are unsafe or unfit for habitation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)  
2. If relying on that condition, give a **signed written notice of intention to vacate under section 91ZD**, specifying today or a later termination date. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) The retrieved documents do not provide a prescribed form for this notice, but they state that a notice of intention to vacate is invalid unless it is in writing and signed. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)  
3. **Ask the rental provider to confirm in writing** that the agreement will end and that they will arrange or pay for the necessary plumbing, electrical and security repairs. The rental provider must maintain the premises in good repair and fit for occupation. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)  
4. For urgent repairs, first take reasonable steps to have the rental provider or agent arrange them immediately; if they do not, you may arrange the repairs yourself and seek reimbursement of the reasonable cost up to **$2,500**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)  
5. If you cannot pay, the repairs exceed **$2,500**, or the rental provider refuses to pay, apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring the repairs; the Act says the application must be heard within **2 business days**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)  
6. Keep photographs, police or insurance records, tradesperson reports, receipts and all messages. The retrieved documents do not state whether rent can be stopped automatically or whether compensation is payable for the burglary damage, so do not assume either without an agreement or Tribunal order.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are present. (1) Reporting: 'The renter must report damage to the rental provider in writing as soon as practicable.' (2) Urgent repairs: 'Plumbing or wiring damage may require urgent repairs' is softly worded, but the answer then says the provider must be asked to 'arrange them immediately; if they do not, you may arrange the repairs yourself and seek reimbursement of the reasonable cost up to $2,500.' (3) Ending the lease: a section 91ZD notice to vacate where the premises are unfit or unsafe can end the agreement 'on the day the notice is given or a later date, even though the fixed term has three weeks remaining.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never makes the renter liable for the burglary damage or bound to stay until the lease ends: it says "The rental provider must maintain the premises in good repair and fit for occupation," lets the renter arrange urgent repairs only if the provider fails to and then "seek reimbursement," and says a notice of intention to vacate "may make the agreement end on the day the notice is given or a later date, even though the fixed term has three weeks remaining."

version-cited.reason: No: the answer correctly names the Act as "Authorised Version No. 115", but it relies on Regulations version 005 (21-3sra005), which was not in force on that date (version 009 was). In step 2 it uses that version's rule that a notice of intention to vacate "is invalid unless it is in writing and signed", and deleting that would change the advice.

question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. The app is run by a payments company my agent uses, and it's that company that charges the card fee. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
## What the law says

The current document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115**, in force from **13 October 2026**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

- The rental provider or agent must ensure that **at least one rent-payment method is reasonably available without additional costs**, apart from bank or account fees payable on the renter’s own bank account. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The Regulations also state that the rental provider must permit at least one fee-free method and allow Centrepay or another electronic funds transfer. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- Before you consent to a payment method, the rental provider or agent must tell you about costs you may incur, including **third-party transaction fees** and electronic-payment-facility fees. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- A person must not charge a renter for the **establishment or use of an electronic payment facility for paying rent**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- The Act also says that a person other than an authorised deposit-taking institution must not demand or receive a fee for a **prescribed matter** relating to payment of rent. The retrieved document does not state what the relevant prescribed matter is. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

On these documents alone, the app’s card fee is **not clearly authorised merely because it is charged by the payments company**. The documents do not expressly decide whether this particular card surcharge is a prohibited charge under section 51(3) or section 51A. They also do not say that the fee becomes lawful because it goes to a third party rather than the agent. Section 51(3) applies to **“a person”**, while section 42(7) expressly refers to **third-party transaction fees**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

You can ask the agent to:

1. Confirm in writing that the manual bank-transfer option is a reasonably available **fee-free rent-payment method**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
2. Identify the legal basis for the card fee and explain whether it is a fee for using an electronic payment facility to pay rent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
3. Provide the required information about all costs of the card-payment method, including the third-party transaction fee, before you consent to use it. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
4. Confirm whether the payments company is an authorised deposit-taking institution, because section 51A contains an exception for such institutions; the retrieved documents do not provide facts that establish the company’s status. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The documents do not state whether the slower bank-transfer option is sufficiently “reasonably available” in your particular circumstances, so they do not conclusively determine that issue.

must-mention.reason: No. The second point is missing. The output never states that fees for paying rent are banned for anyone other than a bank under s 51A with reg 21C, so that it does not matter who collects the fee. Instead it says 'The retrieved document does not state what the relevant prescribed matter is' and 'The documents do not expressly decide whether this particular card surcharge is a prohibited charge'. That is hedged so far that a reader cannot tell which way the point falls. The first point (a reasonably available fee-free method) and a next step (asking the agent) are covered.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the fee is allowed because a fee-free option exists, and never says the landlord or agent is exempt from the fee ban. It states the opposite on both points: the card fee is "not clearly authorised merely because it is charged by the payments company" and "Section 51(3) applies to 'a person'". The only exception it mentions is the one for authorised deposit-taking institutions under section 51A.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Act as "Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115" (link 97-109aa115) and cites "The Regulations" through the link 21-3sra009, which identifies Authorised Version No. 009. Both are the versions in force on that date, and no rule is drawn from any other version.

question: My lease is on the standard form and started in 2024. It has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. I cleaned them myself and they're back to how they were when I moved in, but the agent wants a receipt from a professional cleaner. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?
answer:
## What the retrieved law says

The documents **do not contain the law in force today (9 November 2026)**. The latest retrieved versions ended earlier: **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 110** was in force until 24 November 2025, and **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, version 002** was in force until 30 November 2024. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) Therefore, I cannot definitively state today’s law from these documents.

Under the latest retrieved provisions, a standard-form agreement may require professional cleaning **only if it is needed to restore the premises to their condition immediately before the tenancy began**, taking account of the condition report and fair wear and tear. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) A term requiring professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy, outside that standard-form condition, is a prohibited term; prohibited terms are void and unenforceable. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

So, on the facts you gave, if you cleaned the carpets yourself and restored them to their starting condition, the retrieved documents do **not** support requiring you to pay for a professional cleaner merely to obtain a receipt. They also do not state that a professional-cleaning receipt is required. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

- Ask the agent to identify the specific carpet condition in the **entry condition report** that they say has not been restored, allowing for fair wear and tear. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)  
- Provide the entry and exit photographs, dated and labelled by room or location. The prescribed condition report says photographs should be taken at the beginning and end of the tenancy and may help resolve disputes about condition and cleaning. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)  
- Keep your cleaning records, photographs, correspondence, and any inspection report.  
- Ask the agent to explain why professional cleaning is necessary rather than identifying actual remaining cleaning or damage. Under the retrieved standard terms, the relevant comparison is the carpets’ condition immediately before the tenancy, based on the condition report and fair wear and tear—not simply whether you possess a professional cleaner’s receipt. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The documents do not say what specific tribunal or bond procedure applies to this particular dispute, so I cannot supply that part from the retrieved material.

must-mention.reason: No. The answer never states the renter's general s 63 duty to leave the premises reasonably clean and in the same condition as at the start, fair wear and tear excepted. It only frames condition as a limit on when professional cleaning can be required. It also gives the reg 12 rule incompletely, saying professional cleaning can be required 'only if it is needed to restore the premises' and omitting the limb where cleaning was done before the tenancy and the renter was told.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer never says the renter must pay simply because of the clause or the pet, and instead says the documents "do **not** support requiring you to pay for a professional cleaner merely to obtain a receipt" and that professional cleaning may be required "only if it is needed to restore the premises to their condition immediately before the tenancy began."

version-cited.reason: No: the answer names 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 110' and 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, version 002' rather than the in-force Version No. 115 and Version No. 009. It also applies rules from these superseded versions, such as the professional-cleaning prohibited term and the condition-report photographs, even though it acknowledges they were not in force on the date.

question: When I moved out I agreed the agent could take an amount for cleaning out of my bond, but I never signed a bond claim form for it. Then my full bond came back to me, and a month later the agent sent a separate invoice for the cleaning. Do I have to pay it? Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?
answer:
## What the law says

The current document is **_Residential Tenancies Act 1997_, Authorised Version No. 115**, in force from **13 October 2026**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

- A renter must leave the premises **reasonably clean**, allowing for fair wear and tear. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- A residential rental provider may claim from the bond the **reasonable cost of cleaning** if the premises were not left reasonably clean, having regard to their condition when the tenancy began. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- A bond claim must be made in an **Authority-approved form**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- The renter’s signature is specifically required where the claim is a **joint claim** by the provider and renter for payment of part of the bond to the provider. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The Act does not, in the retrieved text, say that a renter’s signature is required for every type of bond claim.
- Before making a claim for repayment of bond to the provider, the provider or agent must give the renter supporting **bond claim evidence at least 3 days beforehand**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- If the Authority has already repaid the **full bond** to you, the retrieved provisions do not state whether a later, separate cleaning invoice is enforceable, nor whether agreeing to a proposed bond deduction is legally the same as agreeing to pay an invoice. **The documents therefore do not answer those two questions directly.** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

So, on these documents alone, you cannot be told that you definitely must pay the invoice—or that you definitely do not. Your earlier agreement may be evidence of an agreement about the cleaning cost, but the retrieved Act does not establish that it automatically creates liability for a separate invoice after the full bond was returned. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

Ask the agent in writing to provide:

1. the legal basis for the invoice;
2. the cleaning report, condition reports and photographs;
3. the actual cleaning account or receipt; and
4. an explanation of why the full bond was paid to you and why the claim was not made through the Authority.

You can also dispute whether the amount is a **reasonable cleaning cost** and whether the premises actually failed to meet the statutory cleaning requirement. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The retrieved documents state that an application for a Tribunal order requiring repayment of bond to the provider must be made within **14 days after the residential rental agreement terminated**, but they do not state a specific process or deadline for disputing this later invoice. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: No: the first point is missing. The answer never says that agreeing to a bond deduction is agreement to a claim on the bond rather than agreement to pay a separate invoice. Instead it says 'The documents therefore do not answer those two questions directly' and that the agreement 'may be evidence of an agreement about the cleaning cost', which is hedged so far that a reader cannot tell which way it falls. The second point is covered: 'not left reasonably clean, having regard to their condition when the tenancy began'.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer asserts neither forbidden claim, stating instead that "you cannot be told that you definitely must pay the invoice—or that you definitely do not" and that the Act "does not establish that it automatically creates liability for a separate invoice after the full bond was returned."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the only required document with its version, "Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, in force from 13 October 2026", and every citation links to 97-109aa115, the version in force on that date; it relies on no other version.

question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. I've called them twice today. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
## What the law says

**The retrieved documents do not contain the Victorian law in force today, 9 November 2026.** The latest retrieved Act is *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, **Authorised Version 111**, which was in force only from **25 November 2025 to 29 June 2026**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

Under that version, a renter could arrange urgent repairs without waiting if they had taken reasonable steps to arrange for the rental provider or agent to repair the problem **immediately**, but were unable to get them to do so. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) Calling the emergency contact twice and being told that the owner’s tradespeople cannot attend may satisfy that requirement, but the retrieved documents do not specifically address whether a broken tap that requires the whole house’s water to be turned off is legally an “urgent repair.” [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

Only a **suitably qualified person** may carry out urgent or non-urgent repairs. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) Under Authorised Version 111, the renter would then have to give the rental provider **7 days’ written notice** of the repairs and cost, and the provider would owe the reasonable cost—or the prescribed amount, if lower—within **7 days** after receiving that notice. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

You do **not necessarily have to wait** under the latest retrieved Act version: you may arrange a suitably qualified plumber, keep the invoice and evidence of your two calls, and send written notice of the work and cost. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

However, the documents do not establish the reimbursement limit that applies **today**, because the retrieved regulations are *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, **Authorised Version 005**, which was in force only until **9 February 2026**. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) That version states a renter may be reimbursed up to **$2,500**, but I cannot confirm from the retrieved documents that this limit remains in force today. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

If you cannot afford the repair, the cost exceeds the prescribed amount, or the rental provider refuses to pay, the latest retrieved Act allowed an application to the Tribunal for an urgent-repair order, which had to be heard within **2 business days**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) The documents do not confirm the current Tribunal name or procedure for November 2026.

must-mention.reason: No. The answer covers the s 72 reimbursement process, but it misses the other two points. It hedges on the first, saying the documents 'do not specifically address whether a broken tap that requires the whole house's water to be turned off is legally an "urgent repair"' rather than stating that no water supply is an urgent repair. It never says that requiring the owner's nominated tradespeople is a prohibited term (reg 11(e)) or that this policy cannot stop an urgent repair.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the renter must wait or cannot recover costs; instead it states 'You do not necessarily have to wait' and that 'the provider would owe the reasonable cost—or the prescribed amount, if lower—within 7 days', and its date caveats express uncertainty rather than asserting either failure condition.

version-cited.reason: No: the answer never names the in-force versions (Act Authorised Version No. 115, Regulations Authorised Version No. 009). Instead it applies rules from superseded versions, 'Authorised Version 111' of the Act (97-109aa111) and 'Authorised Version 005' of the Regulations (21-3sra005). It presents those rules (arranging urgent repairs, 7 days' written notice, the $2,500 reimbursement cap, the Tribunal application) as steps the user can take, despite caveats.

question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. I haven't moved any of my things in or stayed there yet. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
## What the law says

Today’s applicable documents are:

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115, in force from 13 October 2026** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009, in force from 30 June 2026** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

Because you have **not entered into possession**, section 91L applies. A residential rental agreement terminates if the renter gives the rental provider a notice of termination stating that the premises are, among other things, **not in good repair, unfit for human habitation, do not meet rental minimum standards, or are otherwise unavailable for occupation**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The minimum standards require the premises to be **structurally sound and weatherproof**, and every room to be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) Structural mould or damp is also defined as an **urgent repair**, as is a fault or damage making the premises unsafe or insecure. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The rental provider must provide and maintain the premises in **good repair** and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation, regardless of whether the renter knew about the disrepair before entering into occupation. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

1. **Give written notice terminating the agreement under section 91L.**  
   State that you have not entered into possession and that the damp, mould and rotting timber mean the premises are not in good repair and/or do not meet the rental minimum standards. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Ask for confirmation that the agreement is terminated and for return of any bond or rent paid; the retrieved documents do not specify the refund procedure or timing.

2. **Ask the rental provider to arrange repairs instead.**  
   Ask for suitably qualified tradespeople to investigate and repair the source of the damp, remove the mould safely, and replace or repair the rotting timber. Repairs required to discharge the provider’s repair duty must be done by a suitably qualified person. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The regulations also require each room to be free from structurally caused mould and damp and the premises to be structurally sound. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

3. **Ask to postpone occupation and rent until the work is complete.**  
   The provider must ensure the premises comply with the minimum standards on or before the day you enter occupation. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) If the premises are not vacant and reasonably clean on the agreed occupation day, you are not required to enter occupation and are not required to pay rent for the period until you actually enter occupation. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The documents do not expressly state that rent is automatically suspended solely because of the mould, damp or timber defects before occupation.

4. **Ask for a lower rent, but do not reduce it unilaterally.**  
   The retrieved documents do not give a renter an automatic right to impose a lower rent because the premises are defective. You may ask the provider to agree in writing to a reduced rent, but the documents do not state that the provider must agree. A Tribunal compensation order, where available, may take the form of a rent refund or reduction. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

5. **If the provider disputes the problem or refuses to act, seek a Tribunal remedy.**  
   For non-urgent repairs, the Act permits an application for repair orders after written notice and 14 days without the repairs; the Tribunal may order specified repairs and compensation. Do not simply stop paying or walk away without giving written notice or obtaining written agreement, because the Act says a residential rental agreement can be terminated only in the ways provided by the Act or by agreement. question: Our rental was broken into several times while we were moving out, and there are about three weeks left on our fixed-term lease. The burglars damaged the plumbing and wiring, so we can't even clean properly. What are our options before the lease ends?
answer:
## What the law says

The current document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115** (*rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf*), authorised by the Chief Parliamentary Counsel; its current version began on **13 October 2026**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

- You must notify the rental provider **in writing, as soon as practicable**, of the burglary damage and its nature. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- You must ordinarily leave the premises reasonably clean and in the same condition as at the start, allowing for fair wear and tear—but only **“as far as practicable.”** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The Act also says this cleaning duty does not apply to the extent the rental provider is responsible for keeping the premises clean. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- If the premises are **unfit for human habitation**, or have been destroyed totally or to an extent that makes them unsafe, you may give a notice of intention to vacate with the termination date being **the date the notice is given or a later date**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) This applies despite the fixed term. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- For urgent repairs, you may arrange the repairs yourself if you first take reasonable steps to have the rental provider or agent carry them out immediately and they do not do so. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) You must then give **7 days’ written notice** of the repairs and cost; the rental provider must reimburse the reasonable cost—or the prescribed maximum, if lower—within **7 days** after receiving that notice. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- If you cannot pay, the cost exceeds the prescribed amount, or the rental provider refuses to pay, you may apply to the Tribunal for an urgent-repairs order; the Tribunal must hear that application within **2 business days**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved documents do **not** state whether the particular plumbing and wiring damage in your case legally meets the Act’s “unfit for human habitation” or “unsafe” test, nor do they state the current prescribed monetary limit for urgent repairs.

## What you can do or ask

1. **Immediately send written notice** to the rental provider or agent describing the break-ins, plumbing and wiring damage, safety risks, and inability to clean properly. Keep photographs, police reports, messages, quotations and receipts. The written-notice requirement and the need to report the damage are stated in the Act. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

2. **Ask the rental provider to confirm immediately** whether the premises are safe and to arrange qualified repairs. Do not attempt electrical or plumbing work yourself; the retrieved current Act does not specify who must perform those repairs, so the documents do not provide a more specific rule.

3. If the damage makes the premises uninhabitable or unsafe, **serve a notice under section 91ZD ending the tenancy immediately or on a later date**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) On the documents provided, this is the clearest way to end the fixed-term lease before the remaining three weeks.

4. If the premises are not clearly uninhabitable or unsafe but urgent repairs are needed, either:
   - arrange them after taking the required reasonable steps to obtain immediate repairs and seek reimbursement; or
   - apply to the Tribunal for an urgent-repairs order, especially if you cannot fund the work. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

5. Regarding cleaning, explain in writing that cleaning is not reasonably practicable until the damaged plumbing and wiring are repaired. The Act requires cleaning only **as far as practicable**, and the documents do not say that you must repair burglary damage caused by third parties before vacating. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: No. Point 2 is missing: the answer never says the damaged plumbing and wiring are urgent repairs the landlord must fix immediately. It only says 'if urgent repairs are needed', and it adds that 'the retrieved current Act does not specify who must perform those repairs', so a reader cannot tell whether this damage counts as urgent or that the landlord must fix it. Points 1 (written notice as soon as practicable) and 3 (s 91ZD notice to vacate with an immediate termination date, despite the fixed term) are covered.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never makes the renter liable for the burglary damage and never says they must stay until the lease ends; it says "the documents do not say that you must repair burglary damage caused by third parties before vacating", describes self-arranged urgent repairs as optional and reimbursable, and says that if the premises are unsafe the renter may "serve a notice under section 91ZD ending the tenancy immediately or on a later date".

question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. The app is run by a payments company my agent uses, and it's that company that charges the card fee. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
Based on the retrieved documents, the governing law today is the ***Residential Tenancies Act 1997***, **Authorised Version 111** (in force from 25 November 2025) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), alongside the ***Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021***, **Authorised Version 005** [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

### Can the app charge you the card fee? Does it matter who receives it?
Yes, a third-party payments company can charge a processing fee for using their card service. However, **the law strictly guarantees that you are not forced to use it.** 

Under Section 42(4) of the Act, your rental provider or agent **must ensure that a rent payment method that incurs no additional costs** (other than standard bank fees on your own account) is reasonably available to you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The Regulations also explicitly note that the provider must permit a fee-free payment method and allow you to use Centrepay or another form of electronic funds transfer [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 

Because you already have a manual bank transfer option with no fee, your agent is complying with this legal requirement. The law does not ban third-party card fees, but it mandates that these "third party transaction fees" must be clearly disclosed to you before you consent to use that payment method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). 

It **does not matter** whether the fee goes to the app company or your agent. The legal obligation falls on the rental provider/agent to provide a free alternative, regardless of who profits from the card transaction. As long as a fee-free option (like your bank transfer) is available and you are informed of any third-party costs upfront, the law is satisfied [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

### What you can do:
* **Use the free method:** You are fully entitled to pay via the manual bank transfer option without penalty or pressure. 
* **Check for disclosure:** Ensure your agent has provided you with clear information about the card fee before you agreed to use the app [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). If they haven't, you can ask them to formally disclose these costs in writing.
* **Refuse forced payments:** Your agent cannot require you to pay rent via a paid method if a free one is available. 

*(Note: This information applies to standard residential tenancies in Victoria as of 9 November 2026 based on the provided statutory texts.)*

must-mention.reason: No. The answer misses the second point: it says the law "does not ban third-party card fees" and only requires disclosure, which contradicts the rule that fees for paying rent are banned for anyone other than a bank (s 51A with reg 21C), unless the fee is a surcharge permitted under another law. The first point (a fee-free method must be reasonably available) and the third point (use the fee-free method) are both covered.

must-not-say.reason: No. The answer says the card fee is allowed because a fee-free option exists, stating 'Because you already have a manual bank transfer option with no fee, your agent is complying with this legal requirement' and 'As long as a fee-free option (like your bank transfer) is available and you are informed of any third-party costs upfront, the law is satisfied.' It also relies on Version 111, which the rubric identifies as no longer current.

version-cited.reason: No. The answer cites 'Authorised Version 111' of the Act (97-109aa111) and 'Authorised Version 005' of the Regulations (21-3sra005) instead of the in-force Versions 115 and 009. It also takes the s 42(4) rule and the third-party fee disclosure rule from version 101 (97-109aa101).

question: My lease is on the standard form and started in 2024. It has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. I cleaned them myself and they're back to how they were when I moved in, but the agent wants a receipt from a professional cleaner. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?
answer:
**What the law says**
Under the Victorian residential tenancy laws currently in force today, the rules for professional cleaning are found in:
* **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021** (Authorised Version v005) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)
* **Residential Tenancies Act 1997** (Authorised Version v115) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

The standard form lease explicitly states that a rental provider cannot require you to arrange or pay for professional cleaning at the end of your tenancy unless it is actually *required* to restore the carpets to the condition they were in immediately before you moved in, taking into account fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). This statutory rule is supported by section 27C of the Act, which permits this term only if professional cleaning becomes necessary to achieve that restoration [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Because your legal obligation is tied to the *result* (the condition of the carpets) rather than the *method* (who cleaned them), you do not have to pay for a professional cleaner or provide a receipt if your DIY cleaning successfully restored them to their original state.

**What the renter can do or ask**
1. **Reference the Condition Report:** The law requires the agent to give you two copies of the condition report on or before your move-in date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Use this document as your primary evidence to show that the carpets are back to their starting condition (minus fair wear and tear).
2. **Provide Photographic Evidence:** If you took photos when you moved in, share them alongside photos of the cleaned carpets to prove they match the original state.
3. **Communicate with the Agent:** Politely inform the agent that under clause 12 of the standard form lease, professional cleaning is only mandatory if it is *required* to restore the premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Since you have already achieved this through your own efforts, you are not legally obligated to pay for or provide a receipt from a professional cleaner. If they continue to demand it, you can point them to the specific wording in the current standard form lease and section 27C of the Act.

It also omits the reg 12 ground that professional cleaning can be required if it was done before the tenancy and the renter was told. The condition report point is covered by 'Use this document as your primary evidence to show that the carpets are back to their starting condition'.

It also never names v009. The Act is named as 'Authorised Version v115', although its link shows 97-109aa088.

question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. I've called them twice today. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997** (Authorised Version No. 110), you do **not** have to wait for the owner's tradespeople. 

Here is how the law applies to your situation:

**1. Your broken tap qualifies as an "urgent repair"**
A tap that has broken and forced you to shut off the water to the entire house falls under the legal definition of urgent repairs, specifically a **"burst water service"** or a **"failure or breakdown of... water supply"** [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa097%20authorised.pdf). 

**2. You can arrange your own emergency plumber**
Under Section 72(1) of the Act, you are legally permitted to arrange for urgent repairs yourself if:
* You have taken reasonable steps to get the owner (or their agent) to do the repairs immediately; and 
* You are unable to get them to carry out the repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). 
Since you have already called twice today and been told no tradespeople are available, you have satisfied the requirement of taking "reasonable steps" and being "unable to get" the owner to act.

**3. How to get reimbursed**
If you hire a plumber yourself, you must follow these steps to ensure you get paid back:
* **Get an invoice:** Ensure the tradesperson provides a detailed receipt for the work done.
* **Give written notice:** You must give the residential rental provider written notice of the repairs and the cost within 7 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). 
* **Reimbursement timeline & limit:** The owner is legally liable to reimburse you for the reasonable cost of the repairs (up to a prescribed maximum limit, which is currently $2,500) within 7 days of receiving your written notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). 

**Summary of next steps:**
You can call a licensed plumber immediately. Once the repair is done, send a written message or email to the owner/agent attaching the invoice and stating that you arranged the urgent repair because they were unavailable. They are legally required to reimburse you within 7 days.

*(Note: This advice applies to the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997**, Authorised Version No. 110, which is the most current version of the law available in the provided records.)*

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered: the answer calls a broken tap that forced a whole-house water shut-off a 'burst water service' or 'failure or breakdown of... water supply' urgent repair. It states that after reasonable steps the renter can arrange the repair under s 72 and must be reimbursed the reasonable cost, up to the prescribed $2,500, within 7 days of written notice. It also addresses the preferred-tradesperson policy with 'you do **not** have to wait for the owner's tradespeople', which equivalently means the policy cannot stop an urgent repair, though it does not cite reg 11(e).

question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. I haven't moved any of my things in or stayed there yet. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Authorised Version No. 115)** [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) and the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (Authorised Version No. 009)** [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf), which are the versions of Victorian tenancy law in force today (November 09, 2026), here is what the law says about your situation:

### 🔹 Property Condition Standards
Your landlord is legally required to ensure the premises are **"in a fit condition for occupation"** and comply with all rental minimum standards [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Under these minimum standards, every room in the rented premises must be completely free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). 

### 🔹 Asking for Repairs
Because mould or damp caused by the building structure is legally classified as an **urgent repair**, your landlord must carry out these repairs as soon as you notify them [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
*   You should notify the rental provider in writing about the damp, mould, and rotting timber [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 
*   Only a suitably qualified person may perform these repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
*   If the landlord fails to carry out the urgent repairs after being notified, you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring them to do so [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

### 🔹 Cancelling the Lease or Asking for Lower Rent
The provided documents **do not contain specific provisions** that allow a tenant to cancel a lease before moving in due to property conditions, nor do they outline a process for asking for lower rent in this situation. 

*(Note: While you have strong grounds to demand urgent repairs under the law, the retrieved texts do not explicitly grant statutory rights to terminate the agreement early or reduce rent prior to taking possession for these specific defects.)*

question: Our rental was broken into several times while we were moving out, and there are about three weeks left on our fixed-term lease. The burglars damaged the plumbing and wiring, so we can't even clean properly. What are our options before the lease ends?
answer:
### What the Law Says About Your Situation
Under Victorian tenancy law, your rental provider is legally obligated to maintain the premises in good repair and in a fit condition for occupation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). When damage occurs, you are required to notify the rental provider in writing as soon as practicable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 

Because the burglary damaged your plumbing and wiring, these issues qualify as **urgent repairs** (such as a burst water service or failure of an essential service) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf), [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The rental provider must carry out urgent repairs immediately after being notified [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

### Your Options Before the Lease Ends
1. **Request Urgent Repairs & Claim Reimbursement**: If your rental provider does not arrange for a suitably qualified person to fix the plumbing and wiring immediately, you can take reasonable steps to arrange the repairs yourself [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). You may be reimbursed directly by the provider for the reasonable cost of these urgent repairs, up to **$2500** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). If the cost exceeds $2500 or the provider refuses to pay, you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring them to carry out the repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
2. **Terminate the Lease Early Without Penalty**: If the damage (e.g., lack of plumbing/wiring) makes the premises "unfit for habitation" or "destroyed," you can give your rental provider a notice of intention to vacate under section 91ZD of the Act [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). In this specific scenario, the rental provider **cannot** charge you compensation for the remaining rent on your fixed-term lease [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). They are also legally required to take all reasonable steps to re-let the premises to minimise any losses [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Apply to VCAT for Severe Hardship**: If continuing with the tenancy while repairs are pending would cause you severe hardship due to unforeseen circumstances, you can apply to VCAT for an order to reduce the term of your agreement and make necessary variations under section 91U [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### Your Ongoing Obligations
* You must keep the premises reasonably clean [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 
* Regarding cleaning at the end of the tenancy, the provider cannot require you to pay for professional cleaning unless it is strictly necessary to restore the premises to the condition they were in when you moved in (accounting for fair wear and tear) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. The app is run by a payments company my agent uses, and it's that company that charges the card fee. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
Based on the Victorian residential tenancy law in force today (Monday, November 9, 2026), the relevant governing documents are:
* ***Residential Tenancies Act 1997*** (Authorised Version **rta-1997-v111**, effective from 25 November 2025) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
* ***Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*** (Authorised Version **rt-regs-2021-v005**, effective from 25 November 2025) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

Here is how the law applies to your situation:

**1. Can the app charge you a card fee?**
Yes, a third-party payments company can legally charge a fee for processing your rent by card. However, this is only permitted if your rental provider or agent also provides a reasonably available payment method that incurs **no additional costs** (other than standard bank or account fees on your own banking app) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The current regulations explicitly note in the standard tenancy agreement that the rental provider must permit a fee-free payment method and allow you to use Centrepay or another form of electronic funds transfer [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 

**2. Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or the agent?**
No, it does not matter who collects the fee. The law places the obligation on the rental provider or their agent to ensure a fee-free option is available, regardless of who charges for the alternative card payment service [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). Furthermore, before you consent to use any payment method that has a cost, the provider or agent must give you clear information about those costs upfront. The law explicitly defines these costs to include **"third party transaction fees"** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). 

**What you can do:**
* **Use the fee-free option:** Since your agent offers a manual bank transfer with no fee, you are fully entitled to use this method without penalty or delay from the provider. 
* **Check your agreement:** Review your standard tenancy agreement (under the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*) to confirm the listed payment methods [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
* **Report non-compliance:** If your agent refuses to accept the fee-free bank transfer, penalizes you for using it, or fails to disclose third-party fees upfront, they are breaching their obligations under the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Authorised Version rta-1997-v111) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). 

*(Note: While the specific text of Section 42 regarding fee-free payment methods is substantively maintained in the current version of the Act effective today, the explicit regulatory notes and disclosure requirements confirm your rights under the current framework.)*

question: My lease is on the standard form and started in 2024. It has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. I cleaned them myself and they're back to how they were when I moved in, but the agent wants a receipt from a professional cleaner. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?
answer:
**What the law says**
Under Victorian residential tenancy law, a lease clause requiring professional carpet cleaning does not mean you must hire a professional service if your own cleaning has already met the standard. The law states that a renter is only required to have carpets professionally cleaned (or pay for it) if professional cleaning becomes necessary to restore the premises to the condition they were in immediately before the tenancy started, taking into account fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Because you have already cleaned them yourself and returned them to their original state, you do not have to pay for a professional service or provide a receipt [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask**
To prove the carpets are in the required condition, you should use the **condition report** provided when you moved in. The law requires the rental provider to give you this report (either two paper copies or one emailed copy) on or before your move-in date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 

You can:
* Compare your current carpet condition against the original condition report and any photos or videos you took at the start of your tenancy.
* Politely inform the agent that because you have already restored the carpets to their original state (accounting for fair wear and tear), professional cleaning is no longer required under the regulations [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
* Ask them to inspect the carpets against the condition report to verify they meet the standard, rather than demanding a professional cleaning receipt.

**Documents referenced:**
* *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, version 005 (in force from 25 November 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)
* *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, version 115 (in force from 13 October 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

question: When I moved out I agreed the agent could take an amount for cleaning out of my bond, but I never signed a bond claim form for it. Then my full bond came back to me, and a month later the agent sent a separate invoice for the cleaning. Do I have to pay it? Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Authorised Version No. 115)**, which is in force today (from 13 October 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf):

**Do you have to pay the invoice?**
Not automatically. Because your full bond was already returned to you, the statutory process for claiming money from the bond is closed. The agent cannot retroactively take money from your bond without a signed claim form or a Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) order. Whether you owe the invoice depends entirely on whether you actually left the premises unreasonably dirty (excluding fair wear and tear). If you did, they could theoretically pursue it as a separate debt, but sending an invoice does not automatically make it payable.

**Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?**
No. They are legally distinct:
* A **bond deduction** is a claim against the security deposit held by the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority. It requires specific statutory procedures and must be submitted on an Authority-approved form [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
* An **invoice** is a direct request for payment for services rendered. Agreeing to let money be taken from your bond does not legally equate to agreeing to pay a separate invoice, particularly after the bond has already been fully repaid.

**What the law says about cleaning claims**
Under current Victorian tenancy law, a rental provider is only entitled to claim cleaning costs if two conditions are met:
1. The premises were **not left reasonably clean** by you [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
2. The cost claimed is **reasonable** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 

The law explicitly considers "fair wear and tear" and the condition of the property when you moved in. You cannot be charged for cleaning just to make the property "spotless" or to a professional standard unless it was genuinely necessary to restore it to its original condition, and even then, only the reasonable cost can be claimed [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do:**
* Review your initial condition report and take photos of the property when you moved out. If it was left reasonably clean (accounting for fair wear and tear), you have no obligation to pay the invoice.
* Reply to the agent in writing stating that you do not accept liability for the cleaning costs because the premises were left reasonably clean, and note that the bond process is already closed since the full refund was issued.
* If they continue to demand payment or threaten your rental history, you can seek free advice from the Victorian Tenants Union or apply to VCAT to have the dispute formally resolved.

On the distinction, the answer says a bond deduction 'must be submitted on an Authority-approved form' and that 'agreeing to let money be taken from your bond does not legally equate to agreeing to pay a separate invoice.' On the cleaning test, it says the rental provider can only claim if 'the premises were not left reasonably clean' and that the law 'considers ... the condition of the property when you moved in,' which matches the reasonably-clean test judged against the starting condition.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the one required document with its in-force version, the 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Authorised Version No. 115)', and every citation links to 97-109aa115. It relies on no other version of any document.

question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. I've called them twice today. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
**What the law says**
Under Section 72 of the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Authorised Version No. 110) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), a broken tap that causes water to leak or waste qualifies as an "urgent repair" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa097%20authorised.pdf). The law states that you do not have to wait for the owner's tradespeople if you have already taken reasonable steps to get them to fix it immediately and they are unable to do so [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). 

**What you can do**
You can arrange for a suitably qualified person to carry out the repairs yourself [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). To do this, follow these steps:
1. **Get the repair done:** Hire a qualified tradesperson to fix the tap [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). 
2. **Notify the owner in writing:** Give the owner written notice of the repairs and the cost within 7 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
3. **Claim reimbursement:** The owner is legally required to reimburse you for the reasonable cost of the repairs (up to $2500, as set out in the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* v002) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). They must pay this back within 7 days of receiving your notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

If the repair costs more than $2500 or you cannot afford to pay for it upfront, you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring the owner to carry out the urgent repairs directly [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**Documents applied:**
- *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Authorised Version No. 110) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (Authorised Version No. 002) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
- *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Authorised Version No. 097) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa097%20authorised.pdf) (for the definition of urgent repairs)

must-mention.reason: No: the answer never says that having no water supply, or a burst water service, is an urgent repair. It relies instead on a different ground ('a broken tap that causes water to leak or waste qualifies as an urgent repair'). It does cover the s 72 reimbursement process and the preferred-tradesperson point ('you do not have to wait for the owner's tradespeople if you have already taken reasonable steps').

question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. I haven't moved any of my things in or stayed there yet. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:

### **Landlord's Obligations & Minimum Standards**
The landlord is legally required to ensure the premises comply with rental minimum standards and are in good repair and fit for occupation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Specifically, each room must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). 

### **Repairs (What you can ask for)**
You can absolutely ask for repairs. Under the current Act, the presence of mould or damp caused by the building structure is classified as an **urgent repair** [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
* **Urgent Repairs:** The landlord must carry out urgent repairs after being notified [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). If they fail to act, you may arrange for a suitably qualified person to do the work and claim up to $2500 in reimbursement, or apply to VCAT for an order requiring the repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
* **Non-Urgent Repairs:** For other issues (such as certain types of rotting timber not classified as urgent), you must notify the landlord in writing. They must complete these repairs within a reasonable time, and you can apply to VCAT if they do not act within 14 days of receiving your notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

### **Cancelling the Lease**
The retrieved documents do not contain specific provisions regarding your right to cancel a residential rental agreement before moving in due to property condition. 

### **Asking for Lower Rent**
The retrieved documents do not contain information on how to apply for a rent reduction or lower rent through VCAT or other means.

question: Our rental was broken into several times while we were moving out, and there are about three weeks left on our fixed-term lease. The burglars damaged the plumbing and wiring, so we can't even clean properly. What are our options before the lease ends?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021**, Authorised Version **v009** (which is currently in force as of today, 9 November 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf), here are your options regarding the burglary damage and remaining three weeks of your fixed-term lease:

### 1. Notify Your Provider Immediately
You must notify your rental provider in writing about the damage to the premises as soon as possible [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 

### 2. Pursue Urgent Repairs
The damaged plumbing and wiring likely qualify as **urgent repairs** (such as a burst water service, gas leak, or flood damage) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Your provider is legally required to carry out these repairs immediately after you notify them [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 
* **If they refuse or delay:** You can arrange for a suitably qualified person to fix the issue yourself and claim reimbursement from your provider for reasonable costs up to **$2,500** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

### 3. Terminate the Lease Early (Unfit for Habitation)
Because the damage is severe enough that you cannot even clean properly, the premises may be legally considered **"unfit for habitation."** 
* You can give notice under section 91ZD of the Act to end your fixed-term lease early [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
* **Crucial Protection:** If you terminate on this basis, your rental provider **cannot** claim compensation for the remaining three weeks of rent (known as "rent foregone") [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### 4. Apply to VCAT
If your rental provider refuses to address the urgent repairs or fails to act within a reasonable timeframe, you can apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) for an order requiring them to carry out the necessary work [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 

**Recommended Next Step:** Send a written notice to your provider immediately detailing the damage, classifying it as an urgent repair, and stating that if the premises are deemed unfit for habitation, you reserve the right to terminate the agreement under section 91ZD without liability for the remaining rent.

question: My lease is on the standard form and started in 2024. It has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. I cleaned them myself and they're back to how they were when I moved in, but the agent wants a receipt from a professional cleaner. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?
answer:
**Do you have to pay for professional cleaning?**
No. Under Victorian residential tenancy law, you are **not** required to pay for or arrange professional carpet cleaning if the carpets are back to the condition they were in when you moved in (accounting for fair wear and tear). 

**What the Law Says**
The rules governing your lease are set out in Clause 12 of the standard form residential rental agreement, found in the ***Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*** (**Authorised Version rt-regs-2021-v005**), which is in force today [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 

According to this clause, a rental provider cannot require you to professionally clean the carpets at the end of your tenancy unless one of two specific conditions is met:
1. Professional cleaning was done immediately before you moved in **and** you were explicitly advised that it had been professionally cleaned; OR
2. Professional cleaning is actually required to restore the carpets to the same condition they were in when you started the tenancy, having regard to the condition report and taking into account fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

Since your carpets are back to their original state (minus normal wear and tear), the second condition does not apply, and the agent has no legal basis to demand a professional cleaning receipt.

**What Would Help Show the Carpets' Condition?**
To prove you have met your obligation, you should rely on the following:
* **The Signed Condition Report:** This is the primary legal benchmark for comparing the property's state at move-in versus move-out [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 
* **Dated Photos or Videos:** Clear, timestamped photos or videos you took when you moved in and when you moved out will provide objective evidence that the carpets have not been damaged beyond fair wear and tear.
* **Written Correspondence:** If the agent continues to demand payment, reply in writing referencing Clause 12 of the standard form lease and attach your move-in/move-out photos alongside the signed condition report to demonstrate the carpets are in the required condition [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

If the agent still refuses to return your bond or insists on the fee despite the carpets being in good order, you can apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) to resolve the dispute.

It mentions condition only as part of the reg 12 test and leaves out the 'reasonably clean' obligation, although the reg 12 conditions and the role of the condition report are both covered.
