It also never names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 or its Authorised Version No. 115.

question: When I moved out I agreed the agent could take an amount for cleaning out of my bond, but I never signed a bond claim form for it. Then my full bond came back to me, and a month later the agent sent a separate invoice for the cleaning. Do I have to pay it? Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997**, Authorised Version No. 115 (in force today as of November 09, 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf):

**1. Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?**
No, they are legally distinct processes. Under Victorian law, a bond deduction is a formal statutory claim that must be submitted using a specific form approved by the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority (RTBA) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Because you never signed this required claim form and your full bond was returned to you, no valid bond claim was ever processed against your money [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Verbally agreeing that an agent *could* take money from the bond does not constitute signing the statutory form.

**2. Do you have to pay the separate invoice?**
The Act regulates how bonds are held and claimed, but it does not automatically validate or invalidate private invoices sent after a tenancy ends [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
*   **Bond Claim Rules:** A residential rental provider is only entitled to claim cleaning costs from a bond if the premises were not left reasonably clean by the renter, taking into account fair wear and tear and the initial condition of the property [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Since your bond was returned in full without a signed claim form, the agent cannot retroactively deduct money from the bond.
*   **The Invoice:** Whether you must pay the separate invoice depends on your specific lease agreement and whether the cleaning was actually required under those terms. However, because the tenancy has ended and the bond was fully refunded, the agent cannot force payment through the bond system. 

**What you can do:**
*   **Do not sign anything new** acknowledging the debt unless you agree with the amount and the work was genuinely required.
*   **Request evidence** of the property's condition at move-out versus move-in to verify if professional cleaning or restoration was actually necessary under the lease terms [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
*   If the agent continues to demand payment, you can seek advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria or consider disputing the invoice through small claims processes if it is unreasonable.

It misses the second point. It confines the "reasonably clean… taking into account… the initial condition" test to bond claims, and says the invoice instead "depends on your specific lease agreement and whether the cleaning was actually required under those terms." question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. I've called them twice today. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
**What the Law Says**
Under Victorian residential tenancy law, a broken tap that forces you to shut off your water supply qualifies as an **urgent repair** (specifically classified as a "burst water service" or failure of a water supply) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa097%20authorised.pdf). 

The current law states that if a renter has taken reasonable steps to get the owner or their agent to carry out urgent repairs immediately, but is unable to get them to do so, the renter is legally permitted to arrange for those repairs themselves [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). An owner's policy of only using their own tradespeople does not override this statutory right if those tradespeople are unavailable.

**What You Can Do Now**
You do not have to wait. Since you have already called twice today and they cannot attend immediately, you can proceed with the following steps:

1. **Hire a qualified professional:** Only a suitably qualified person may carry out urgent repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). 
2. **Keep detailed records:** Ensure you obtain a formal invoice/receipt itemising the work done and the cost.
3. **Notify the owner in writing:** Within 7 days of the repairs being completed, you must give the owner written notice detailing the repairs carried out and the cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). 
4. **Claim reimbursement:** The owner is legally liable to reimburse you for the reasonable cost of the repairs (up to a prescribed limit of $2,500) within 7 days of receiving your written notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). 

**If the Cost Exceeds $2,500 or You Cannot Pay Upfront**
If the repair costs more than $2,500, or if you cannot afford to pay for it yourself first, you do not have to arrange the repairs. Instead, you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring the owner (or their agent) to carry out the urgent repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The Tribunal is required to hear your application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

*Note: This advice applies under the current Victorian residential tenancy laws in force today, specifically the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (v110)** and the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (v002)**.*

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered, and the hardest one (the preferred-tradesperson policy cannot stop an urgent repair) is met by: "An owner's policy of only using their own tradespeople does not override this statutory right if those tradespeople are unavailable."

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer says neither failing statement: it tells the renter "You do not have to wait" and that the owner's tradesperson policy "does not override this statutory right," and it says "The owner is legally liable to reimburse you for the reasonable cost of the repairs (up to a prescribed limit of $2,500)."

question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. I haven't moved any of my things in or stayed there yet. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
Based on the Victorian residential tenancy laws in force today (Monday, 9 November 2026), here is how the situation applies to you. The relevant documents are the ***Residential Tenancies Act 1997*** (Authorised Version No. 115) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) and the ***Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*** (Authorised Version No. 009) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### What the law says about your situation
* **Landlord's obligations:** The rental provider must ensure that the premises comply with rental minimum standards, are vacant and reasonably clean when you move in, and are maintained in good repair and in a fit condition for occupation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 
* **Mould and damp standards:** Under the rental minimum standards, each room in the rented premises must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
* **Classification of the issue:** The presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure is explicitly classified as an "urgent repair" under the Act [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do or ask
* **Ask for repairs:** You can notify the rental provider in writing about the damp, mould, and rotting timber. Because this qualifies as an urgent repair, the rental provider must carry out the repairs after being notified [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). If they fail to act, you may apply to VCAT for an order requiring them to carry out the urgent repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
* **Cancel the lease:** The provided documents do not contain information regarding your right to cancel a residential tenancy agreement before moving in due to property condition issues. 
* **Ask for lower rent:** The provided documents do not contain information regarding your options to request a rent reduction prior to taking possession of the premises. 

*(Note: While the retrieved regulations outline repair obligations and minimum standards, they do not address pre-move-in cancellation or rent negotiation rights. You may need to consult the full Act or seek legal advice for those specific remedies.)*

question: Our rental was broken into several times while we were moving out, and there are about three weeks left on our fixed-term lease. The burglars damaged the plumbing and wiring, so we can't even clean properly. What are our options before the lease ends?
answer:
Based on the current date (November 09, 2026), the relevant regulations in force are found in the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021**, Authorised Version Number **S.R. No. 3/2021** (Version 009) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

Here are your options before your fixed-term lease ends, based on this document:

### 1. Demand Urgent Repairs
Damaged plumbing and wiring likely constitute urgent repairs (such as a burst water service or failure of an essential service) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). You must notify your rental provider in writing immediately [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The provider is responsible for ensuring these are fixed [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). If they fail to act, you may arrange for a suitably qualified person to do the work and claim reimbursement for reasonable costs up to $2,500, or apply to VCAT if the costs exceed this amount or you cannot afford them [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

### 2. Terminate the Agreement Early (Premises Unfit for Habitation)
Because the break-in caused significant damage that prevents you from living in or cleaning the property, you can give your rental provider notice of intention to vacate under section 91ZD of the Act on the basis that the premises are destroyed or unfit for habitation [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). 
* **Key Benefit:** If you terminate under this ground, the rental provider **cannot** charge you compensation for "rent foregone" (the money they claim they will lose because you are leaving early) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### 3. Apply to VCAT for Severe Hardship
Alternatively, if the situation causes you severe hardship due to unforeseen circumstances, you may apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) for an order to reduce the term of your agreement [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### 4. Document Everything Thoroughly
To ensure you are not held financially responsible for the burglary damage at the end of your tenancy, you must document everything. Take dated photos showing the condition of the premises and note the burglary-related damage on your condition report [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The condition report is specifically designed to help resolve disputes over damage and cleaning, ensuring that fair wear and tear or third-party damage is not unfairly attributed to you [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

*Note: While the Regulations provide these standard terms, they reference specific sections of the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (such as section 91ZD). The provided documents do not contain the current version of the Act itself, but the Regulations confirm your right to use these sections to end the agreement without penalty for rent foregone.*

(3) The hardest point, termination: "you can give your rental provider notice of intention to vacate under section 91ZD of the Act on the basis that the premises are destroyed or unfit for habitation." question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. The app is run by a payments company my agent uses, and it's that company that charges the card fee. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
**Document used:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", version 115, in force from 13 October 2026. It is the version in force today (9 November 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Card fee on rent.** Under s 51(3)(b), a person must not demand or receive from a renter a charge for "the establishment or use of direct debit facilities or any other electronic payment facility for payment of rent". The penalty is 60 penalty units [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A card payment through a rent app looks like an "electronic payment facility", so this section probably covers your fee. That is my reading, because the text doesn't mention card surcharges by name.
- **A second prohibition.** Under s 51A, a person "other than an ADI" must not demand or receive a fee for "any prescribed matter" in relation to the payment of rent. The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person and 400 for a body corporate [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents I retrieved don't include the regulations, so I can't say whether a card fee is a "prescribed matter". They also don't define "ADI". An earlier version spelled it out as an authorised deposit-taking institution under the *Banking Act 1959* (Cth) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **The free bank transfer doesn't make the fee lawful.** Under s 42(4), the agent must make sure a payment method with no additional costs, other than your own bank or account fees, is "reasonably available" to you [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This is a separate duty. Nothing in the text says that offering a free option allows a fee on another method. The text also doesn't say whether a slower free option still counts as "reasonably available".
- **Disclosure.** Under s 42(7), the agent must tell you about any costs, expressly including "third party transaction fees" and "electronic payment facility fees", before you consent to a payment method [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This is a disclosure duty. It doesn't make a fee permitted.

## Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or the agent?

On the current text, it doesn't appear to.

- **Section 51(3)** applies to "a person", not only to the agent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Section 51A in version 115** exempts only an ADI. The agent and the provider are not exempt [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The earlier version 111 (25 November 2025 to 29 June 2026) expressly exempted a residential rental provider and the provider's agent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). That exemption is not in the current section.
- **Section 42(4) and (7)** bind the provider and the agent, so the agent stays responsible for the payment options and for the disclosure even though a third party runs the app [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't say whether the agent is liable for a fee the app company charges, or how any liability is shared.

## What you can do

The documents describe your rights but don't set out a complaint or refund process, so these are practical steps based on the provisions above.

1. **Use the free bank transfer.** Section 42(4) requires it to be reasonably available [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask the agent in writing** to remove the card fee, citing s 51(3)(b) and s 51A. You could also ask for a refund of any fee already paid.
3. **Ask for the cost information** the agent must give you under s 42(7) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Check the regulations** on what counts as a "prescribed matter" under s 51A. They aren't in the documents I retrieved.

I can't say from these documents how a refund would be recovered or where to complain.

(2) The hardest point is covered by 's 51(3)(b) ... probably covers your fee', 'Section 51A in version 115 exempts only an ADI. The agent and the provider are not exempt', and, on who collects, 'On the current text, it doesn't appear to [matter]'. The answer could not confirm reg 21C or the prescribed-matter detail and omits the surcharge-under-another-law caveat, but a reader can still tell the fee is likely banned whoever collects it. (3) It gives next steps: use the free bank transfer and ask the agent in writing to remove or refund the fee.

## What the law says

- **Professional cleaning terms are generally prohibited.** A residential rental agreement must not include a term requiring professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy, or requiring the renter to pay for it, unless that term is in the standard form [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **A prohibited term is void.** If an agreement contains a prohibited term, it is "void and unenforceable" [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **The standard form allows only a limited cleaning term.** The rental provider must not require professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy unless one of two things applies [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf):
  1. Professional cleaning was done immediately before the tenancy started, and the renter was told so.
  2. Professional cleaning is needed to restore the premises to their condition at the start of the tenancy, "having regard to the condition report and taking into account fair wear and tear".
- **The renter's duty is the same test.** The renter must have the premises professionally cleaned, or pay for it, only if cleaning becomes required to restore them to their starting condition, again by reference to the condition report and fair wear and tear [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Pets.** The standard-form pet clause only deals with seeking the rental provider's consent to keep a pet. It says nothing about carpet cleaning [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). The documents contain no pet-specific or carpet-specific cleaning rule.

**Applied to you:** A pet clause that flatly requires professional carpet cleaning looks like an extra term of the kind s 27B(1)(d)–(e) prohibits, so it would be void [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Under the standard-form test, the agent can only insist on professional cleaning if the carpets actually need it to match their starting condition, or if they were professionally cleaned before you moved in and you were told. If the carpets are back to how they were, the documents give no basis for requiring a receipt.

## What you can do or ask

- **Rely on the condition report.** The law measures the carpets against the condition report [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). The standard form says you must be given 2 copies (or one emailed copy) on or before the day you move in [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Compare the carpet entries in that report with their condition now.
- **Ask the agent which basis they rely on.** Ask whether the carpets were professionally cleaned before your tenancy and whether you were told, or whether they say the carpets need cleaning to match the condition report. The agent has to show one of these [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Apply to the Tribunal if needed.** A renter may apply to the Tribunal to have a term declared invalid or varied if it is harsh or unconscionable [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**Evidence:** Apart from the condition report, the retrieved documents don't say what else counts as evidence of the carpets' condition, such as photos or cleaning records. I can't say more on that from these sources.

must-mention.reason: No. The point about the renter's s 63 duty is missing: the answer never says the renter must leave the premises reasonably clean and in the same condition as at the start, fair wear and tear excepted. Its 'renter's duty' bullet only covers when professional cleaning must be paid for. The reg 12 conditions and the condition report as evidence of the starting condition are both covered.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the renter must pay simply because of the clause or the pet; it says a clause that "flatly requires professional carpet cleaning... would be void" and that "the agent can only insist on professional cleaning if the carpets actually need it to match their starting condition, or if they were professionally cleaned before you moved in and you were told."

It never names either of those versions, and its substance would collapse if the material from the non-in-force versions were deleted.

question: When I moved out I agreed the agent could take an amount for cleaning out of my bond, but I never signed a bond claim form for it. Then my full bond came back to me, and a month later the agent sent a separate invoice for the cleaning. Do I have to pay it? Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?
answer:
## Which document I used
The version in force today (9 November 2026) is the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf". It is labelled version 115 and has been in force since 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The excerpt I retrieved does not print the words "Authorised Version No.", so the version number comes from the file's metadata.

## What the Act says
- **A bond claim by the agent has to be made in a set way.** A claim to the Authority for repayment of a bond must be in a form approved by the Authority and must include the claimant's address or email address [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Cleaning is a permitted bond claim, within limits.** A rental provider (which includes an agent) may claim from the bond "the reasonable cost of cleaning any part of the premises, if the premises were not left reasonably clean by the renter". That is judged against the condition of the premises at the start of the agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The agent must give you evidence first.** At least 3 days before a claim to take bond money is made, the provider or agent must give each renter bond claim evidence supporting the claim. That evidence must not conflict with a statement in a condition report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Undisputed claims are paid out.** The Authority repays the bond where the claim is joint, or where the provider claims repayment to the renter, or where nobody disputes the claim within 14 days of notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Tribunal applications about the bond have a deadline.** An application to the Tribunal for a bond repayment order must be made within 14 days after the agreement has terminated [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Your two questions
**Do you have to pay the invoice?** The documents I retrieved do not say. They cover claims against the bond. They don't say whether an agent can invoice a former renter separately after the full bond has been refunded. I can't answer that from them.

**Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?** The documents don't say either. The Act treats a deduction as a bond claim, made on an approved form with supporting evidence [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Nothing in the retrieved text turns an informal agreement about a deduction into a separate debt. Nothing in it rules that out either.

## What you can do
- **Ask the agent for the evidence.** Request the cleaning evidence and the condition reports. The 3-day evidence rule is written for bond claims [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The same test is a sensible benchmark for the invoice: was the place not left reasonably clean compared with how it started, and is the cost reasonable? [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- **Dispute in writing if you disagree.** You can say that the bond has been refunded, that no claim form was signed, and that you want the evidence before paying anything. That is a practical step. The Act doesn't prescribe it.
- **Check the cleaning term.** An older version (version 110, dated 6 August 2025) says an agreement can't require professional cleaning, or require the renter to pay for it, unless that term is in the standard form [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). I did not retrieve the equivalent section from version 115, so confirm it is still current before relying on it.
- **Get advice about the Tribunal.** The only Tribunal route in the retrieved text is the 14-day bond repayment application, and that window has probably passed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether the Tribunal can hear a dispute over a post-refund invoice. A tenant advocacy service or VCAT could advise on that.

must-mention.reason: No. The answer misses the first point, that agreeing to a bond deduction is agreement to a claim on the bond and not to a separate invoice: it says "Nothing in the retrieved text turns an informal agreement about a deduction into a separate debt. Nothing in it rules that out either," which leaves the reader unable to tell which way it falls (the reasonably-clean test against the starting condition is covered).

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer asserts neither forbidden claim: on paying, it says "The documents I retrieved do not say," and on whether the agreement creates a debt, it says "Nothing in the retrieved text turns an informal agreement about a deduction into a separate debt. Nothing in it rules that out either."

version-cited.reason: No. The answer correctly names the in-force version ('version 115', file 'rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf'), but under 'Check the cleaning term' it presents a rule from 'version 110, dated 6 August 2025' as a step the user can take: an agreement can't require professional cleaning unless the term is in the standard form. The caveat that the user should confirm it is still current does not save it, and deleting that material would remove an actionable step, so the answer relies on a version not in force on that date.

question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. I've called them twice today. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
**Short answer:** You may not have to keep waiting. The documents say a renter can arrange urgent repairs once they have taken reasonable steps to get the rental provider to act and it hasn't happened. They don't settle whether two calls today count as "reasonable steps".

**Which documents I relied on**
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021**, file "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf", version 009, in force from 30 June 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). It is the latest version I retrieved and shows no end date. I take it to be the version in force today, but I can't confirm no later version exists. The version number comes from the file's metadata, not from the text.
- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997**: the version in force today was not retrieved. I only found "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf" (version 110, in force 6 Aug 2025 to 24 Nov 2025) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) and "rta-1997-v097-2021-03-28.pdf" (version 097, 28 March 2021) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa097%20authorised.pdf). Both are out of date for today. I use them only as background and flag where I do.

**What the law says (current Regulations, version 009)**
- The standard rental agreement summary says the rental provider must carry out urgent repairs after being notified. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- A renter may arrange urgent repairs if they have taken reasonable steps to get the rental provider to do them immediately and the provider has not carried them out. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- The renter may be reimbursed directly by the rental provider for the reasonable cost of repairs, up to $2500. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- The same summary says only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, urgent or non-urgent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

**Is a broken tap an "urgent repair"?**
The current definition wasn't retrieved. The 2021 Act (version 097) lists, among others, a burst water service, a failure or breakdown of the water supply to the premises, and a water-using fitting malfunctioning so that a substantial amount of water is wasted. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa097%20authorised.pdf) Your situation may fit one of these, but I can't confirm it under today's Act.

**What you can do or ask**
1. **Put it in writing now.** Tell the rental provider or agent that the water is off and ask for an immediate repair. The 2025 Act (version 110, not current) requires written notice of breakdowns as soon as practicable [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Written notice also helps show you took reasonable steps.
2. **If it still isn't done**, you can arrange the repair yourself using a suitably qualified person, as above. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) The documents say nothing on whether the owner can insist on using only their own tradespeople. That policy doesn't appear in the text I found, so I can't say it overrides your right to arrange the repair.
3. **Afterwards**, under the 2025 Act (version 110, not confirmed as current), you must give 7 days' written notice of the repairs and their cost. The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days of that notice. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
4. **If you can't pay, the cost is over $2500, or the provider refuses to pay**, you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring the provider to carry out the urgent repairs. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) Under version 110, VCAT must hear such an application within 2 business days. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

**Not covered:** the documents don't define "reasonable steps" or say how many contact attempts are enough. I also couldn't retrieve today's version of the Act itself, so please check it, or Consumer Affairs Victoria, before you spend money.

must-mention.reason: No. The point that the preferred-tradesperson policy is a prohibited term (reg 11(e)) and cannot stop an urgent repair is missing: the answer says only that "The documents say nothing on whether the owner can insist on using only their own tradespeople... so I can't say it overrides your right," which leaves a reader unable to tell which way the point falls.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer asserts neither failure condition; it says "You may not have to keep waiting" and "I can't say it overrides your right to arrange the repair," and that the renter "may be reimbursed directly by the rental provider for the reasonable cost of repairs, up to $2500."

question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. I haven't moved any of my things in or stayed there yet. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
## What the law says

The version in force today (9 November 2026) is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file **rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf**, in force from 13 October 2026 with no end date shown [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Its metadata gives the version number as 115. The retrieved text doesn't print an "Authorised Version No." label, so I can't confirm that wording. Only the termination provisions below were retrieved from this version.

- **Cancelling before you move in.** A residential rental agreement terminates if you haven't entered into possession and you give the provider a notice of termination on the ground that the premises:
  - are not in good repair,
  - are unfit for human habitation,
  - do not meet any rental minimum standards, or
  - are for any other reason unavailable for occupation [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 91L).
- **Unfit for habitation.** A renter may also give a notice of intention to vacate if the premises are unfit for human habitation or destroyed or unsafe. The termination date can be the date of the notice or a later date [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 91ZD).
- **No break fee under the standard agreement.** The standard-form agreement says the provider cannot claim rent foregone if you end the agreement through a s 91ZD notice on the "unfit for habitation" basis [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) (*Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, version 009, in force from 30 June 2026).
- **Provider's duties.** The standard agreement states that the provider must ensure the premises meet the rental minimum standards when you move in. It also states that the provider must maintain the premises in good repair and in a fit condition for occupation [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do

**1. Cancel the agreement.**
- Section 91L is the closest fit. It is available only because you haven't taken possession, so avoid moving in or staying there [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- "Not in good repair" and "unfit for human habitation" are separate grounds. You don't need to prove the house is uninhabitable to use the first one [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The retrieved text doesn't say what form the notice must take or how much notice is needed. Put it in writing and attach photos.
- The documents also don't say whether damp, mould and rotting timber breach the rental minimum standards. The content of those standards wasn't retrieved.

**2. Ask for repairs.**
- These repair provisions come from older versions of the Act. I did not retrieve them from v115, so check they haven't changed.
- Under v111 (in force 25 Nov 2025 to 29 Jun 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) and v110 (from 6 Aug 2025) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf):
  - You give the provider written notice that repairs are needed.
  - If they aren't done within 14 days, you can apply to the Director to investigate, or to VCAT [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (ss 74–75).
  - VCAT must hear a non-urgent repairs application within 7 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
  - VCAT can order specified repairs by a suitably qualified person, with a deadline and compensation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 76).
- The standard agreement also says you can go to VCAT if non-urgent repairs aren't done within 14 days of notice [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- v110 also says the provider must ensure the premises meet the rental minimum standards on or before the day you enter into occupation [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 65A).
- The documents don't say whether your problems count as "urgent repairs". The definition wasn't retrieved.

**3. Ask for lower rent.**
- The retrieved documents contain **no provision allowing a rent reduction** for damp, mould or rot.
- The closest tools are in the older versions:
  - **No rent until you enter.** If the premises aren't vacant and reasonably clean on the agreed day, you don't pay rent from that day until you actually enter [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 65(3)). It covers only vacancy and cleanliness, so it may not apply to damp or rot.
  - **Rent Special Account.** After you've given repair notice and the provider hasn't done the repairs, you can apply to VCAT to pay rent into this account [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 77). The provider can resist by showing financial hardship [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). I haven't confirmed this section in v115.

## Gaps
I did not retrieve the rental minimum standards or the definition of "urgent repairs". I also didn't retrieve v115 text for the repair provisions or the rent provisions. For a firm answer on your situation, check the current text of these with Consumer Affairs Victoria or VCAT.

must-mention.reason: No: the point that the rental minimum standards include a mould and damp standard is missing. The output does say the s 65A standards must be met "on or before the day you enter into occupation", but it states "The documents also don't say whether damp, mould and rotting timber breach the rental minimum standards," so it never says those standards cover mould and damp linked to the building structure.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. Neither banned claim is made: the answer tells the renter to 'avoid moving in or staying there' to keep the s 91L cancellation option, and states 'The retrieved documents contain no provision allowing a rent reduction for damp, mould or rot', framing the Rent Special Account as something the renter can 'apply to VCAT' for, which is a Tribunal order and is permitted.

version-cited.reason: No. The answer correctly names the Act as 'version number as 115' (rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf) and the Regulations as 'version 009', but it presents the repair process (ss 74–76) and the Rent Special Account (s 77) as steps the user can take, citing 'v111 (in force 25 Nov 2025 to 29 Jun 2026)' and 'v110 (from 6 Aug 2025)', which were not in force on 9 November 2026, and deleting that material would remove most of the repairs and rent options, so the answer relies on non-current versions.

question: Our rental was broken into several times while we were moving out, and there are about three weeks left on our fixed-term lease. The burglars damaged the plumbing and wiring, so we can't even clean properly. What are our options before the lease ends?
answer:
**Documents applied:** the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", Version 115, in force from 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). For the standard-form terms I used the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (file "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf", Version 009, in force from 30 June 2026) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). These are the versions in force today, 9 November 2026. The excerpts don't show an "Authorised Version" label, so the version numbers come from the document metadata.

## What the law says

- **Unfit or unsafe premises:** A renter may give a notice of intention to vacate if the premises are unfit for human habitation, or have been destroyed totally or to such an extent as to be rendered unsafe. The termination date can be the day you give the notice or any later date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 91ZD).
- **Ordinary notice doesn't help here:** A normal notice of intention to vacate needs at least 28 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 91Z). On a fixed term, it has no effect if it ends the agreement before the end of the term [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 91ZA). With about three weeks left, that route adds nothing.
- **Landlord's duties:** The rental provider must keep the premises in good repair and in a fit condition for occupation [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) (cl 26). The rental provider must also carry out urgent repairs after being notified [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) (cl 30).
- **Your duties:** You must notify the rental provider in writing of damage to the premises, and keep the premises reasonably clean [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) (cl 25).

## What you can do or ask

1. **Notify the rental provider in writing now.** Describe the burglaries and the plumbing and wiring damage [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) (cl 25, 31).
2. **Request repairs.**
   - Urgent repairs: the rental provider must act once notified. If you've taken reasonable steps to get the rental provider to do them immediately and they haven't, you may arrange them. You can be reimbursed the reasonable cost up to $2500. You can apply to VCAT if you can't meet the cost, the cost is over $2500, or the rental provider refuses to pay [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) (cl 30).
   - Non-urgent repairs: you can apply to VCAT if they aren't done within 14 days of notice [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) (cl 31).
   - Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, so don't fix the plumbing or wiring yourselves [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) (cl 29).
3. **Consider ending the tenancy early under s 91ZD.** This is only available if the premises are truly unfit for habitation or unsafe, which depends on the facts. Damaged plumbing and wiring may support it, but the documents don't say whether this damage qualifies [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You can name the same day or a later date. Keep photos and any tradesperson's report.
4. **Expect a possible notice from the other side.** The rental provider has the same ground and can also give notice to vacate for unfit or unsafe premises, effective the same day or later [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 91ZL).
5. **Repeated break-ins and locks.** The rental provider must ensure the premises have window locks and deadlocks that meet the rental minimum standards [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) (cl 28). A separate right to end a fixed term applies only after the rental provider has breached the same duty three times, with breach of duty notices given on the two earlier occasions [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 91ZF).

## What the documents don't answer

- Whether the plumbing and wiring damage counts as an "urgent repair". The regulations point to the Act's definition in s 3(1), which isn't in the retrieved text [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- Whether you owe any lease-break compensation if you end the tenancy under s 91ZD. The retrieved text of s 91ZD is silent on this [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Who is liable for the burglary damage, or how your bond or cleaning obligations are affected when you can't clean because of the damage.
- Any hardship application to VCAT. I only found s 91U in a 2019 version, not the current one, so I can't confirm it applies today.

For those points, I'd suggest getting advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy advice service.

question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. The app is run by a payments company my agent uses, and it's that company that charges the card fee. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
**Short answer:** Under the current Act, the app company can't safely charge you the card fee just because a free option exists. Section 51(3) and section 51A are separate prohibitions. Whether this particular card fee breaches them depends on a point the documents don't settle (see "What the documents don't answer").

**Source used:** *rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf*, the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Version 115, in force from 13 October 2026. I take this as the current version, since it is the latest in the documents. The search tool also failed twice on my follow-up searches, so I could not retrieve the regulations on prescribed fees.

## What the law says

- **A free method must be reasonably available.** The provider or their agent must ensure a rent payment method with no additional costs, other than your own bank or account fees, is reasonably available to you. The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person and 400 for a body corporate (s 42(4)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Your free bank transfer may satisfy this. The Act doesn't say whether a slower method still counts as "reasonably available", so I can't say.
- **Fees must be disclosed first.** The provider or agent must tell you about costs you may incur by using a payment method, including third party transaction fees and other electronic payment facility fees. They must do this before you consent to that method (s 42(7)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Some charges are banned outright.** A person must not demand or receive a charge from a renter for the first issue of a rent payment card. Nor can they charge for the establishment or use of direct debit or "any other electronic payment facility for payment of rent". The penalty is 60 penalty units (s 51(3)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Rent payment fees can be banned by regulation.** A person, other than an ADI (authorised deposit-taking institution, i.e. a bank-type lender), must not demand or receive a fee for any "prescribed matter" in relation to the payment of rent. The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person and 400 for a body corporate (s 51A) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Does it matter who receives the fee?

- **For ss 51(3) and 51A, the wording is not limited to the agent.** Both apply to "a person" who demands or receives the fee [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A payments company collecting the fee is therefore not outside them just because it isn't the agent.
- **Section 51A's current wording is wider than before.** Version 111 (*rta-1997-v111-2025-11-25.pdf*, in force 25 November 2025 to 29 June 2026) excluded residential rental providers and their agents. It also excluded ADIs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Version 115 says only "a person, other than an ADI", and notes that s 51A was substituted by No. 46/2025 s 13 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If the app company is an ADI, s 51A would not apply to it. Section 51(3), as printed, has no ADI exception [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Sections 42(4) and 42(7) bind only the provider and the agent.** They don't bind the app company directly [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). They still apply to your agent, because the agent chose the app.

## What the documents don't answer

- **Whether a card surcharge is a banned fee.** I couldn't retrieve the regulations that list the "prescribed matters" under s 51A. The regulations I did retrieve (*rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf*) were only forms [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The Act also doesn't say whether a card surcharge is a charge for using an "electronic payment facility" under s 51(3) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I can't confirm either way.
- **Remedies.** The documents I retrieved don't cover refunds or complaint processes.

## What you can do

1. **Ask your agent in writing** to confirm the fee-free method that is reasonably available to you. Ask them also to disclose all the app's fees (s 42(4), (7)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Use the free bank transfer** to avoid the card fee. It is slower, so pay early.
3. **Query the card fee itself.** Ask the agent or the app company to explain why it is lawful given ss 51(3) and 51A, and ask for it to be removed or refunded if they can't. Whether it must be removed turns on the unresolved point above.

must-mention.reason: No. The second point is missing: the answer correctly says s 51A applies to 'a person, other than an ADI', so it doesn't matter who collects the fee. But it does not state that rent payment fees are banned. It says 'Whether a card surcharge is a banned fee... I can't confirm either way', which leaves the reader unable to tell which way the ban falls.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer rejects the first point, stating the company "can't safely charge you the card fee just because a free option exists", and it attributes the agent exemption only to the earlier version ("Version 111 ... excluded residential rental providers and their agents"), noting that the current Version 115 applies to "a person, other than an ADI".

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Act as "Version 115" (rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf) and the Regulations as "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf" (link 21-3sra009), both in-force versions, and it cites Version 111 only to show that s 51A was different earlier, without relying on it for any rule it applies.

question: My lease is on the standard form and started in 2024. It has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. I cleaned them myself and they're back to how they were when I moved in, but the agent wants a receipt from a professional cleaner. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?
answer:
## What the law says

**Document and version:** The *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, version 115 (file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", in force from 13 October 2026), is the latest version I retrieved. It has no end date, so I treat it as the one in force today [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

- A residential rental agreement must not include a term requiring professional cleaning, or requiring the renter to pay for it, unless that term is in the standard form [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- A prohibited term is void and unenforceable [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The standard form can only carry a prescribed term. That term applies if professional cleaning becomes required to restore the premises to their condition at the start of the tenancy, taking fair wear and tear into account [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**Regulations:** The prescribed wording is in regulation 12 of the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*. The provider must not require professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy unless one of two things applies:
- (a) Professional cleaning was done immediately before the tenancy started, and the renter was told so.
- (b) Professional cleaning is needed to restore the premises to their starting condition, "having regard to the condition report and taking into account fair wear and tear" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

The standard form repeats this in its professional cleaning clause [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Its pet clause only says the renter must get consent and that the provider must not unreasonably refuse [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). It says nothing about carpet cleaning.

**Caveat on the Regulations:** The retrieved versions are v002 (1 June 2022 to 30 November 2024) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf) and v004 (1 July 2025 to 24 November 2025) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). I did not retrieve a version in force today. Regulation 12 reads the same in both. I can't confirm the current wording from these documents. Also, my second search failed, so I did not look for anything beyond these.

**What this means for you:** Your pet clause is an additional term, not part of the standard form. As you describe it, a blanket "professionally clean the carpets" requirement looks like a prohibited term, and so would be void and unenforceable [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I haven't seen your exact wording, so check it. Even without that, the standard-form test is about condition, not receipts. If the carpets are back to their starting condition, professional cleaning isn't "required" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

One exception to check: if the premises were professionally cleaned just before you moved in and you were told, the provider can require professional cleaning (a) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do

- **Put it in writing.** Tell the agent that the carpets are in the same condition as at move-in, and that under regulation 12 and section 27B a receipt can't be demanded [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Challenge the term.** A renter may apply to the Tribunal (VCAT) to have a term declared invalid or varied if it is harsh or unconscionable [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What helps show the carpets' condition

The condition report form (Form 4) says:
- **Keep your copy.** It helps resolve cleaning disputes at the end of the tenancy [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Take photos.** They should be taken at the beginning and at the end of the tenancy, be dated and labelled, show the room, and include close-ups and wider shots [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Check your move-in comments and photos.** Floor coverings are an item the condition report lists [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Renters can add comments and photos against each item [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Attend the final inspection.** The agent must complete the end-of-tenancy inspection and report within 10 days after the agreement ends. They must give you an opportunity to attend if possible. They must also allow for fair wear and tear, which isn't damage caused by the renter [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

The documents I retrieved don't cover whether a cleaning receipt or other evidence would be accepted at VCAT. They also don't cover how a bond dispute would proceed.

must-mention.reason: No. The answer never states the renter's own duty under s 63 to leave the premises reasonably clean and in the same condition as at the start, fair wear and tear excepted. It mentions fair wear and tear only in the context of reg 12 and the end-of-tenancy inspection, so the second point is missing.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the renter must pay simply because of the clause or the pet; it says the opposite: 'a blanket "professionally clean the carpets" requirement looks like a prohibited term, and so would be void and unenforceable' and 'If the carpets are back to their starting condition, professional cleaning isn't "required"'.

version-cited.reason: No. The answer correctly names the Act as 'version 115' (97-109aa115), but it never names Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 Authorised Version No. 009. Instead it applies regulation 12, the standard form and the Form 4 condition report guidance from 'v002 (1 June 2022 to 30 November 2024)' and 'v004 (1 July 2025 to 24 November 2025)', which were not in force on that date. It presents these as the law and as steps the user can take, despite a caveat, and deleting that material would change the answer's substance.

question: When I moved out I agreed the agent could take an amount for cleaning out of my bond, but I never signed a bond claim form for it. Then my full bond came back to me, and a month later the agent sent a separate invoice for the cleaning. Do I have to pay it? Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?
answer:
## Which document applies

Today (9 November 2026) the applicable text is **rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf**, the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, in force from 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Its metadata gives the version as **115**. The retrieved pages don't include the cover page, so I can't quote an "Authorised Version No." line from it. Treat "115" as the version number shown in the file's metadata.

## What the law says

- **Cleaning is a proper bond deduction.** A provider (which includes the agent) may claim from the bond the reasonable cost of cleaning if the premises weren't left reasonably clean. This is judged against the condition at the start of the tenancy [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **A bond claim must be made on a form.** The claim must be in a form approved by the Bond Authority [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A joint claim by provider and renter for repayment of bond to the provider is one of the permitted routes [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Safeguards on the form.** The provider must not request or obtain your signature on a claim form that doesn't state the amount of bond to be refunded and how it is apportioned. The penalty is 60 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Evidence.** At least 3 days before a claim for repayment of bond to the provider is made, the provider or agent must give each renter bond claim evidence. That evidence must not conflict with a statement in a condition report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Your two questions

**Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?**
The documents don't say. They only set out the bond-claim process above. That process runs through a signed or approved form and the Authority [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You never signed a claim form, and the full bond was returned to you. These facts don't match the bond-claim route. But the retrieved text doesn't say whether your agreement to a deduction could also support a separate invoice.

**Do you have to pay the invoice?**
The retrieved documents don't answer this. They don't cover a cleaning charge billed after the bond has been refunded in full. I won't guess beyond that.

One related point comes from an older version only. Version 110 (in force 6 August 2025 to 24 November 2025) says a tenancy agreement can't require the renter to pay for professional cleaning unless the term is in the standard form. It also allows a prescribed standard-form term where professional cleaning is needed to restore the premises to their starting condition, allowing for fair wear and tear [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). I can't confirm that wording appears in version 115, because the retrieved pages of 115 don't include those sections.

## What you can do

- **Ask the agent in writing** for the basis of the charge: the amount, the cleaning evidence, and the condition report comparison. The evidence rules above apply to bond claims [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), so this is a reasonable thing to ask for.
- **Check your agreement and condition report.** See whether there is a professional-cleaning term and whether the premises were left reasonably clean compared with the start of the tenancy [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Don't treat the invoice as settled just because you agreed to a deduction.** The documents give no basis for that.
- **Get tenancy advice before paying or ignoring it.** The retrieved documents don't cover the law on a post-refund debt claim. The Tribunal application for a bond order (s 419A) must be made within 14 days after the tenancy ended [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and your bond has already been repaid.

question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. I've called them twice today. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
## What the law says

I used the versions in force today (9 November 2026):
- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997**, file *rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf*, version 115, in force from 13 October 2026 [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021**, file *rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf*, version 009, in force from 30 June 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**You don't have to wait indefinitely.** Under section 72 of the Act, a renter may arrange urgent repairs if both of these are true [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf):
1. You have taken reasonable steps to get the rental provider (or their agent) to carry out the repairs immediately.
2. You are unable to get them to carry out the repairs.

The regulations' standard form says the same. It also says the rental provider must carry out urgent repairs after being notified [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do

1. **Notify the provider or agent in writing now.** You must give written notice as soon as practicable of a breakdown of facilities or fixtures the provider supplied [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Written notice also helps show you took "reasonable steps".
2. **If they still can't act, arrange the repair yourself.** The regulations say only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, urgent or not [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Use a qualified tradesperson rather than doing it yourself.
3. **Give written notice of the repair and its cost.** You must give the provider 7 days' written notice of the repairs carried out and the cost [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Claim reimbursement.** The provider is liable for the reasonable cost, or any greater prescribed amount, whichever is less. This includes GST, and they must pay within 7 days of receiving your written notice [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The regulations' form summary says reimbursement is up to $2500 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
5. **Go to VCAT if needed.** You can apply for an order requiring the urgent repairs if you can't meet the cost, the cost is over the prescribed amount, or the provider refuses to pay [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The form states that amount as $2500 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). VCAT must hear the application within 2 business days [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't answer

- **"Owner only uses their own tradespeople."** Nothing I retrieved says a provider can limit repairs to their own tradespeople. Section 72 turns on whether you took reasonable steps and couldn't get the repair done [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether two calls in one day, with the provider saying no one is available yet, is enough. I can't say how a tribunal would see that.
- **Whether a broken tap counts as "urgent".** The definition of "urgent repairs" is in section 3(1), and that section isn't in the current Act text I retrieved. The 2021 version (*rta-1997-v097-2021-03-28.pdf*, version 097, dated 28 March 2021) lists a "burst water service", a failure or breakdown of water supply, and a water-using fitting malfunctioning so that a substantial amount of water is wasted [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa097%20authorised.pdf). That is an old version, so I can't confirm the current wording from these documents. Check section 3(1) of version 115 before relying on it.
