question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. I haven't moved any of my things in or stayed there yet. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
**Document applied:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", in force from 13 October 2026 and the version current today [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Its metadata labels it version 115. The excerpts I retrieved don't print an "Authorised Version No." line, so that number comes from the metadata only.

## What the law says

- **Provider's duties.** The provider must keep the premises in good repair and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation. This applies even if you knew of the disrepair before moving in [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Minimum standards.** The provider must make sure the premises meet the prescribed rental minimum standards on or before the day you enter occupation [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The regulation text I retrieved for those standards is from an earlier version, *rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf* (in force 1 July to 24 November 2025). It says the premises must be "structurally sound and weatherproof" and that "each room … must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). The current regulations (*rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf*) were retrieved only for the forms section, so I can't confirm the wording in force today [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs.** "Urgent repairs" includes a failure to comply with rental minimum standards. It also includes any fault or damage that makes the premises unsafe, including "the presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Day of occupation.** The provider must make sure the premises are vacant and reasonably clean on the agreed day. You aren't required to move into premises that fail this, and you don't pay rent from the agreed day until you actually move in [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). That section mentions only vacancy and cleanliness. It doesn't mention damp, mould or rot, so whether this rent-free rule applies to your situation isn't clear from the documents.

## What you can do

**1. Ask for repairs**
- Give the provider or agent written notice of the problem. A renter must give written notice of damage as soon as practicable [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs:** The provider can be asked to fix urgent repairs. If you take reasonable steps and can't get them done, you can arrange the repairs yourself and give 7 days' written notice of the work and its cost. The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days of that notice [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If you can't afford the repairs, or the provider refuses to pay, you can apply to VCAT, which must hear the application within 2 business days [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Non-urgent repairs:** If the provider hasn't done the work within 14 days of your written notice, you can apply to the Director (Consumer Affairs Victoria) to investigate. You can also apply to VCAT, which must hear the application within 7 days [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- VCAT can order specified repairs by a suitably qualified person and award compensation [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The Act says a renter "may issue a request" for urgent repairs under the minimum-standards section if premises don't comply "on or immediately after" the day you enter occupation [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You haven't moved in, so check with Consumer Affairs Victoria or VCAT whether you can use that route yet.

**2. Cancel the lease**
- **Current Act:** In the current Act I found only s 91ZD. It lets a renter give a notice of intention to vacate if the premises are "unfit for human habitation" or destroyed or unsafe, and the termination date can be the date of the notice [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Whether your damp, mould and rot meet "unfit for human habitation" isn't answered by the documents.
- **Earlier text:** An earlier document, *rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf* (in force 2 July to 3 December 2019), contains a "termination by renter before possession" rule. It applies where you haven't entered into possession and give notice because the premises are not in good repair, are unfit for habitation or don't meet minimum standards [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). That text appears only in the 2019 version. I did not find it in the current version, so I can't say it applies today. I wouldn't rely on it without checking.

**3. Ask for lower rent**
- I found no provision in the retrieved documents that gives a general right to a rent reduction. The related rent provisions are:
  - **No rent before you move in:** If the premises fail the vacant-and-clean duty, you don't pay rent until you move in (above) [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
  - **Rent Special Account:** After you give notice requiring repairs, you can apply to VCAT to pay your rent into the Rent Special Account. VCAT must order this if the provider hasn't done the repairs and hasn't shown financial hardship [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Any other rent reduction would have to be agreed with the provider. The documents don't cover the details of VCAT compensation under s 212.

## Next steps
Document the problems with photos and the condition report, and send your notice in writing. Check with VCAT or Consumer Affairs Victoria before you give any notice to end the lease.

must-mention.reason: No. The s 91L point is missing because the answer hedges it too far: it says the 'termination by renter before possession' rule 'appears only in the 2019 version… so I can't say it applies today. I wouldn't rely on it without checking.' A reader therefore cannot tell that a renter who has not taken possession can currently end the agreement by notice for failure to meet minimum standards, disrepair or unfitness. The other two points are adequately covered: s 65A minimum standards, including mould and damp, must be met by the day of occupation, and both the urgent repair and good-repair routes are described.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the renter must move in and pay rent before acting, and it never claims a legal right to lower rent; it says "I found no provision in the retrieved documents that gives a general right to a rent reduction" and "Any other rent reduction would have to be agreed with the provider."

version-cited.reason: No. The answer names both required documents, 'rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf' (version 115) and 'rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf', but it applies rules from versions not in force on the date. It quotes the minimum-standards wording ('structurally sound and weatherproof', 'free from mould and damp') from Regulations version 004, 'rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf'. It also presents the 'termination by renter before possession' rule from Act version 088, 'rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf', as a possible way to cancel. The caveats do not change this, and deleting that material would change the substance of the answer.

question: Our rental was broken into several times while we were moving out, and there are about three weeks left on our fixed-term lease. The burglars damaged the plumbing and wiring, so we can't even clean properly. What are our options before the lease ends?
answer:
**Short answer:** If the burglary damage makes the premises unfit to live in or unsafe, you can give notice and leave early without waiting for the lease to end. Whether the damage reaches that level is a factual question the documents can't settle.

**Which version I used.** The version in force today (9 November 2026) is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", Version 115, in force from 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The retrieved text doesn't print the words "Authorised Version No." The number 115 comes from the document's metadata and file name. The current regulations I found are the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf", Version 009, in force from 30 June 2026 [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). I didn't retrieve any later versions.

## What the law says

- **Leaving early because of the condition of the premises (s 91ZD).** A renter may give the rental provider a notice of intention to vacate if the premises are unfit for human habitation, or have been destroyed totally or to such an extent as to be rendered unsafe [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Timing.** The notice can give the day you send it, or a later date, as the termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). That means no 28-day wait.
- **Why the usual route doesn't fit.** In a fixed-term lease, an ordinary notice that ends the lease before the term ends is of no effect [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The usual notice period is 28 days. That wording is not in the v115 excerpt. It appears in earlier versions, such as Version 110 (6 August 2025) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Either way, with about three weeks left, s 91ZD is the relevant route.
- **Lease break fees.** The regulations' form for agreements of more than 5 years says no "rent foregone" is payable if the renter ends the agreement under s 91ZD [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). I did not find the equivalent clause for the standard form. Check your own agreement.

## What you can do or ask for

1. **Report the damage in writing now.** The regulations' summary of renter duties says a renter must notify the rental provider in writing when damage occurs [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The Act's own duty is s 72AA, but I only found it in Version 111 (25 November 2025) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Include the plumbing and wiring damage and the break-ins.
2. **Ask for urgent repairs.** The summary says urgent repairs include failure of essential services. The rental provider must carry them out after being notified [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
   - You may arrange them yourself if you've taken reasonable steps to get the provider to act and they haven't. You can then be reimbursed the reasonable cost up to $2500 [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
   - You can apply to VCAT if you can't meet the cost, the cost is over $2500, or the provider refuses to pay [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
   - Only a suitably qualified person may do the repairs [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
   - The Act's sections on this (ss 72–73) appear in the documents only in Version 111 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), which is not the current version. I couldn't confirm the wording in Version 115.
3. **Consider a s 91ZD notice** if the premises are genuinely unfit or unsafe, for example because the plumbing and wiring faults make them uninhabitable. You could give it for the day you send it or a later date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Non-urgent repairs.** You can apply to VCAT if the provider hasn't done them within 14 days of notice [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't cover

- The documents don't say who is liable for burglary damage, or what happens to your bond.
- They don't say how the cleaning obligation works when you can't clean because of third-party damage. The regulations' form says a renter must keep the premises reasonably clean and pay for professional cleaning only if it is needed to restore the premises to their starting condition, allowing for fair wear and tear [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- They don't say whether your premises meet the "unfit" or "unsafe" test.
- I found no mention of insurance or police reports.

For a firm answer on those points, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria or VCAT.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. Point 1: the answer says to 'Report the damage in writing now' and cites the written-notice duty (s 72AA). Point 2 is the hardest: the answer says to 'Ask for urgent repairs' for the plumbing and wiring damage and that 'the rental provider must carry them out after being notified', and adds that the renter may arrange them and 'be reimbursed the reasonable cost up to $2500'. Point 3: under s 91ZD, a renter in a fixed-term lease may give notice if the premises are 'unfit for human habitation' or 'rendered unsafe', with 'the day you send it' as the termination date.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer asserts neither forbidden claim. It says the renter "can give notice and leave early without waiting for the lease to end" under s 91ZD, and it says the rental provider "must carry them out" for urgent repairs, with self-arranged repairs offered only as a reimbursable option ("be reimbursed the reasonable cost up to $2500").

version-cited.reason: Yes: the answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as "Version 115, in force from 13 October 2026" (file rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf, link 97-109aa115) and draws its rules from v115 and the in-force Regulations "Version 009"; its mentions of Version 110 (the 28-day period) and Version 111 (ss 72AA, 72–73) only add detail, since removing them leaves the answer's substance unchanged.

question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. The app is run by a payments company my agent uses, and it's that company that charges the card fee. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
**Document used:** *rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf*, the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, in force from 13 October 2026 with no end date shown [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Its metadata gives the version as 115. I found no later version. The retrieved text doesn't show a separate "Authorised Version No." label, so I'm relying on that metadata.

## What the law says

- **A fee-free method must be available.** The agent must ensure a rent payment method with no additional costs is reasonably available to you. Your own bank or account fees don't count as additional costs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Your free bank transfer option may satisfy this. The Act doesn't say whether "slower" affects whether it is "reasonably available".
- **Fees must be disclosed first.** The agent must tell you about costs you may incur by using a payment method before you consent to it. The Act expressly lists "third party transaction fees" and "any other electronic payment facility fees" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This suggests some third-party fees are contemplated, as long as they are disclosed.
- **Some charges are prohibited.** A person must not demand or receive from a renter a charge for "the establishment or use of direct debit facilities or any other electronic payment facility for payment of rent". The penalty is 60 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Some payment fees are also banned.** A person other than an ADI must not demand or receive a fee for any *prescribed matter* in relation to the payment of rent. The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person and 400 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Does it matter who gets the fee?

On the wording, probably not.

- The ban on charges for electronic payment facilities applies to "a person", not just the agent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The same is true of the fee ban [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A payments company is therefore not obviously outside them.
- The fee ban exempts an "ADI" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The retrieved text doesn't define that term, so I can't say whether your app company falls within the exemption.
- The disclosure and fee-free-method duties are placed on the rental provider and their agent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The agent can't avoid them by using a third-party app.

## What the documents don't answer

- **Is a card surcharge banned?** The documents don't say whether a card fee is a charge for an "electronic payment facility". They also don't say whether it is a "prescribed matter" under the fee ban. The retrieved Regulations extract (version 009, in force from 30 June 2026) only notes that the provider must permit at least one fee-free payment method [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). It doesn't list prescribed matters. So I can't say definitively that the app may or may not charge you.
- **Does the fee-free option cure the problem?** The Act doesn't say that offering a fee-free alternative makes a card fee lawful under the prohibition on charges for electronic payment facilities.

## What you can do

1. Ask the agent, in writing, to disclose the card fee and confirm that the fee-free bank transfer is a compliant method. Disclosure before you consent is required [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. Don't consent to card payments if you don't want the fee. Pay by the fee-free method, which the agent must keep reasonably available [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. If you think the fee is prohibited, raise it with the agent, naming the provisions on electronic payment facility charges and rent payment fees [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). For a definitive view, seek advice from a tenancy advocate or Consumer Affairs Victoria. The retrieved documents don't cover that.

must-mention.reason: No: the answer misses the second point. It says the fee ban applies to 'a person other than an ADI', but it leaves open whether a card fee is a banned 'prescribed matter' ('I can't say definitively that the app may or may not charge you'). That is hedged too far to state that rent-payment fees are banned whoever collects them, and it never identifies reg 21C or the surcharge-under-another-law exception. The first point (a fee-free method must be reasonably available) and the third point (next steps such as using the fee-free method or contacting Consumer Affairs Victoria) are covered.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer does not claim either failure condition: it states that "The Act doesn't say that offering a fee-free alternative makes a card fee lawful," and that the fee ban applies to "a person" with only an "ADI" exempt, never saying the landlord or agent is exempt.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as 'rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf' (link 97-109aa115) and the Regulations as 'version 009, in force from 30 June 2026' (link 21-3sra009), both in-force versions, and relies on no other version.

question: My lease is on the standard form and started in 2024. It has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. I cleaned them myself and they're back to how they were when I moved in, but the agent wants a receipt from a professional cleaner. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?
answer:
## What the law says

I checked the Act in force today, which is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Version 115, in force from 13 October 2026** [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The only Regulations I retrieved are older. See the caveat at the end.

- **Professional cleaning terms are restricted.** An agreement must not include a term requiring professional cleaning, or requiring the renter to pay for it, unless that term is in the standard form [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Prohibited terms are void.** If an agreement contains a prohibited term, that term is void and unenforceable [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The standard form only allows a conditional cleaning term.** It allows professional cleaning only if it "becomes required to restore the premises to the condition they were in immediately before the start of the tenancy, taking into account fair wear and tear" [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The prescribed wording matches.** Regulation 12 says the rental provider must not require professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy unless one of two things applies:
  - (a) professional cleaning was done before the tenancy started and the renter was told so; or
  - (b) it is needed to restore the premises to their starting condition, "having regard to the condition report and taking into account fair wear and tear" [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

  The standard form (Form 1, clause 11) repeats this wording [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

## Applying it to you

On these documents, a pet clause that flatly requires professional carpet cleaning goes further than the standard form allows. That is my reading of how the sections apply, not something the documents say about pet clauses specifically.

If the carpets are in the same condition as when you moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear, professional cleaning is not "required". The renter's obligation to have premises professionally cleaned or to pay for it only arises if it becomes required [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). So you should not have to pay for a professional clean.

The documents don't say anything specific about receipts. They also don't say whether you can refuse one. They only say when professional cleaning can be required.

## What you can do

1. **Ask the agent in writing** which part of the condition report shows the carpets need professional cleaning. The test refers to the condition report and fair wear and tear [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
2. **Use evidence of the carpets' condition.** The condition report form (Form 4) in the older Regulations I retrieved says [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf):
   - Keep the condition report. It "will help to resolve disputes over cleaning, damage, safety or missing items."
   - Take photos at the start and end of the tenancy.
   - Photos should be dated, labelled and show the room. Take close-ups for detail and wider shots for perspective.
   - Compare against your own entry or comments on the start-of-tenancy report. Renters fill in and return it within 5 business days of moving in.
   - Use the final inspection. The agent must complete it within 10 days after the agreement ends and give you a chance to attend. It must allow for fair wear and tear.
3. **Challenge the term.** A renter may apply to the Tribunal (VCAT) for an order declaring a term invalid or varying it if it is harsh or unconscionable [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Caveat

I did not retrieve a version of the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 in force today. The latest was Version 004, in force from 1 July 2025 to 24 November 2025 [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). I also saw Version 002, in force from 1 June 2022 to 30 November 2024 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf), which may cover the start of your 2024 lease. The photo and inspection guidance above comes from Version 002 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Check the current Regulations, and your own lease, before relying on it.

must-mention.reason: No. The answer is missing the s 63 point: it never says the renter must leave the premises reasonably clean and in the same condition as at the start, fair wear and tear excepted. It does cover reg 12 ('professional cleaning was done before the tenancy started and the renter was told so; or... needed to restore the premises to their starting condition') and the condition report as evidence. It also says the carpets need not be professionally cleaned if they match their starting condition, but it frames that only as a limit on the cleaning term, not as the renter's general end-of-tenancy duty.

question: When I moved out I agreed the agent could take an amount for cleaning out of my bond, but I never signed a bond claim form for it. Then my full bond came back to me, and a month later the agent sent a separate invoice for the cleaning. Do I have to pay it? Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents don't say whether you have to pay the invoice. They also don't say whether agreeing to a bond deduction is the same as agreeing to pay an invoice. What they do cover is how the bond-claim process works.

I used the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 115 (file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). It is the latest version in the documents, so I treated it as the law in force today (9 November 2026).

## What the Act says

- **Cleaning can be claimed from a bond.** A provider (which includes an agent) may claim from the bond "the reasonable cost of cleaning any part of the premises, if the premises were not left reasonably clean by the renter". This is judged against the condition of the premises when the agreement started [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Bond claims follow a set process.**
  - A claim to the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority "must be in a form approved by the Authority" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
  - If the claim is made jointly by provider and renter, the Authority must repay the bond as claimed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
  - A provider must not request or obtain a renter's signature on a claim form unless it specifies the amount of bond to be refunded and any apportionment. The penalty is 60 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Evidence is required for bond claims.** At least 3 days before a claim for repayment of bond to the provider is made, the provider must give each renter "bond claim evidence" supporting it. That means an invoice, receipt, quote, photograph or other prescribed evidence. The evidence must not conflict with the condition report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What this means for you

- The Act treats a bond deduction as something done through the approved claim process. Your agreement to a deduction was informal, and no claim form was signed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The agent then refunded the full bond. The retrieved text says nothing about whether an agent can bill you separately for cleaning after the bond has been repaid. It also says nothing about whether an informal agreement to a deduction creates a debt outside the bond. I can't say either way without guessing.

## What you can do or ask

- **Ask the agent in writing** what the invoice is based on. Ask for the supporting evidence (invoice, receipt, quote or photos) and for a comparison against the condition report. The Act requires that evidence for bond claims, and the cleaning cost must be "reasonable" and judged against the condition at the start of the tenancy [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Check your records.** Look at the condition report and any messages in which you agreed to the deduction. They matter because the cleaning claim depends on how clean the premises were left compared with the start of the tenancy [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Get advice before paying or ignoring it.** The documents don't cover whether the invoice is enforceable, so it's worth checking with a tenancy advice service.

I also retrieved earlier versions of the Act and a 2021 version of the Regulations. They are superseded, and I haven't relied on them.

I can't say either way without guessing.' A reader cannot tell that agreeing to a deduction is agreement to a bond claim rather than to a separate invoice. question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. I've called them twice today. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
## What the law says

**Documents applied:** the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version 115, in force from 13 October 2026 (rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf) [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I also used the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, version 009, in force from 30 June 2026 (rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). These are the latest versions I found, and neither shows an end date. The version numbers come from the file names and metadata, not from text printed in the document.

- **You don't have to wait indefinitely.** Under section 72(1), a renter may arrange urgent repairs if both of these apply [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf):
  - you have taken reasonable steps to arrange for the rental provider or their agent to carry out the repairs immediately; and
  - you are unable to get them to carry out the repairs.
- **Use a suitably qualified person, not a DIY fix.** The standard agreement terms say that only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, urgent or non-urgent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **The owner's "own tradespeople only" rule.** The documents I retrieved don't mention any right for the owner to limit which tradespeople do urgent repairs. The test in section 72(1) is whether you can get the rental provider or agent to carry out the repair [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether a rental provider can lawfully restrict who does the work, so I can't say more on that.
- **Does your tap count as an "urgent repair"?** Section 3(1) defines urgent repairs, but I didn't retrieve that definition. The regulations' form refers to it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf), and one form gives "a burst water service" as an example of an urgent repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). I can't confirm from these documents that a broken tap with the water off to the whole house qualifies, so check section 3(1).
- **Are two calls enough?** The Act doesn't define "reasonable steps" in the text I retrieved. Two unsuccessful calls today is a good start, but it is not confirmed to be enough.

## What you can do

1. **Give written notice now.** The standard agreement says that if you need an urgent repair, you should notify the rental provider in writing [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). You must also give written notice of a breakdown of facilities or fixtures as soon as practicable [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Email counts as written notice [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **If they still don't act, arrange the repair yourself** through a suitably qualified person [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Tell the rental provider afterwards.** You must give 7 days written notice of the repairs carried out and their cost [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Claim reimbursement.** The rental provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days of receiving that written notice. The Act caps this at the reasonable cost or the prescribed amount, whichever is less [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The regulations' form summary gives that amount as **$2500** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). I didn't retrieve the operative regulation that sets it.
5. **If they don't pay, go to VCAT.** There are two routes:
   - You can apply to the Tribunal for a compensation or compliance order if you gave written notice of the repairs and cost and were not reimbursed within 7 days [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
   - You can apply for an order requiring the rental provider to carry out urgent repairs if you can't meet the cost, the cost exceeds the prescribed amount, or the rental provider refuses to pay. The Tribunal must hear that application within 2 business days [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**Practical tip:** keep a record of your calls (times and numbers), your written notice, and the tradesperson's invoice.

It is also missing the point that a nominated-tradesperson term is prohibited (reg 11(e)) and cannot stop an urgent repair, since it says only that 'the documents don't say whether a rental provider can lawfully restrict who does the work, so I can't say more on that'. question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. I haven't moved any of my things in or stayed there yet. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
## Documents used

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997**, file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", in force from 13 October 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This is the version in force today, but only its definitions section was retrieved.
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021**, file "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf", in force from 30 June 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- The identifiers I can see are "version 115" for the Act and "version 009" for the Regulations. The retrieved excerpts don't show the words "Authorised Version No." printed on the page. I'm taking the numbers from the file metadata.
- I did not rely on the 2022 Act (v101, "rta-1997-v101-2022-09-07.pdf") or the 2025 Regulations (v004). Both are superseded [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says about your situation

- **Minimum standards.** The rented premises must be structurally sound and weatherproof. Each room must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Rotting timber isn't named in the excerpts. It may relate to structural soundness, but I can't confirm that from these documents.
- **The rental provider's duty at move-in.** Under the standard-form agreement, the rental provider must ensure the premises comply with the rental minimum standards. They must also be vacant and reasonably clean when you move in, and be kept in good repair and fit for occupation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs.** The Act's definition includes a failure to comply with any rental minimum standards. It also includes any fault or damage that makes the premises unsafe or insecure, including mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do

**1. Ask for repairs.** The documents support this.
- Notify the rental provider in writing. If the mould or damp is an urgent repair, the provider must carry it out after being notified [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- You may arrange urgent repairs yourself only if you have taken reasonable steps to get the provider to do them immediately and they haven't. You can then be reimbursed the reasonable cost up to **$2500** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- You may apply to VCAT for an order requiring urgent repairs if you can't meet the cost, the cost is over $2500, or the provider refuses to pay [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- For non-urgent repairs, notify the provider in writing. You may apply to VCAT if the repairs aren't done within **14 days** of the provider receiving notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**2. Record it in the condition report.** The prescribed condition report form says you should note anything unsafe or needing repair. Where the report lists something needing repair, that gives the provider written notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). You have 5 business days after moving in to complete it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). If you later find something wrong, you can apply to VCAT to correct the report within **30 days** after the start date of the agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). You haven't moved in, so take dated photos and send them to the provider with your written notice.

**3. Cancel the lease.** The retrieved documents don't answer this.
- The only reference is in the over-5-years form. It mentions a notice to vacate under section 91ZD "on the basis the premises are destroyed or unfit for habitation" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). That is a form clause, not the operative section, so I can't say what it requires or whether it applies to you.
- The operative provisions of the Act on ending an agreement were not in the retrieved text, so I can't say whether you can cancel before moving in.

**4. Lower rent.** The retrieved documents don't answer this either. The rent provisions I found only deal with challenging a proposed rent increase as excessive [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). They don't cover a rent reduction for a defective property.

## Before you decide

You should check the operative sections of the Act on termination and rent reduction, or get advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria or VCAT. I wouldn't treat your lease as cancelled, or stop paying rent, until you have done that.

question: Our rental was broken into several times while we were moving out, and there are about three weeks left on our fixed-term lease. The burglars damaged the plumbing and wiring, so we can't even clean properly. What are our options before the lease ends?
answer:
**Source and version:** The version in force today (9 Nov 2026) is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", in force from 13 October 2026 and not shown as ended [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Its metadata gives "version 115". The text I retrieved doesn't show a separate "Authorised Version No." label, so I can only give you the 115 from the metadata. For the matching regulations I used "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf", in force from 30 June 2026 [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Unfit premises:** A renter may give a notice of intention to vacate if the premises are unfit for human habitation, or destroyed to the point of being unsafe. The notice can take effect on the day it is given or on a later date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 91ZD).
- **Ordinary notice doesn't fit your timing:** A standard notice of intention to vacate needs at least 28 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 91Z). On a fixed term, a notice with a termination date earlier than the end of the term has no effect, unless an exception applies [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 91ZA). Section 91ZD is the route that avoids the 28 days.
- **Reporting damage:** A renter must give the provider written notice of damage as soon as practicable, describing what it is. Email is allowed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 62).
- **Cleaning duty:** At the end of the tenancy you must leave the premises reasonably clean and in the starting condition "as far as practicable", allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 63(2)). The duty not to damage the premises covers damage that a renter or visitor causes intentionally or negligently [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 61). The retrieved text doesn't say who bears the cost of damage done by burglars.
- **Urgent repairs:** The current Act's definition of "urgent repairs" wasn't in the retrieved v115 text. The 2021 version of the Act (rta-1997-v097-2021-03-28.pdf) listed a burst water service, a dangerous electrical fault, failure of the gas, electricity or water supply, and "any fault or damage that makes rented premises… unsafe or insecure" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa097%20authorised.pdf). That is an older version, so check the current wording. The current regulations point to the Act's definition [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask for

1. **Notify the provider or agent in writing now.** Describe the break-ins and the plumbing and wiring damage, and ask for urgent repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
2. **If the damage makes the home unfit or unsafe, give a s 91ZD notice.** You can set the termination date to the day you give it, or later [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Arrange urgent repairs yourself if the provider won't act.** Under the regulations, you must first take reasonable steps to get the provider to do them immediately. Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, and you can be reimbursed the reasonable cost up to $2500 [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). An earlier version of the Act (rta-1997-v111-2025-11-25.pdf, in force 25 Nov 2025 to 29 Jun 2026) also required 7 days' written notice of the repairs and their cost, and reimbursement within 7 days [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). I didn't retrieve the current wording of s 72.
4. **Apply to VCAT for an urgent repairs order** if you can't pay, the cost exceeds $2500, or the provider refuses to pay [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The v111 Act required VCAT to hear these applications within 2 business days [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). I didn't retrieve the current s 73.
5. **Ask the provider to agree in writing** to how the cleaning and condition will be handled, given that you can't clean properly. The retrieved documents don't give a specific rule for this situation.

## Not covered by the documents

- Whether you owe a lease break fee under s 91ZD. The no-fee rule I found is in s 91ZB(5), which applies only to the circumstances listed in that section [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Bond and compensation for the burglary damage, rent reductions, and insurance or police reporting.
- Whether any change was made to the repair provisions between v111 and v115.

This is general information from the retrieved documents, not legal advice. A tenancy advice service or VCAT can confirm how it applies to you.

question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. The app is run by a payments company my agent uses, and it's that company that charges the card fee. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the retrieved documents, the app probably cannot charge you a card fee for paying rent. Who receives the fee does not change that. The documents don't address every detail of your situation, so I've noted the gaps.

**Which versions apply today (9 November 2026):**
- *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version **115**, in force from 13 October 2026 (file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf") [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised Version **009**, in force from 30 June 2026 (file "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf") [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**What the law says**

- **Fees for paying rent are restricted.** Under s 51A of the Act, "a person, other than an ADI, must not demand or receive a fee for any prescribed matter in relation to an application to enter into a residential rental agreement or the payment of rent" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Regulation 21C, effective from 31 March 2026, lists "rent payment (other than payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act)" as a prescribed matter [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). So a card surcharge for rent is caught unless another Act permits a payment surcharge. The retrieved documents don't identify any such Act.
- **A no-cost option must be available.** Under s 42(4), the provider or agent "must ensure that a rent payment method that incurs no additional costs (other than bank fees or account fees payable on the renter's bank account) is reasonably available to the renter" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Your bank transfer may meet this, but the documents don't define "reasonably available," so whether a slower method counts is not settled by the text.
- **Costs must be disclosed.** Under s 42(7), the provider or agent must tell you about costs, "including third party transaction fees," before you consent to a payment method [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Separate charge rule.** Under s 51(3)(b), a person must not demand or receive a charge "in relation to the establishment or use of direct debit facilities or any other electronic payment facility for payment of rent" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This prohibition has no ADI exception.

**Does it matter who gets the fee?**

Not on the wording of these provisions. Section 51A and s 51(3) apply to "a person," not only the agent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The one carve-out is that s 51A does not apply to an ADI (an authorised deposit-taking institution, such as a bank). The documents don't say whether your payments company is an ADI. Even if it were, s 51(3)(b) would still apply. The agent's duties under s 42(4) and s 42(7) also apply regardless of who collects the fee [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask**

1. Ask the agent in writing what the card fee is, who receives it, and the legal basis for charging it, referring to s 42(7) and s 51A.
2. Ask for a fee-free method, such as bank transfer, to be confirmed as available under s 42(4). Note that the documents don't say what "reasonably available" means in practice.
3. Ask whether Centrepay is available. The provider or agent must permit Centrepay under s 42(5) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. If you pay, ask for a receipt. Under s 43(1), a receipt must be given immediately for in-person payments, or within 5 business days if requested for other payments [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover**

- Whether you can recover card fees you've already paid.
- How to enforce these rules or complain. The documents set penalties (for example, 80 penalty units for a natural person under s 51A and s 42(4), and 400 for a body corporate) but don't set out a complaint procedure [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Whether any other Act permits a payment surcharge for rent.

Because this is a legal question, consider checking with Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy advice service before taking formal action.

question: My lease is on the standard form and started in 2024. It has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. I cleaned them myself and they're back to how they were when I moved in, but the agent wants a receipt from a professional cleaner. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?
answer:
**Short answer:** Probably not, if the carpets are already back to their move-in condition. The law makes the professional-cleaning obligation conditional, and the documents don't say a receipt is required.

**What the law says**

- A standard-form lease can require professional cleaning only in limited cases. The Regulations say the landlord "must not require the renter to arrange professional cleaning or cleaning to a professional standard at the end of the tenancy" unless the premises were professionally cleaned before the tenancy started and the renter was told so, or professional cleaning "is required to restore the rented premises to the same condition they were in immediately before the start of the tenancy, having regard to the condition report and taking into account fair wear and tear" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- The renter must have the premises professionally cleaned, or pay for it, only "if professional cleaning becomes required to restore the premises to the condition they were in immediately before the start of the tenancy, having regard to the condition report and taking into account fair wear and tear" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- At the end of a tenancy, the renter must leave the premises "as far as practicable" reasonably clean and "in the same condition as when the renter entered into possession of the premises, taking into account fair wear and tear to the premises" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

So the key question is whether professional cleaning is actually *required* to restore the carpets. If your own cleaning achieved that, the documents suggest the condition is met. The documents don't say how to decide this in a particular case.

**Versions relied on**

- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021**, version 009, in force from 30 June 2026 (per its file metadata) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997**, Authorised Version 115, in force from 13 October 2026 (per its file metadata) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't show the wording in force when your 2024 lease began, so I can't say whether that wording differed.

**What would help show the carpets' condition**

The documents point to the **condition report** as the reference point. Professional cleaning is judged "having regard to the condition report" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf), and any bond claim evidence "must not conflict with a statement in a condition report" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Your move-in condition report is therefore the most important document. Compare the carpets against it.

Beyond that, the documents don't list specific evidence (such as photos or cleaning receipts) that would be accepted. Dated photos and a note of the cleaning method are sensible practical steps, but they're my suggestion, not something the documents require.

**What you can do or ask**

- **Ask the agent in writing** which part of the condition report they say the carpets fail to meet, and whether they say professional cleaning is required to restore them. This ties the request to the legal test.
- **If the bond is claimed**, the landlord may claim only for "the reasonable cost of cleaning any part of the premises, if the premises were not left reasonably clean by the renter, having regard to the condition of the premises at the commencement of the residential rental agreement" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The landlord must give you bond claim evidence at least 3 days before claiming from the bond [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If you disagree, you can give written notice that the claim is subject to a Tribunal application within 14 days of notice [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **If a term is harsh or unconscionable**, you may apply to the Tribunal to declare it invalid or vary it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't say whether a professional-cleaning receipt is ever a required form of proof. For a firm answer on your specific lease, check with the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal or a tenancy advice service.

must-mention.reason: Yes. The answer covers all three points. It quotes the reg 12 exceptions: professional cleaning only if the premises were professionally cleaned before the tenancy and the renter was told, or if it is required to restore pre-tenancy condition allowing for fair wear and tear. It states the s 63 duty to leave the premises reasonably clean and in the same condition, fair wear and tear excepted. For the hardest point, it says 'Your move-in condition report is therefore the most important document. Compare the carpets against it.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the renter must pay because of the clause or the pet. It says 'Probably not, if the carpets are already back to their move-in condition' and treats the duty as conditional on whether professional cleaning 'is required to restore the rented premises to the same condition they were in immediately before the start of the tenancy.'

question: When I moved out I agreed the agent could take an amount for cleaning out of my bond, but I never signed a bond claim form for it. Then my full bond came back to me, and a month later the agent sent a separate invoice for the cleaning. Do I have to pay it? Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents don't say that agreeing to a bond deduction counts as agreeing to pay a separate invoice. Under the Act, though, a bond deduction for cleaning has to go through a formal claim, and the agent's later invoice doesn't fit that process. Whether you must pay depends on facts the documents don't cover, so you should get advice on your specific situation.

Current versions: the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* is Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* is S.R. No. 3/2021, version 009, in force from 30 June 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

---

### What the law says

- **Cleaning can be claimed from the bond.** A landlord may claim from the bond "the reasonable cost of cleaning any part of the premises, if the premises were not left reasonably clean by the renter, having regard to the condition of the premises at the commencement of the residential rental agreement" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A renter must leave the premises "as far as practicable" reasonably clean [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Bond claims follow a set process.** A claim must be "in a form approved by the Authority" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A provider must not request or obtain a renter's signature on a claim form unless the form states the amount of bond to be refunded and any apportionment [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Evidence is required.** Before a claim is made to the provider, the provider must give each renter "bond claim evidence" (such as an invoice, receipt, quote or photograph) at least 3 days beforehand, and that evidence must not conflict with the condition report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Other parties get notice.** If a claim is made without the consent of all parties, the Authority must notify the other parties. The Authority pays the claim unless a party gives written notice within 14 days that the claim is subject to a Tribunal application [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **A bond refund doesn't end the matter.** A person who has recovered compensation from a bond "is not precluded from taking proceedings... to recover an additional amount by way of compensation" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Tribunal must also consider whether money "has been paid to or recovered by the applicant... including money recovered or entitled to be recovered from the bond" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Limits on cleaning terms.** A term requiring professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy, or requiring the renter to pay for it, is prohibited unless it is in the standard form [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations prescribe the standard-form wording, which applies only if professional cleaning is required to restore the premises to their condition at the start of the tenancy, "having regard to the condition report and taking into account fair wear and tear" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### Your situation

- **Verbal agreement vs. claim form:** The Act's mechanism is a formal claim, not an informal agreement. I can't confirm from the documents whether a verbal agreement to a deduction has any legal effect on its own.
- **Invoice after refund:** The provider's later invoice came after the bond was released. The documents don't say how the bond was released to you. A claim for cleaning must rest on evidence that is given before the claim is made [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), so the timing of the invoice is relevant.
- **Can they still pursue you?** Yes, in principle. The provider may still bring compensation proceedings despite the bond refund [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't set the time limit for that kind of claim. The time limits in the retrieved text (for example, 14 days after termination for a bond repayment application under s 419A(2) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)) relate to bond applications, not general compensation claims.

### What you can do or ask

1. **Ask for the bond claim evidence and the claim form.** Ask the agent to show what claim, if any, was made to the Authority, and the evidence they relied on.
2. **Check your condition report.** It is the key comparison for cleaning [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Compare it with the state of the property at the end of the tenancy.
3. **Check whether the invoice is reasonable.** The cost must be "reasonable" and the premises must not have been left reasonably clean [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Consider a dispute.** Under the Act, disputes go to the Tribunal (VCAT) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The documents don't set out the procedure for disputing an invoice sent after bond refund, so check the current process.

**Gaps in the documents:** The retrieved documents don't address whether a verbal bond-deduction agreement binds you, the time limit for compensation claims made after a bond refund, or what happens when a provider sends an invoice after the bond has been paid out. For those points, you should get advice from a tenancy service or the Tribunal.

For the first, the answer says 'a bond deduction for cleaning has to go through a formal claim, and the agent's later invoice doesn't fit that process' and that 'the documents don't say that agreeing to a bond deduction counts as agreeing to pay a separate invoice.' For the second, it quotes the test that the premises were 'not left reasonably clean by the renter, having regard to the condition of the premises at the commencement' and treats the condition report as the key comparison.

question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. I've called them twice today. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
**Short answer:** You don't necessarily have to wait. Under the law, you may be able to arrange urgent repairs yourself if you meet certain conditions. Those conditions are set out below, and I can't confirm from the documents that they are all met in your case.

The governing document is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, version 115, in force from 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, version 009, in force from 30 June 2026, is also relevant [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **This is likely an urgent repair.** "Urgent repairs" include work to repair "a burst water service" and "a failure or breakdown of the gas, electricity or water supply to rented premises" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A tap that has cut off water to the whole house may fall within these categories, though that depends on the facts.
- **The provider must act on notice.** "The rental provider must carry out urgent repairs after being notified" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **You can arrange repairs only if both conditions are met.** A renter may arrange urgent repairs if (a) they have taken reasonable steps to get the provider or agent to carry out the repairs immediately, and (b) they are unable to get the provider or agent to do so [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs.** This applies to both urgent and non-urgent repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). A "suitably qualified person" includes a registered or licensed tradesperson where the work requires registration or licensing [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do

1. **Put it in writing.** The documents say that if there is a need for an urgent repair, the renter should notify the rental provider in writing [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Your two phone calls may not count as written notice, so send an email or text as well, if that is how the agreement allows notices to be served.
2. **Hire a suitably qualified person.** Use a registered or licensed tradesperson for the plumbing work.
3. **Give written notice of the repair and its cost.** You must give the provider 7 days' written notice of the repairs and the cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days after receiving that notice. The renter's reimbursement is limited to the lesser of the reasonable cost or the prescribed amount [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Know the cap.** The Regulations summary says the renter may be reimbursed "for the reasonable cost of repairs up to $2500" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
5. **If the cost is over $2500, or the provider refuses to pay,** you may apply to VCAT for an order requiring the provider to carry out the repairs. The grounds include that the cost is more than $2500 or that the provider refuses to pay the cost of repairs carried out by you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). VCAT must hear such an application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't cover

- **Whether the owner can insist on using only their own tradespeople.** The documents don't address this. They only say that repairs must be done by a suitably qualified person [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **How many attempts count as "reasonable steps."** The documents don't define this. Two calls today may or may not be enough, and you should keep a record of every attempt.
- **Whether a single tap counts as "urgent" in your case.** The documents list water supply failures as urgent, but they don't say how the definition applies to a broken tap in your situation.

For a full list of urgent repairs, the Regulations point to consumer.vic.gov.au/urgentrepairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Given the uncertainties, you may want to check with Consumer Affairs Victoria before paying for the work.

The first two points are covered: it quotes 'a burst water service' and 'a failure or breakdown of the... water supply' as urgent repairs, and explains reasonable steps, the renter arranging repairs, and reimbursement within 7 days of written notice up to the cap.

question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. I haven't moved any of my things in or stayed there yet. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents I retrieved set out a landlord's repair duties and your repair remedies. They do not say whether you can cancel the lease before moving in, and they do not give you a right to a rent reduction for these defects.

The sources are the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (version 009, in force from 30 June 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) and the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (version 115, in force from 13 October 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Both are in force today, 9 November 2026.

## What the law says about your situation

- **Mould and damp:** Each room must be "free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The Act treats "the presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure" as a fault that makes premises unsafe or insecure, which is a type of urgent repair [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Structure:** The premises "are to be structurally sound and weatherproof" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The retrieved text does not mention rotting timber specifically, so whether it counts depends on this general standard.
- **Timing:** The landlord must ensure the premises comply with the rental minimum standards and are vacant and reasonably clean "when the renter moves in," and must maintain them "in good repair and in a fit condition for occupation" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Condition report:** You must be given the condition report on or before the day you move in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). You can note anything that needs repair on it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). If you later find something not working or in poor repair, you may apply to VCAT to correct the report, within 30 days after the start date of the agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## Your options

**1. Ask for repairs (available now)**
- Give the landlord written notice as soon as practicable after becoming aware of the damage [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Your notice should describe the damp, mould and timber problems.
- **Urgent repairs:** You may arrange them if you have taken reasonable steps to get the landlord to do them immediately and they cannot or do not. You must then give 7 days' written notice of the repairs and cost, and the landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations summarise the reimbursement limit as up to $2500 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). You can apply to VCAT for an order requiring urgent repairs if the cost is more than $2500 or the landlord refuses to pay [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Non-urgent repairs:** If the landlord has not carried out repairs within 14 days of your written notice, you can apply to the Director to investigate [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You can also apply to VCAT for an order requiring the repairs, and VCAT must hear that application within 7 days [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

If you have given notice requiring repairs, you can apply to VCAT for an order that you pay rent into that account instead of to the landlord, if the landlord has failed to carry out the repairs and has not shown financial hardship [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Money held there must be paid to the landlord at the end of the period unless VCAT orders otherwise [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The retrieved text does not explain its requirements, so I cannot say whether it applies to you.

## Practical next steps
- Put your complaint in writing now, listing each defect, and keep photos with dates.
- Note the defects on the condition report and add comments and photos. Do not sign it without noting them.
- Before paying more money or moving in, get advice from VCAT or Consumer Affairs Victoria about cancellation. The Regulations refer to consumer.vic.gov.au/renting for further information [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
