question: Our rental was broken into several times while we were moving out, and there are about three weeks left on our fixed-term lease. The burglars damaged the plumbing and wiring, so we can't even clean properly. What are our options before the lease ends?
answer:
**Short answer:** The Act requires your landlord to fix urgent problems like burst pipes and dangerous electrical faults, and gives you a route to get them fixed if they don't act. You can also consider ending the lease early, but only if the premises are unfit for habitation or unsafe. The documents don't say whether those grounds apply to your situation.

**Which law applies:** The *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 115 (in force from 13 October 2026), is the version in force today [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised Version No. 009 (in force from 30 June 2026), also applies [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Notice:** A renter must give the landlord written notice "as soon as practicable" after becoming aware of damage to the premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs:** "Urgent repairs" include a burst water service, a dangerous electrical fault, and "any fault or damage that makes rented premises... unsafe or insecure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Renter's duty:** A renter must not intentionally or negligently cause damage, and fair wear and tear is excluded [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Renters must also leave the premises "as far as practicable" reasonably clean [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Cleaning limits:** A landlord cannot require professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy unless the premises were professionally cleaned before the tenancy started, or professional cleaning is needed to restore them to their starting condition, taking fair wear and tear into account [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## Options before the lease ends

1. **Give written notice now.** Tell the landlord or agent in writing about the break-ins and the damage to plumbing and wiring [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Electronic notice is allowed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

2. **Ask for urgent repairs.** Your landlord must carry out urgent repairs once notified [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). If the landlord doesn't act, you may arrange repairs yourself only if you have "taken reasonable steps" to get the landlord to repair immediately and they are unable to do so [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

3. **If you pay for repairs yourself:**
   - You must give the landlord **7 days written notice** of the repairs and their cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
   - The landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost within **7 days** after receiving written notice of the repairs and cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
   - The regulations state that reimbursement is available for reasonable cost "up to $2500" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
   - Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

4. **Apply to VCAT if needed.** You can apply to VCAT for an urgent repairs order if you cannot meet the cost, if the cost is more than the prescribed amount, or if the landlord refuses to pay for repairs you arrange [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). VCAT must hear the application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

5. **End the lease early (possible but conditional).** A renter may give a notice of intention to vacate if the premises are "unfit for human habitation" or have been "destroyed totally or to such an extent as to be rendered unsafe." The termination date can be the date of notice or a later date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If this applies, the landlord cannot claim rent foregone under the standard terms [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Whether your premises meet this test is a factual question the documents don't resolve.

   Otherwise, for a fixed-term agreement, a notice that specifies a termination date earlier than the end of the term is of no effect, unless the agreement has a specific early-termination clause [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Check your lease for that clause.

6. **Cleaning.** If you can't clean because of the damage, document the situation in writing and notify the landlord. The landlord cannot require professional cleaning unless one of the conditions above applies [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The bond can cover cleaning costs if premises weren't left reasonably clean, having regard to their condition at the start of the lease [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

7. **Bond exposure.** A landlord can claim from the bond for repair costs from damage "caused by the renter or a renter's visitor" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A "visitor" is someone on the premises with the renter's permission [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Burglars would not normally be there with permission, but the documents don't address this directly. Keep your records of the break-ins.

## What the documents don't cover

- Whether burglary damage counts as renter-caused damage for bond or compensation purposes.
- Whether your premises are "unfit for human habitation" or "unsafe" enough to support early termination.
- How the lease-break fee cap ("no more than one month's rent for each year left") applies when only about three weeks remain [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- Police reports, insurance claims, or changing locks after break-ins, beyond the general lock rules [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

For advice on your specific facts, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria on 1300 558 181 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

(3) The hardest point is covered by: "A renter may give a notice of intention to vacate if the premises are 'unfit for human habitation' or ... 'rendered unsafe.' The termination date can be the date of notice or a later date." It then contrasts this with ordinary fixed-term notices that are "Otherwise" of no effect, which shows the ground applies to their fixed-term lease.

question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. The app is run by a payments company my agent uses, and it's that company that charges the card fee. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
**Short answer:** Probably not. Under the current law, a card surcharge for rent payment is likely prohibited unless another Act permits it, and the documents I found don't identify any such Act. Whether the fee goes to the app company or the agent doesn't change the basic rule, though it may affect who is liable.

**Documents used:**
- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997**, Authorised Version (metadata "version 115"), in force from 13 October 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021**, Authorised Version (metadata "version 009"), in force from 30 June 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). These are S.R. No. 3/2021 as amended.

I'm relying on the version metadata for the version numbers, since the text itself doesn't state them.

---

### What the law says

- **Fee ban:** "A person, other than an ADI, must not demand or receive a fee for any prescribed matter in relation to an application to enter into a residential rental agreement or the payment of rent." [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person or 400 penalty units for a body corporate [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Rent payment is a prescribed matter:** Regulation 21C, effective from 31 March 2026, lists "rent payment (other than payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act)" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **The exception:** A surcharge is only allowed if "any other Act" permits it. The documents don't identify any such Act, so I can't confirm whether one applies to your app.
- **Fee-free option:** The provider or agent "must ensure that a rent payment method that incurs no additional costs (other than bank fees or account fees payable on the renter's bank account) is reasonably available to the renter." [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- **Bank transfer:** Electronic funds transfer is the prescribed payment method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Providers must also permit Centrepay [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Cost disclosure:** Before you agree to a payment method, the provider or agent "must give the renter information about any costs (including third party transaction fees ...)" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Who the ban covers:** Section 51A applies to "a person," not only the landlord or agent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). That means the payments company could be caught if it demands or receives a rent payment fee.

### Does it matter who gets the fee?

Based on these documents, the ban applies whether the money goes to the app company or the agent, so the recipient doesn't change whether the fee is prohibited. The recipient matters for who may be liable. The agent has its own duties under the Act to offer a fee-free method and disclose costs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say how liability works when a third-party company charges the fee, so that point needs specific advice.

### What you can do or ask

1. **Ask the agent in writing** to confirm which payment methods incur no additional costs and whether the card fee is permitted under an Act other than the Residential Tenancies Act.
2. **Ask for the cost information** the Act requires the agent to give before you choose a method [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Ask to pay by bank transfer (EFT)**, which is the prescribed fee-free option [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The law requires a no-extra-cost method to be "reasonably available" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't define "reasonably available," so a slower transfer may or may not meet that test.

### What the documents don't cover

- Whether any other Act permits a payment surcharge for rent.
- Whether the payments company is an ADI, which would take it outside the ban.
- How to make a complaint or seek enforcement, such as through VCAT or Consumer Affairs Victoria.
- How "reasonably available" should be interpreted for a slower method.

If you want to act on this, a tenancy advice service such as Consumer Affairs Victoria can help with the next steps.

question: My lease is on the standard form and started in 2024. It has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. I cleaned them myself and they're back to how they were when I moved in, but the agent wants a receipt from a professional cleaner. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?
answer:
**Short answer:** Probably not, if the carpets are back to their move-in condition. The law requires a professional clean only when one is actually needed to restore the premises, and the documents don't say what the agent can demand as proof.

**Which law applies:** The current *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* is Authorised Version No. 115, in force from 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The current *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* is Version No. 009, in force from 30 June 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Because the lease started in 2024, the documents don't show whether the 2024 standard form had the same wording.

**What the law says**

- A standard-form lease may require professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy only if professional cleaning becomes required to restore the premises to the condition they were in immediately before the tenancy started, taking fair wear and tear into account [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The regulations say the provider must not require professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy unless either (a) professional cleaning was carried out before the tenancy started and the renter was told so, or (b) professional cleaning is required to restore the premises to their move-in condition, having regard to the condition report and fair wear and tear [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- Under the standard form, the renter must have the premises professionally cleaned, or pay for it, only if professional cleaning becomes required to restore the premises to their move-in condition [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- At the end of a tenancy, a renter must leave the premises "as far as practicable" reasonably clean and in the same condition as when they moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- A provider can claim the reasonable cost of cleaning from the bond only if the premises were not left reasonably clean, judged against their condition at the start of the tenancy [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask**

- **Check the condition report.** The standard form requires you to have been given two copies (or one emailed copy) of the condition report on or before you moved in [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). This is the main benchmark for "move-in condition" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Check whether a professional clean was done before you moved in.** If it was, and you were told so, the provider may have a stronger basis to require one [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). If not, the regulations limit what can be required [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Ask the agent in writing** what professional cleaning is said to be required to restore the carpets to move-in condition, and by reference to what. The documents don't set out a procedure for this.
- **If there's a bond claim,** you can dispute it. Bond claim evidence must not conflict with a statement in a condition report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If a claim is made without your consent, the Authority must notify you, and you can stop it being paid automatically by notifying the Authority in writing within 14 days that the claim is subject to a Tribunal application [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **If the term is harsh or unconscionable,** you can apply to VCAT for an order declaring it invalid or varying it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What helps show the carpets' condition**

The documents name the **condition report** as the key reference point [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). They don't list other types of evidence. Practical steps not covered by the documents include keeping dated photos or video of the carpets before and after your clean, and keeping your own cleaning receipts or notes.

**What the documents don't answer**

- Whether an agent can insist on a professional-cleaner receipt, or what counts as proof.
- What the 2024 version of the standard form said.
- Whether your own cleaning meets the "restore to move-in condition" test. That depends on facts in your condition report and on fair wear and tear, which the documents don't assess for your case.

This is general information from the retrieved documents, not legal advice. For a firm answer, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria or VCAT.

question: When I moved out I agreed the agent could take an amount for cleaning out of my bond, but I never signed a bond claim form for it. Then my full bond came back to me, and a month later the agent sent a separate invoice for the cleaning. Do I have to pay it? Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents don't establish that you must pay a separate invoice after your full bond has been returned. Agreeing to a bond deduction and agreeing to pay an invoice are different things under the Act. The documents don't say whether a verbal agreement to a deduction binds you, so I can't answer that part.

I'm relying on the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 115 (incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, S.R. No. 3/2021 (version 009, in force from 30 June 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). These are the current versions as of today.

### What the law says

- **Cleaning is a permitted bond claim.** A landlord may claim from the bond "the reasonable cost of cleaning any part of the premises, if the premises were not left reasonably clean by the renter, having regard to the condition of the premises at the commencement of the residential rental agreement" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **A bond claim needs paperwork.** A claim must be "in a form approved by the Authority" and include the claimant's address or email [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). At least 3 days before a claim is made to the landlord, the landlord or agent "must give each renter bond claim evidence that supports the claim" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Bond claim evidence includes "an invoice," "a receipt," "a quote," or "a photograph" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The claim must match the condition report.** Bond claim evidence "must not conflict with a statement in a condition report" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Signing is a separate step.** A landlord "must not request or obtain a renter's signature to a claim form" unless the form specifies the amount to be refunded and any apportionment [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Landlords can still pursue more money.** A person who has recovered compensation from a bond "is not precluded from taking proceedings under this Part to recover an additional amount by way of compensation" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This suggests a landlord may still seek extra money through the Tribunal, but the documents don't set out how a post-bond invoice would be enforced.
- **Professional cleaning limits.** A standard-form term can require a renter to pay for professional cleaning only if it is needed to restore the premises to their starting condition, "taking into account fair wear and tear" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The landlord also must not require professional cleaning unless the premises were professionally cleaned before the tenancy started, or it's needed to restore the premises to that condition [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do or ask

1. **Ask for bond claim evidence.** Request the invoice, quote, receipts, and photos the agent relies on. The Act requires these to be given at least 3 days before a claim is made [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Check your condition report.** Compare the cleaning charge with the condition report from the start of the tenancy, since the cleaning must be measured against that condition [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Check whether the cleaning was "reasonable."** The Act only allows the "reasonable cost" of cleaning, so ask whether the amount is reasonable and whether it was professional cleaning [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
4. **Ask whether a claim form was ever lodged.** If no form was lodged and your full bond was released, you can ask the agent to explain the basis for the separate charge.
5. **Seek advice or dispute it.** If the agent pursues the amount, the Tribunal handles compensation disputes. I haven't retrieved the full procedure for those applications, so please check that before taking steps.

### What the documents don't cover

- Whether a verbal agreement to a bond deduction counts as agreeing to pay an invoice.
- How a landlord recovers a cleaning invoice after the bond has been fully returned, including the time limits and procedure for that claim.
- Whether the bond was released through a valid claim process in your case.

It applies no rule from any other version.

question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. I've called them twice today. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
**Short answer:** You probably don't have to wait indefinitely. Under the Victorian rules, a renter can arrange urgent repairs if the owner doesn't carry them out after reasonable steps to get them done. The documents don't say how long you must wait, and they don't say whether a broken tap qualifies, so check that point before you act.

**What the law says**

I'm relying on two current instruments:
- *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, version 115 (in force from 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, version 009 (in force from 30 June 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

- **Is this an urgent repair?** "Urgent repairs" include work to repair "a burst water service" and "a failure or breakdown of the gas, electricity or water supply to rented premises" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A tap that has caused you to shut off the whole house's water may fall within these categories, but the documents don't define "burst water service," so this is a judgement call.
- **Can the renter arrange repairs?** Yes, if the renter "has taken reasonable steps to arrange for the rental provider to immediately do the repairs" and the provider "has not carried out the repairs" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Who can do the work?** "Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs—both urgent and non-urgent" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The Act says a suitably qualified person "includes a tradesperson who is registered or licensed in respect of relevant work" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Does the owner's tradesperson rule stop you?** The documents don't say whether an owner can restrict repairs to its own tradespeople. They only say the work must be done by a suitably qualified person, and that the renter may arrange urgent repairs when the provider hasn't carried them out.

**What you can do**

1. **Give written notice now.** The regulations say that if urgent repairs are needed, the renter "should notify the rental provider in writing" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Your two phone calls may count as reasonable steps, but a written notice (email is fine if the lease allows it) makes the record clearer. Include the emergency contact's name and the time of each call.
2. **Arrange a suitably qualified person** if the owner's tradespeople still can't attend. Keep the invoice and receipts.
3. **Notify the owner in writing of the repairs and the cost.** The rental provider must reimburse "the reasonable cost of repairs" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The reimbursement is capped at "up to $2500" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
4. **Expect reimbursement within 7 days.** A renter can apply to the Tribunal for compensation or a compliance order if the provider doesn't reimburse within 7 days of receiving written notice of the repairs and cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. **Go to VCAT if needed.** The renter can apply to VCAT for an order requiring urgent repairs if the renter cannot meet the cost, the cost is more than $2500, or the provider refuses to pay [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover**

- How many attempts or how much time counts as "reasonable steps."
- Whether a broken tap alone counts as an urgent repair.
- Whether an owner can insist on its own tradespeople.
- The full text of section 72, which the Act's compensation provision refers to for arranging urgent repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I couldn't retrieve it, so check it before relying on this answer.

If the leak is ongoing, consider contacting Consumer Affairs Victoria. The regulations refer renters to its website for the full list of urgent repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The documents don't give its contact details.

must-mention.reason: No (fail). The third point is missing: the answer never says that a term requiring the landlord's nominated tradesperson is prohibited, or that the preferred-tradesperson policy cannot stop an urgent repair. It says instead that 'The documents don't say whether an owner can restrict repairs to its own tradespeople' and lists this as uncovered. The first two points (water supply failure or burst water service is an urgent repair; the renter can arrange the repair after reasonable steps and be reimbursed up to $2500 within 7 days of written notice) are covered.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer says neither forbidden thing; it states "You probably don't have to wait indefinitely" and that the renter can arrange urgent repairs, and it says "The rental provider must reimburse 'the reasonable cost of repairs'" (capped at "up to $2500"), so it neither requires waiting for the owner's tradespeople nor denies cost recovery.

question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. I haven't moved any of my things in or stayed there yet. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents support asking for repairs, and in some cases arranging urgent repairs yourself. They don't provide a right to a rent reduction. On cancelling, they only partly answer the question, so get advice before you act.

I'm treating the documents as current. The Residential Tenancies Act 1997 is version 115, in force from 13 October 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 is version 009, in force from 30 June 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The retrieved text doesn't use the phrase "Authorised Version," so these numbers come from the document metadata.

## What the law says

- **Rental minimum standards:** The property must be "structurally sound and weatherproof" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Each room must be "free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Condition at move-in:** The landlord must ensure the premises comply with the rental minimum standards and are "vacant and reasonably clean when the renter moves in" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Mould and damp count as urgent:** "Urgent repairs" include "any fault or damage that makes rented premises... unsafe or insecure, including... the presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure," and "a failure to comply with any rental minimum standards" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Condition report:** Before you move in, the landlord must give you a signed condition report stating the state of repair [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If you aren't given one, you may complete one yourself, and it is taken as notice to the landlord of any defects it records [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You may apply to VCAT to amend an inaccurate report within 30 days of the agreement starting [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do

1. **Notify the landlord in writing now.** You must give written notice "as soon as practicable after becoming aware" of damage [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Put the mould, damp and rotting timber in writing and attach photos.
2. **Ask for urgent repairs.** You may arrange urgent repairs if you have taken reasonable steps to get the landlord to do them immediately and the landlord cannot be reached or doesn't act [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You must give 7 days' written notice of the repairs and their cost, and the landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations' summary says reimbursement can be up to $2500 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Apply to VCAT for urgent repairs** if you cannot meet the cost, the cost is more than $2500, or the landlord refuses to pay for repairs you arrange [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). VCAT must hear the application within 2 business days [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Ask for non-urgent repairs.** If the work isn't urgent, you can apply to the Director after giving written notice and waiting 14 days without repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You can then apply to VCAT [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. **Rent into the Rent Special Account.** If you have given notice requiring repairs, you can apply to VCAT to pay rent into the Rent Special Account if the landlord has failed to carry out the repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This holds rent back. It is not a reduction, and the Tribunal decides whether it applies [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Your three questions

- **Ask for repairs:** Yes, as described above.
- **Lower rent:** The retrieved documents don't contain a provision that reduces rent for disrepair. The closest option is the Rent Special Account in point 5 above.
- **Cancel:** The retrieved documents don't set out a clear right for you to end the agreement over these conditions. Form 2 refers to notice of intention to vacate under section 91ZD "on the basis the premises are destroyed or unfit for habitation" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf), but the text of section 91ZD was not retrieved, so I can't tell you its conditions. Section 80 also says renters can't use the repair remedies where a Housing Act 1983 declaration that the house is unfit for habitation is in force [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I can't tell whether that applies to you.

## Gaps

I could not retrieve the text of section 68 (the landlord's duty to comply with minimum standards), section 91ZD, or the Tribunal's powers on termination. Before deciding whether to end the agreement, check those provisions and get advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy advocate. Consumer Affairs also publishes guidance at consumer.vic.gov.au/renting [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

Instead it says the documents "don't set out a clear right for you to end the agreement over these conditions" and hedges on s 91ZD. The move-in minimum standards point and the urgent repairs route are covered.

question: Our rental was broken into several times while we were moving out, and there are about three weeks left on our fixed-term lease. The burglars damaged the plumbing and wiring, so we can't even clean properly. What are our options before the lease ends?
answer:
**Sources:** The main source is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), version 115, in force from 13 October 2026, the current version as of today. The *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf), version 009, in force from 30 June 2026, is also relevant. The documents show these as "version" numbers in their metadata, not as "Authorised Version" numbers.

## What the law says

- **Damage must be reported in writing.** A renter must give written notice to the provider "as soon as practicable after becoming aware of" damage to the premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Notice can be given electronically [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs include the problems you describe.** The Act's definition covers a burst water service, a dangerous electrical fault, and "any fault or damage that makes rented premises... unsafe or insecure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Your plumbing and wiring damage likely falls within this, and so may the broken locks, though that depends on the facts.
- **The renter is not automatically liable for break-in damage.** The renter's duty not to damage the premises covers damage caused intentionally or negligently by the renter or a visitor, and "damage does not include fair wear and tear" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Whether the burglars count as visitors (someone on the premises with the renter's permission) is a question the documents don't answer.
- **Cleaning is limited.** At the end of the agreement, the renter must leave the premises "as far as practicable" reasonably clean, allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

1. **Notify the provider in writing now.** Describe the break-in, the plumbing and wiring damage, and the security problems, and say which items are unsafe or unusable. Keep a copy.
2. **Ask for urgent repairs.** You may arrange urgent repairs yourself only if you have "taken reasonable steps" to get the provider to repair immediately and cannot get them done [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You must then give the provider 7 days' written notice of the repairs and their cost, and the provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days of that notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Reimbursement is capped at the lesser of the reasonable cost or the prescribed amount [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations summary gives the prescribed amount as up to $2,500 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Apply to VCAT if needed.** You can apply to VCAT for an order requiring urgent repairs if you cannot meet the cost, the cost is more than the prescribed amount, or the provider refuses to reimburse you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). VCAT must hear the application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Locks.** The Regulations say a renter must get consent to change a lock in a master key system, and the provider must not unreasonably refuse [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
5. **Document the condition now.** The Regulations recommend taking dated photos showing the condition of items [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The provider must complete the end-of-tenancy condition report within 10 days after the agreement ends and give you a chance to attend if possible [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
6. **Ending the lease early.** A renter may give a notice of intention to vacate on the basis that the premises are "unfit for human habitation" or "destroyed totally or to such an extent as to be rendered unsafe." The termination date may be the date of the notice or a later date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Whether your premises meet this test depends on the facts. Ordinary notice periods are not enough: a notice to end a fixed-term agreement before its term ends is generally of no effect [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If you rely on this route, the Regulations say the provider cannot claim rent foregone where the agreement ends on this basis, but that rule is in a standard form for agreements over 5 years [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Your lease may not be on that form.

## What the documents don't cover

- Whether a three-week gap before the fixed term ends is covered by any specific early-termination rule beyond the notice provisions above.
- Whether the burglary is covered by insurance, or whether police reporting affects the renter's rights.
- Whether the provider can claim the cost of damage from the bond.

If you rely on the "unfit or unsafe" route or plan to withhold rent for repairs, get advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy lawyer before acting.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are present. The answer says a renter must give written notice 'as soon as practicable after becoming aware of' damage. It says burst water services and dangerous electrical faults are urgent repairs that the renter may arrange and have reimbursed if the provider does not repair immediately. On the hardest point, it says a renter may give a notice of intention to vacate because the premises are 'unfit for human habitation' or unsafe, and that 'the termination date may be the date of the notice', presenting this to a fixed-term renter as an exception to the rule that ordinary notices cannot end a fixed term early.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer says neither: it states "The renter is not automatically liable for break-in damage" and offers a way out of the lease if the premises are "unfit for human habitation" or "destroyed totally or to such an extent as to be rendered unsafe"; its note that ordinary early notice "is generally of no effect" is not a claim that the renter must stay whatever the condition.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as "version 115, in force from 13 October 2026" (link 97-109aa115), which is the required in-force version, and the only other document it relies on is the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 "version 009, in force from 30 June 2026" (link 21-3sra009), which is also in force on that date.

question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. The app is run by a payments company my agent uses, and it's that company that charges the card fee. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the retrieved documents, the card fee is probably not allowed. The documents do not say who the payments company is or whether any other Act permits a payment surcharge, so that point needs checking. Who receives the fee does not change the answer.

**What the law says**

- **Fee ban:** A person other than an ADI (authorised deposit-taking institution) must not demand or receive a fee for any prescribed matter in relation to an application or the payment of rent. The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person or 400 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The prescribed matters include "rent payment (other than payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act)" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The documents do not identify any Act that permits such a surcharge.
- **Charges for electronic payment:** A person must not demand or receive a charge for establishing or using "any other electronic payment facility for payment of rent," with a penalty of 60 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Free method must be available:** The provider or agent must ensure that a rent payment method incurring no additional costs (other than the renter's own bank or account fees) is reasonably available to the renter [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Electronic funds transfer is the prescribed payment method [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Disclosure:** Before the renter consents to a payment method, the provider or agent must tell the renter about any costs, including third-party transaction fees and other electronic payment facility fees [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**Does it matter who gets the fee?**

No, on these documents. The fee ban applies to "a person," not only to the landlord or agent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The payments company receiving the fee is therefore caught, and so is the agent if the fee is passed on. The duties to offer a free method and disclose costs sit with the provider or agent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and the agent using the app is the one responsible for those duties.

**What you can do or ask**

1. Ask the agent in writing to confirm the card fee is not charged, or to identify the Act that permits it.
2. Ask for the bank transfer option as the free method the agent must make reasonably available [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). question: My lease is on the standard form and started in 2024. It has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. I cleaned them myself and they're back to how they were when I moved in, but the agent wants a receipt from a professional cleaner. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?
answer:
**Short answer:** Probably not, if the cleaning was not professional-standard work at the start. The law limits when a provider can require professional cleaning at the end of a tenancy. The documents don't say you must provide a cleaner's receipt, and they don't show the wording of your 2024 lease.

## What the law says

- **The provider's limit:** A provider must not require the renter to arrange professional cleaning, or cleaning to a professional standard, at the end of the tenancy unless either (a) professional cleaning was done before the tenancy started and the renter was told so, or (b) professional cleaning is required to restore the premises to the condition they were in before the tenancy started, having regard to the condition report and taking into account fair wear and tear [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **The renter's duty:** The renter must leave the premises as far as practicable reasonably clean, and in the same condition as when they moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Bond claims:** A provider can claim for the reasonable cost of cleaning only if the premises were not left reasonably clean, having regard to their condition at the start of the agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Standard form:** The standard form repeats the same limit on professional cleaning [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

1. **Check the start-of-tenancy facts.** Find out whether professional cleaning was done before you moved in and whether you were told. If not, the first limb of the rule does not apply, and the provider must rely on the second limb, which depends on the condition report [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
2. **Pull your condition report.** The report's statements are conclusive evidence of the state of repair or general condition if signed by both parties [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Check whether it describes the carpets, and whether you added comments [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Gather evidence of the carpets' condition.** The condition report form advises renters to take photos at the start and end of the tenancy, and to keep the report safe because it helps resolve disputes over cleaning . Photos should be dated, labelled by location, and sent to the agent with any amended report .
4. **Attend the final inspection.** The provider must complete the end-of-tenancy report within 10 days after the end of the agreement, and give you an opportunity to attend if possible . Note any disagreement in writing.
5. **Respond to any bond claim.** Before a claim is made, the provider must give you bond claim evidence at least 3 days in advance, and that evidence must not conflict with the condition report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If there is a dispute, a party can apply to VCAT for a bond repayment order, which must be made within 14 days after the agreement ends [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Limits of these documents

- I could not find the wording of the 2024 lease, so I can't confirm whether its clause matches the current prescribed term.
- The documents don't say whether a receipt from a professional cleaner is required as evidence.
- Whether the carpets are restored to their pre-tenancy condition is a factual question. The documents don't say how a renter should prove it beyond the condition report and photos.

**Sources used:**
[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115 (in force from 13 October 2026), rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf.
[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Version 009 (in force from 30 June 2026), rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf (regulation 12 and Form 1, clause 11).
 The Form 4 condition report in the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Version 009 (in force from 30 June 2026), rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf.

If you tell me what your condition report says about the carpets, I can help you work out which limb applies. For a formal view on your specific lease, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria or VCAT.

The output covers all three points: the reg 12 limit on requiring professional cleaning ('unless either (a) professional cleaning was done before the tenancy started and the renter was told so, or (b) professional cleaning is required to restore the premises to the condition they were in before the tenancy started... taking into account fair wear and tear'), the renter's duty to leave the premises 'reasonably clean, and in the same condition as when they moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear', and the condition report as the deciding evidence ('The report's statements are conclusive evidence of the state of repair or general condition if signed by both parties', plus start-of-tenancy photos).

question: When I moved out I agreed the agent could take an amount for cleaning out of my bond, but I never signed a bond claim form for it. Then my full bond came back to me, and a month later the agent sent a separate invoice for the cleaning. Do I have to pay it? Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents don't say whether a renter who agreed to a bond deduction is also bound to pay a later separate invoice. They do set out rules that an agent must follow before taking cleaning costs from a bond, and those rules suggest the agent's route was not followed.

## What the law says

The current version is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

- **Cleaning is a valid bond claim, with limits.** A provider may claim from the bond "the reasonable cost of cleaning any part of the premises, if the premises were not left reasonably clean by the renter, having regard to the condition of the premises at the commencement of the residential rental agreement" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Renters must leave the premises reasonably clean.** At the end of the agreement, the renter must leave the premises "as far as practicable" reasonably clean [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Evidence must be given first.** "At least 3 days before a claim for repayment of a bond to the residential rental provider is made," the provider must give each renter "bond claim evidence that supports the claim" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Bond claim evidence means "an invoice," "a receipt," "a quote," "a photograph," or other prescribed evidence [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Claims go through the Authority.** A bond claim is made to the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority, and must be in a form the Authority approves [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Signing a claim form.** A provider must not request or obtain a renter's signature on a claim form unless the form specifies the amount of bond to be refunded and any apportionment [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Professional cleaning.** The Regulations say the provider must not require professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy unless specific conditions are met, such as the premises having been professionally cleaned at the start of the tenancy and the renter having been told so [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Compensation outside the bond.** A person who has recovered compensation from a bond is not precluded from taking proceedings under Part 5 to recover an additional amount by way of compensation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents do not explain how that process works or what limits apply.

## What this means for your situation

- **Your bond was fully returned.** The documents indicate that a cleaning charge should have been claimed through the bond process, with supporting evidence provided at least 3 days beforehand [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Since your full bond was refunded, it appears that no valid bond claim for cleaning was made.
- **Whether you must pay the invoice:** The documents don't say whether a later invoice is enforceable once the bond has been refunded. They also don't say whether a verbal or informal agreement to a bond deduction counts as agreement to pay a separate invoice. I can't answer either point from these sources.

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask the agent in writing** what bond claim evidence supports the charge, and whether a claim was lodged with the Authority, and when [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Check the cleaning terms** in your residential rental agreement against the professional cleaning rules in the Regulations [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Also compare the invoice with the condition report and your move-in condition.
3. **Get advice before paying.** A tenancy advice service, or the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT), can tell you whether the charge is enforceable. The documents I retrieved don't cover the Tribunal's process for these disputes, so please verify that separately.

I can't answer either point from these sources.' The second point is covered by the quote about premises 'not left reasonably clean by the renter, having regard to the condition of the premises at the commencement'.

question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. I've called them twice today. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
**Short answer:** You may not have to wait. If the conditions in the Act are met, you can arrange the urgent repair yourself and seek reimbursement, but you must follow the notice steps and use a suitably qualified person.

**Documents used:** The *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 115, in force from 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Version 009, in force from 30 June 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### What the law says

- **Urgent repairs:** The Act defines urgent repairs to include a "failure or breakdown of the gas, electricity or water supply to rented premises" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A broken tap may not clearly fall within that wording, so whether this counts as urgent is not settled by the documents. The definition also covers "a burst water service" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **When you can arrange repairs:** You may arrange urgent repairs only if (a) you have taken reasonable steps to get the provider or their agent to carry out the repairs immediately, and (b) you cannot get them to do it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Written notice:** You must give the provider written notice of the repairs and their cost within 7 days of doing them [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Reimbursement:** The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days after receiving that written notice. Their liability is the lesser of the reasonable cost or the prescribed amount [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations summary gives that amount as up to $2500 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Who can do the work:** Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, both urgent and non-urgent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). This includes a registered or licensed tradesperson where the work requires it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do

1. **Put it in writing now.** The Act requires written notice of breakdowns as soon as practicable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and the Regulations say that urgent repair requests should be made in writing [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Your two calls may not be enough on their own to show "reasonable steps," so send an email or letter to the emergency contact with the date, time and details of your calls.
2. **Hire a suitably qualified person** if the provider still cannot attend [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Choose someone registered or licensed for the work.
3. **Keep the receipts** and send the provider written notice of the repairs and cost within 7 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Seek reimbursement**, which the provider must pay within 7 days of receiving your notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. **If the provider refuses or the cost is too high,** you may apply to VCAT for an order requiring the repairs. This applies if you cannot meet the cost, the cost is more than $2500, or the provider refuses to pay you back [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). VCAT must hear an urgent repair application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What the documents don't cover

- They don't say whether the owner can insist on using only their own tradespeople when the urgent-repair conditions are otherwise met.
- They don't say whether two phone calls alone satisfy the "reasonable steps" requirement.
- They don't confirm whether a broken tap alone is an "urgent repair," or whether the whole-house water shut-off changes that.
- The $2500 figure is taken from the Regulations summary, not from the prescribed amount itself [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

Because whether this is urgent and whether your steps are "reasonable" depend on the facts, Consumer Affairs Victoria (consumer.vic.gov.au/urgentrepairs) is listed in the documents as the source for the full urgent-repairs list [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: No. The third point is missing: the answer never says a term requiring the renter to use the landlord's nominated tradesperson is prohibited (reg 11(e)), or that the preferred-tradesperson policy cannot stop an urgent repair. Instead it says the documents "don't say whether the owner can insist on using only their own tradespeople."

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the renter must wait for the landlord's preferred tradesperson or that the cost cannot be recovered; it states "You may not have to wait... you can arrange the urgent repair yourself and seek reimbursement" and that "The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days after receiving that written notice."

Every rule it applies is cited to those versions, and it relies on no other version.

question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. I haven't moved any of my things in or stayed there yet. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
## What the law says

- **The landlord must maintain the home.** The provider must ensure the premises comply with the rental minimum standards and are vacant and reasonably clean when the renter moves in, and must maintain them in good repair and a fit condition for occupation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The standards require the home to be structurally sound and weatherproof, and each room must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Mould, damp and structural faults can be urgent repairs.** "Urgent repairs" includes any fault or damage that makes premises unsafe or insecure, including mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure, and any failure to comply with rental minimum standards [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Whether the rotting timber is an urgent repair will depend on whether it makes the home unsafe or insecure. The documents don't say how to classify it.
- **Condition report.** Before you move in, the provider must give you a signed condition report stating the state of repair [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If you're given a report, you can record disagreement with any statement, and a report you return is taken as notice to the provider of any defects it states [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Within 30 days after the agreement starts, either party can apply to VCAT to amend an inaccurate or incomplete statement [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A signed report is conclusive evidence of the condition on the day specified, except for matters you dispute in writing or that couldn't reasonably have been discovered on inspection [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Your options

1. **Give written notice now.** You must give written notice to the provider as soon as practicable after becoming aware of damage [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Write to them listing the mould, damp and timber problems.
2. **Arrange urgent repairs yourself (if they are urgent).** You may do this if you have taken reasonable steps to get the provider to repair immediately and they can't or don't [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You must give 7 days' written notice of the repairs and cost. The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days, up to the lesser of that cost or the prescribed amount [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The prescribed amount is summarised as up to $2,500 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Apply to VCAT for an urgent repairs order.** You can do this if you can't meet the cost, the cost is more than $2,500, or the provider refuses to pay for repairs you arrange [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). VCAT must hear the application within 2 business days [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Non-urgent repairs.** Give written notice that repairs are needed. If the provider doesn't carry them out within 14 days, you can apply to the Director [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) or to VCAT for an order requiring repairs. VCAT must hear that application within 7 days [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). VCAT can order specified repairs, use of a suitably qualified person, and compensation [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. **Pay rent into the Rent Special Account.** After giving a repair notice, you can ask VCAT to order that rent be paid into the Rent Special Account if the provider fails to carry out repairs and cannot show financial hardship [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This holds your rent. It does not reduce it.

## Lower rent

The retrieved documents do not contain a provision that lets you reduce rent for these defects. The closest options are compensation through a VCAT repairs order [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and rent held in the Rent Special Account [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The compensation provision refers to section 212(2), but its text is not in the retrieved material.

## Cancelling

The documents mention a notice to vacate under section 91ZD where premises are destroyed or unfit for habitation. In that case, the provider cannot claim rent foregone [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). However, the retrieved material does not include the text of section 91ZD, so I can't tell you the procedure, the test, or the notice period. The documents also don't say explicitly whether these rights apply before you've moved in. Section 80 also says you can't use the repair remedies if the house is subject to a Housing Act declaration that it's unfit for habitation [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**Sources and versions:** The Residential Tenancies Act 1997 retrieved is version 115, in force from 13 October 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 retrieved is version 009, in force from 30 June 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The retrieved metadata doesn't show a separate "Authorised Version" label, so I have used the version numbers shown.

Because I don't have the full text of sections 68 and 91ZD, I'd recommend checking the current Act on the Victorian legislation website, or speaking to Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy lawyer before you decide whether to cancel.
