question: Our rental was broken into several times while we were moving out, and there are about three weeks left on our fixed-term lease. The burglars damaged the plumbing and wiring, so we can't even clean properly. What are our options before the lease ends?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved law gives you several options before the lease ends: written notice, urgent repairs with reimbursement, and possibly ending the lease early if the premises are unsafe. The documents do not address damage caused by burglars specifically, so some points below are inferences.

**Sources:** The Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Version 115 (in force from 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Version 009 (in force from 30 June 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Reporting damage:** You must give the landlord written notice "as soon as practicable" after becoming aware of damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Who is liable for damage:** A renter must not intentionally or negligently cause damage, and fair wear and tear is excluded [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The duty covers the renter and any "visitor," meaning a person with the renter's permission [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Intruders are not covered by that definition, but the documents do not expressly say whether burglary damage falls outside the renter's liability.
- **Landlord's repair duty:** The landlord must "maintain the premises in good repair and in a fit condition for occupation" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs:** The Act's definition includes "a burst water service," "a dangerous electrical fault," and "any fault or damage that makes rented premises... unsafe or insecure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Plumbing and wiring damage may fall within these categories.
- **Cleaning:** A renter must leave the premises "as far as practicable" reasonably clean [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The landlord can claim cleaning costs only if the premises were not left reasonably clean, "having regard to the condition of the premises at the commencement" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Early exit:** A renter may give a notice of intention to vacate if the premises "are unfit for human habitation" or "have been destroyed totally or to such an extent as to be rendered unsafe." The termination date may be the date of the notice or later [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents do not say whether a lease-break fee applies on this ground.

## What you can do or ask

1. **Send written notice now.** List the plumbing damage, wiring damage, break-ins, and any safety or security issues. Include photos and dates. The Regulations also say that where damage occurs, the renter must notify the rental provider in writing [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
2. **Request urgent repairs.** Ask the landlord to fix the plumbing and wiring immediately. If they cannot or do not, you may arrange repairs yourself, but only after taking reasonable steps to get the landlord to act immediately [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You must then give the landlord 7 days' written notice of the repairs and their cost, and the landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days of receiving that notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Know the reimbursement cap.** The Regulations state that a renter may be reimbursed directly "for the reasonable cost of repairs up to $2500" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
4. **Go to VCAT if needed.** You may apply to VCAT for an urgent repairs order if you cannot meet the cost, the cost is more than $2500, or the landlord refuses to pay for repairs you arranged [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). VCAT must hear such an application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. **Non-urgent items.** If repairs are not urgent, you may apply to VCAT if the landlord has not carried them out within 14 days of your notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
6. **Security.** The landlord must not unreasonably refuse consent to "reasonable security measures" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Changing a lock in a master key system requires the landlord's consent, which must not be unreasonably refused [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
7. **Cleaning.** Clean as far as practicable. Professional cleaning may only be required in the circumstances listed in the standard form [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Keep records showing why you could not clean fully.
8. **Document everything.** Take dated photos. The Regulations recommend photos at the start and end of the tenancy and state that the landlord must complete the end-of-tenancy condition report within 10 days after the agreement ends [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
9. **Consider ending the lease early.** If the premises are unsafe or unfit, you may give a notice of intention to vacate under the ground described above [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Seek advice before doing so, since the documents do not confirm whether a break fee applies.

**Not covered by the documents:** insurance claims, police reporting, and whether burglary damage counts as the renter's responsibility. Please check these with the relevant body or a qualified adviser. The Regulations point to the Consumer Affairs Victoria renting website for further information [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. The hardest is urgent repairs: the answer hedges with 'may fall within these categories' but then advises 'Ask the landlord to fix the plumbing and wiring immediately. If they cannot or do not, you may arrange repairs yourself... the landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost.' Written notice 'as soon as practicable' and the notice to vacate for unfit or unsafe premises 'may be the date of the notice', applied to ending this lease early, are also stated.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer asserts neither failing claim. It places the repair duty on the landlord: "The landlord must 'maintain the premises in good repair and in a fit condition for occupation'". It treats renter-arranged repairs as reimbursable: "the landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost". It offers an early exit: "you may give a notice of intention to vacate".

question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. The app is run by a payments company my agent uses, and it's that company that charges the card fee. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
## What the law says

The current documents are:

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version v115, in force from 13 October 2026** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version v009, in force from 30 June 2026** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

A rental provider or agent must make reasonably available a rent-payment method with **no additional cost**, except the renter’s own bank or account fees. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The Regulations prescribe **electronic funds transfer** as a payment method that must be permitted. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The Act also prohibits a person **other than an ADI** from demanding or receiving a fee for a prescribed matter concerning rent payment. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The Regulations prescribe **rent payment**, except for “payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act.” [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

Therefore, the documents do **not** establish that the card fee is lawful merely because:

- it is charged by the payments company rather than the agent; or
- a fee-free bank-transfer option exists, if that option is reasonably available.

The documents do not define **ADI**, do not identify whether the payments company is an ADI, and do not explain when a card fee is a “payment surcharge fee permitted under any other Act.” Accordingly, the documents do not contain enough information to conclude that this particular card fee is permitted.

The agent or rental provider must also give you information about costs—including **third-party transaction fees** and **electronic payment facility fees**—before you consent to use the payment method. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

Ask the agent to confirm, in writing:

1. why the card fee is permitted under section 51A and regulation 21C;  
2. whether the payments company is an **ADI**;  
3. what other Act allegedly permits the fee as a “payment surcharge fee”; and  
4. that the manual electronic-funds-transfer option is available without additional cost and is reasonably usable. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

On the documents retrieved, you can insist on using the fee-free electronic-funds-transfer option, but they do not state that the agent must make the slower option as fast as card payment. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. (1) The answer says the agent 'must make reasonably available a rent-payment method with no additional cost, except the renter's own bank or account fees.' (2) It says the Act 'prohibits a person other than an ADI from demanding or receiving a fee' for rent payment, subject to the exception for 'payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act,' and that the fee is not lawful 'merely because it is charged by the payments company rather than the agent.' This covers the hardest point, despite the caveat about ADI status. (3) It gives next steps: ask the agent for written confirmation, and 'insist on using the fee-free electronic-funds-transfer option.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes: neither failing claim is made, since the answer rejects the fee-free-option reasoning ('the documents do **not** establish that the card fee is lawful merely because... a fee-free bank-transfer option exists') and applies the ban to any 'person **other than an ADI**', with no exemption for the landlord or agent.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names both required documents in their in-force versions, "Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version v115, in force from 13 October 2026" (link 97-109aa115) and "Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version v009, in force from 30 June 2026" (link 21-3sra009), and relies on no other version.

question: My lease is on the standard form and started in 2024. It has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. I cleaned them myself and they're back to how they were when I moved in, but the agent wants a receipt from a professional cleaner. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?
answer:
## What the law says

The current retrieved versions are **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115 (in force 13 October 2026)** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) and **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009 (in force 30 June 2026)** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

You **do not automatically have to pay for professional carpet cleaning or provide a professional cleaner’s receipt**. The standard-form term only permits professional cleaning when it is required to restore the premises to their condition immediately before the tenancy, considering the condition report and fair wear and tear. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

A clause requiring professional cleaning in every case is not enforceable if it is an additional prohibited term: the Act prohibits terms requiring professional cleaning or payment for it unless the term is contained in the standard form. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The standard-form wording is conditional, not an unconditional requirement. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

Because the Act requires you to leave the premises reasonably clean and in the same condition as when you moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear, cleaning the carpets yourself may be sufficient if you have restored them to that condition. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) A rental provider may claim only the **reasonable cost of cleaning** if the premises were not left reasonably clean, having regard to their condition at the start of the tenancy. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

- Reply in writing that the carpets were cleaned and returned to their starting condition, and ask the agent to identify the specific condition requiring professional cleaning under the condition report.  
- Provide the signed condition report and **dated, labelled photographs** of the carpets from the start and end of the tenancy; the prescribed condition-report form specifically says these records can help resolve cleaning disputes. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)  
- Ask the agent to conduct or document the final inspection with you present or given a reasonable opportunity to attend. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)  
- If the agent seeks money from the bond, ask for the evidence supporting the claim: they must give bond-claim evidence at least **3 days before** making a claim, and that evidence must not conflict with the condition report. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved documents do not say that a professional receipt is required where the carpets have otherwise been restored to the required condition.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered, though point 1 is satisfied only through its alternatives rule. Point 1: the answer says the standard-form term "only permits professional cleaning when it is required to restore the premises to their condition immediately before the tenancy, considering the condition report and fair wear and tear." It leaves out the other limb (cleaning done before the tenancy with the renter told). The rubric allows any one alternative, and the restoration limb is the one that applies here. Point 2: the answer says the Act requires leaving the premises "reasonably clean and in the same condition as when you moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear." Point 3: the answer relies on the signed condition report and dated move-in and move-out photographs as the evidence for resolving the cleaning dispute.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the renter must pay simply because of the clause or the pet. It says the opposite: 'You do not automatically have to pay for professional carpet cleaning or provide a professional cleaner's receipt', and that professional cleaning is permitted only 'when it is required to restore the premises to their condition immediately before the tenancy.'

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names both required documents with their in-force versions, 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115 (in force 13 October 2026)' (link 97-109aa115) and 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009 (in force 30 June 2026)' (link 21-3sra009), and relies on no other version.

question: When I moved out I agreed the agent could take an amount for cleaning out of my bond, but I never signed a bond claim form for it. Then my full bond came back to me, and a month later the agent sent a separate invoice for the cleaning. Do I have to pay it? Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?
answer:
## What the law says

Under the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997**, current **Authorised Version No. 115**, incorporating amendments as at **13 October 2026**, a renter must leave the premises reasonably clean, allowing for fair wear and tear. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) A rental provider may claim from the bond the **reasonable cost of cleaning** if the premises were not left reasonably clean, having regard to their condition at the start of the tenancy. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

A bond claim must be made in an Authority-approved form. A renter’s signature is specifically required where the claim is a **joint claim** allocating part of the bond to the rental provider. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The Act does not say that a renter’s agreement to a proposed bond deduction, by itself, is the same as agreeing to pay a separate invoice.

The Act allows a rental provider to seek compensation for loss or damage arising from a failure to comply with the rental agreement or the Act. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Therefore, the return of the full bond does **not, by itself, establish that no cleaning claim can ever be made**; the documents do not state that repayment of the bond bars a separate compensation claim. However, they also do not say that a later invoice is automatically payable merely because the renter previously agreed that an amount could be taken from the bond. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Any professional-cleaning requirement must also comply with the prescribed rules: professional cleaning may generally be required only where it is needed to restore the premises to their starting condition, taking account of the condition report and fair wear and tear, or where professional cleaning was carried out before the tenancy and the renter was told about it. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

You do **not have to assume that the invoice is automatically enforceable**. Ask the agent to provide:

- the condition report and evidence that the premises were not left reasonably clean;
- the cleaning invoice, receipt or other evidence of the actual reasonable cost; and
- the legal or contractual basis on which they say your earlier agreement to a bond deduction also created a separate obligation to pay an invoice. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

You can state that your agreement concerned a **possible deduction from the bond**, that no bond claim form was signed, and that the full bond was subsequently repaid. Whether your particular communication amounted to a separate binding agreement to pay remains a factual and contractual question that the retrieved documents do **not** answer.

If the agent insists on payment, you can dispute the invoice and ask the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal to determine whether compensation is payable and, if so, the reasonable amount. The Act permits the Tribunal to make a compensation order where a party failed to comply with the residential rental agreement or the Act. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The documents do not provide a specific deadline for the agent’s separate cleaning invoice in these circumstances. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered. The first is addressed by 'The Act does not say that a renter's agreement to a proposed bond deduction, by itself, is the same as agreeing to pay a separate invoice' and 'your agreement concerned a possible deduction from the bond'. The second is addressed by 'if the premises were not left reasonably clean, having regard to their condition at the start of the tenancy', together with the reference to VCAT determining compensation.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer asserts neither failure condition: it says agreeing to a deduction is not automatically the same as agreeing to pay an invoice ('The Act does not say that a renter's agreement to a proposed bond deduction, by itself, is the same as agreeing to pay a separate invoice'), and it rejects the idea that full repayment bars any further claim ('the return of the full bond does not, by itself, establish that no cleaning claim can ever be made').

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, current Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026', and the only other version it relies on is the Regulations via link '21-3sra009' (version 009), which is the version in force on that date.

question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. I've called them twice today. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
## What the law says

The current document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115, in force from 13 October 2026**, authored by **Barbara Hargreaves**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The prescribed standard agreement is in **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009, in force from 30 June 2026**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

A failure or breakdown of the **water supply** to rented premises is an **urgent repair**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) However, the Act does not expressly say that every broken tap is urgent; a water-using fixture is urgent where it is malfunctioning in a way that results, or will result, in a substantial amount of water being wasted. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

You do **not** have to wait indefinitely for the owner’s preferred tradespeople. A renter may arrange urgent repairs if they have taken reasonable steps to get the rental provider or agent to arrange them immediately and are unable to do so. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Calling twice today and being told that none of those tradespeople can attend yet may satisfy that requirement, but the documents do not define exactly how many calls or how much waiting is “reasonable.” [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

- Arrange the repair **now**, provided you use a **suitably qualified person**; you should not personally carry out work requiring a qualified tradesperson. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- Keep records of your calls, the emergency contact’s response, photographs, and the invoice.
- Give the rental provider **written notice within 7 days** stating what repair was carried out and its cost. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- The rental provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within **7 days** after receiving that notice, up to **$2,500** under the prescribed agreement information. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- If you cannot afford the repair, it costs more than **$2,500**, or the rental provider refuses to pay, you can apply to the Tribunal for an urgent-repair order; the Tribunal must hear that application within **2 business days**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The documents do not state that the owner may require you to wait for their own tradespeople after you have taken reasonable steps and they cannot arrange the repair immediately. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. Water supply failure is stated as urgent. Self-arranged repair after reasonable steps, with reimbursement up to $2,500 within 7 days of written notice, is stated. The hardest point, that the preferred-tradesperson policy cannot stop an urgent repair, is covered by 'You do not have to wait indefinitely for the owner's preferred tradespeople' and 'The documents do not state that the owner may require you to wait for their own tradespeople after you have taken reasonable steps and they cannot arrange the repair immediately.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer says neither forbidden thing: it states "You do **not** have to wait indefinitely for the owner's preferred tradespeople" and "The rental provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within **7 days**... up to **$2,500**," so it affirms the renter's right to arrange the repair and recover the cost.

version-cited.reason: Yes: the answer names both required documents with their in-force versions, 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115, in force from 13 October 2026' and 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009, in force from 30 June 2026', and every rule it applies is cited only to those versions (links 97-109aa115 and 21-3sra009).

question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. I haven't moved any of my things in or stayed there yet. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
## What the law says

The current documents are **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115, in force from 13 October 2026** (“the Act”) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009, in force from 30 June 2026** (“the Regulations”) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

The premises must meet rental minimum standards. They must be **structurally sound and weatherproof**, and every room must be free from mould and damp caused by, or related to, the building structure. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) The rental provider must also ensure the premises comply with those standards and are maintained in good repair and fit for occupation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

Mould or damp related to the building structure is expressly included in the Act’s definition of **urgent repairs**; a failure to comply with rental minimum standards is also an urgent repair. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Rotting timber may indicate that the premises are not structurally sound, but the retrieved documents do not specifically address rotting timber.

The fact that you have collected the keys but have not moved in does not, by itself, appear in the retrieved documents as a right to cancel the signed agreement. The standard agreement says that if a renter ends the agreement early, the rental provider may seek compensation for actual rent lost, capped at **no more than one month’s rent for each year remaining**, and must take reasonable steps to re-let the premises or otherwise minimise the loss. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

1. **Do not move your belongings in, and document everything.** Take dated photographs and videos of the mould, damp and timber, and keep all communications. The condition report is intended to record the premises’ state before occupation, and defects or outstanding repairs recorded in it count as notice to the rental provider. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

2. **Write immediately to the rental provider or agent.** State that the premises do not appear to meet the structural-soundness, weatherproofing, mould-and-damp, and fit-for-occupation requirements; attach the evidence; and request that the agreement be ended by mutual written agreement, with any bond and rent paid returned. The retrieved documents do not state that the provider must agree to cancel on that basis.

3. **Ask for repairs.** You can require the provider to address the defects. For urgent repairs, you must first take reasonable steps to have the provider or agent arrange them immediately; if that fails, you may arrange the repairs, give **7 days’ written notice** of the work and cost, and seek reimbursement of the reasonable cost, subject to the Act. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The Regulations prescribe **$2,500** as the amount relevant to a renter’s application to the Tribunal for urgent repairs. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

4. **Apply for an order if repairs are not done.** For non-urgent repairs, give written notice; if the provider has not carried them out within **14 days**, you may apply to the Tribunal for an order. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The Tribunal can order specified repairs, use of a suitably qualified person, and compensation. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

5. **Ask for lower rent, but do not assume you are entitled to it automatically.** The retrieved documents do not provide a specific right to reduce the agreed rent merely because defects were discovered before moving in. You may negotiate a temporary or permanent rent reduction, or seek compensation, but any agreement should be in writing. The Act does provide for compensation where the provider is in breach and, in some repair situations, allows the Tribunal to authorise rent being paid into the **Rent Special Account** rather than directly to the provider; that is not the same as unilaterally paying less rent. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

6. **Do not simply stop paying or treat the lease as cancelled without advice.** If the provider will not agree to end the agreement, ending it yourself may expose you to a claim for rent actually lost, subject to the agreement’s limits and the provider’s duty to minimise the loss. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) The retrieved documents do not contain a general pre-move-in cancellation right for this situation.

must-mention.reason: No. The answer misses the s 91L right: a renter who has not taken possession can end the agreement by notice if the premises do not meet the minimum standards, are not in good repair, or are unfit for habitation. Instead it says the opposite: 'The retrieved documents do not contain a general pre-move-in cancellation right for this situation.' It also does not say the minimum standards must be met by the day the renter moves in (s 65A), though it does cover the repair route.

The answer never says the renter must move in or pay rent first (it advises "Do not move your belongings in" and to "Write immediately to the rental provider"), and it denies an automatic rent-reduction right: "do not assume you are entitled to it automatically... any agreement should be in writing."
