question: Our rental was broken into several times while we were moving out, and there are about three weeks left on our fixed-term lease. The burglars damaged the plumbing and wiring, so we can't even clean properly. What are our options before the lease ends?
answer:
## What the law says

The current document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115, in force from 13 October 2026**, authored by **Barbara Hargreaves**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Damage to plumbing or wiring may be an **urgent repair** if it involves, for example, a burst water service, blocked or broken lavatory, dangerous electrical fault, failure of the water or electricity supply, or damage making the premises unsafe or insecure. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

A renter may end a fixed-term agreement immediately by giving a notice of intention to vacate if the premises are **unfit for human habitation** or have been destroyed, totally or substantially, so as to be **unsafe**; the termination date may be the date the notice is given or a later date. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The documents do not say whether the particular damage in your home meets that threshold, so that factual question cannot be decided from the documents alone. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

You must give written notice of damage as soon as practicable after becoming aware of it. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) At the end of the agreement, you must leave the premises reasonably clean **as far as practicable**, but only to the extent that the rental provider is responsible for the condition. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

1. **Write immediately to the rental provider or agent.** Describe the break-ins, plumbing and wiring damage, security issues, and why cleaning is not reasonably practicable. Request immediate urgent repairs and state that you are considering ending the agreement under section 91ZD. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

2. **If the premises are unfit or unsafe, give a notice of intention to vacate under section 91ZD.** That notice can specify an immediate termination date, despite the remaining three weeks of the fixed term. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

3. **If the premises are not yet established to be unfit or unsafe, do not rely only on a normal 28-day notice.** For a fixed-term agreement, an ordinary notice specifying a date before the fixed term ends has no effect. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

4. **Arrange urgent repairs yourself only after taking reasonable steps to have the provider or agent arrange them immediately and being unable to get them to do so.** You must then give seven days’ written notice of the repairs and cost; the provider must reimburse the reasonable cost, or the prescribed amount if lower, within seven days after receiving that notice. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

5. **Apply to the Tribunal for urgent-repair orders** if you cannot afford the repairs, they exceed the prescribed amount, or the provider refuses to pay; the Tribunal must hear that application within two business days. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

6. **If you give repair notice and the provider fails to repair, you may apply for permission to pay rent into the Rent Special Account.** Do not simply stop paying rent without such an order. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Keep photographs, police or incident reports, repair assessments, invoices, emails, and evidence showing why cleaning could not reasonably be completed. The retrieved documents support documenting the damage and repair evidence, but do not state any special compensation rule for burglary damage. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three required points are covered. (1) Written reporting: "You must give written notice of damage as soon as practicable after becoming aware of it." (2) Urgent repairs: the answer treats plumbing and wiring damage as urgent repairs, tells the renter to request immediate repairs, and says the renter can "Arrange urgent repairs yourself only after taking reasonable steps to have the provider or agent arrange them immediately... the provider must reimburse the reasonable cost." This is the hardest point because the opening line is hedged with "may be," but the rest of the answer makes the position clear. (3) Ending the lease: "If the premises are unfit or unsafe, give a notice of intention to vacate under section 91ZD. That notice can specify an immediate termination date, despite the remaining three weeks of the fixed term."

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer asserts neither failure condition. It places repair responsibility on the provider ('the provider must reimburse the reasonable cost') and says the renter may leave early ('A renter may end a fixed-term agreement immediately... if the premises are unfit for human habitation'). Its warning that an ordinary 28-day notice has no effect is conditional on the premises not being unfit, so it does not say the renter must stay whatever the condition.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the required document with its version, 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115, in force from 13 October 2026', and cites the matching link 97-109aa115. Every rule it applies is sourced to that in-force version, and no other version is relied on.

question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. The app is run by a payments company my agent uses, and it's that company that charges the card fee. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
## What the law says

The current **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, in force from 13 October 2026** says the rental provider or agent must ensure that a rent-payment method with **no additional cost**—apart from the renter’s own bank or account fees—is reasonably available. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The Act also prohibits a person other than an **ADI** from demanding or receiving a fee for a prescribed matter relating to payment of rent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The current **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 009, in force from 30 June 2026**, prescribe **“rent payment”** as such a matter, except for payment-surcharge fees permitted under another Act. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The Act separately prohibits charges for establishing or using a direct-debit facility or any other electronic payment facility for rent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) It also requires the rental provider or agent to tell the renter, before the renter consents to a payment method, about costs including **third-party transaction fees** and electronic-payment-facility fees. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Therefore:

- **The card fee is not automatically lawful merely because the payments company—not the agent—charges it.** The prohibition applies to “a person other than an ADI,” and the retrieved documents do not say whether this particular payments company is an ADI. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- **The fee may be covered by the prohibition** if it is a fee for rent payment or use of an electronic payment facility. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- **The documents do not establish that a card surcharge is permitted under another Act**, so they do not provide enough information to confirm that exception applies. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- A no-fee manual bank-transfer option may satisfy the fee-free-method requirement, but the documents do not define when a method is “reasonably available” or say whether being slower makes this option unreasonable. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- The rental provider or agent must permit electronic funds transfer as a prescribed payment method. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

## What the renter can ask or do

Ask the agent, in writing:

1. Whether the payments company is an **ADI**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
2. What legal authority under another Act is relied on for the card surcharge, if any. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
3. Why the no-fee bank-transfer method is considered reasonably available despite being slower. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
4. For the required information about all costs, including third-party transaction fees, before consenting to use the card method. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

On the documents provided, you can plainly say that **it is not established that the card fee is lawful**, and that directing the fee through the payments company does not, by itself, answer the issue. The documents do not state who is legally responsible where a third-party payments company imposes the fee, so that specific point cannot be answered more definitively from them.

must-mention.reason: Yes. The answer states that a no-extra-cost payment method must be reasonably available. It also covers the hardest point: 'The card fee is not automatically lawful merely because the payments company—not the agent—charges it. The prohibition applies to "a person other than an ADI"', which makes clear the ban turns on bank (ADI) status rather than who collects the fee, subject to the surcharge-under-another-Act exception. Finally, it gives a reasonable next step: asking the agent in writing about the fee's legal basis and the costs involved.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the fee is allowed just because a fee-free option exists, and never says the landlord or agent is exempt from the fee ban. It says a no-fee transfer "may satisfy the fee-free-method requirement" but concludes "it is not established that the card fee is lawful." It also applies the ban to "a person other than an ADI" without exempting the agent or landlord.

version-cited.reason: Yes: the answer names the 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, in force from 13 October 2026' and the 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 009, in force from 30 June 2026', with links 97-109aa115 and 21-3sra009, and it relies on no other version.

question: My lease is on the standard form and started in 2024. It has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. I cleaned them myself and they're back to how they were when I moved in, but the agent wants a receipt from a professional cleaner. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?
answer:
## What the law says

The current documents are:

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115, in force 13 October 2026** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009, in force 30 June 2026** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

A term requiring professional cleaning at the end of a tenancy is prohibited **unless it is contained in the standard form**; a prohibited term is void and unenforceable. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The standard-form professional-cleaning term does **not** require professional cleaning merely because the lease says so. It applies only if professional cleaning is needed to restore the premises to their condition immediately before the tenancy, considering the condition report and fair wear and tear. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The Act also requires you to leave the premises reasonably clean and in the same condition as at the start, allowing for fair wear and tear. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Therefore, on the facts you gave—carpets cleaned by you and restored to their starting condition—you do **not appear to have to pay for a professional cleaner or provide a professional-cleaning receipt**. The retrieved documents do not state that a professional receipt is required where professional cleaning is not necessary. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The rental provider may claim reasonable cleaning costs from the bond only if the premises were not left reasonably clean, having regard to their condition at the beginning of the tenancy. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

- Send the agent the signed **condition report**, pointing to the carpets’ condition at the start and explaining that they have been cleaned to the same condition, allowing for fair wear and tear. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- Provide dated, labelled photographs or video of the carpets after cleaning, showing both close-up detail and the room’s wider context; the prescribed condition-report form specifically says photographs should be taken at the beginning and end and may help resolve cleaning disputes. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- Ask the agent to identify the specific carpet condition they say requires professional restoration and to provide evidence supporting any proposed bond claim. Before claiming bond, the rental provider or agent must give you bond-claim evidence at least **3 days** beforehand, and that evidence must not conflict with the condition report. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- If the agent seeks bond money, you can dispute the claim through the bond process or apply to the Tribunal; the documents do not say that an agent may require a professional receipt simply because a pet lived at the premises. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: No. Point 1 is only partly covered: the answer says the standard-form term applies "only if professional cleaning is needed to restore the premises to their condition immediately before the tenancy," which leaves out the other limb (professional cleaning was done before the tenancy and the renter was told) and materially narrows the rule. Points 2 and 3 are covered.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the renter must pay for professional cleaning just because of the clause or the pet. It states the standard-form term "does **not** require professional cleaning merely because the lease says so" and that the renter does "**not** appear to have to pay for a professional cleaner or provide a professional-cleaning receipt", and it notes "the documents do not say that an agent may require a professional receipt simply because a pet lived at the premises."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names both required documents with their in-force versions, 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115, in force 13 October 2026' (link 97-109aa115) and 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009, in force 30 June 2026' (link 21-3sra009), and every rule it applies is sourced only from these versions.

question: When I moved out I agreed the agent could take an amount for cleaning out of my bond, but I never signed a bond claim form for it. Then my full bond came back to me, and a month later the agent sent a separate invoice for the cleaning. Do I have to pay it? Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?
answer:
## What the law says

The current document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115**, incorporating amendments as at **13 October 2026** (Author: Barbara Hargreaves). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

- You had a duty to leave the premises **reasonably clean**, allowing for fair wear and tear. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- The rental provider may claim from the bond the **reasonable cost of cleaning** if the premises were not left reasonably clean, having regard to their condition at the start of the tenancy. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- A bond claim must use an Authority-approved form. If the provider claims without everyone’s consent, the Authority must notify the other parties, who have **14 days** to notify the Authority that the claim is subject to a Tribunal application. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- Before making a claim for payment to the provider, the provider must give the renter supporting **bond claim evidence** at least **3 days** beforehand; an invoice is one type of bond claim evidence. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- The Act does **not** say in the retrieved documents that agreeing to a proposed bond deduction automatically means agreeing to pay a separate invoice. Nor does it expressly say that receiving the full bond prevents a later claim for cleaning. **So the documents do not provide a definitive yes-or-no answer to whether this particular invoice must be paid.**
- The Act does say that the Tribunal can award compensation where a party failed to comply with the rental agreement or the Act, and that the Tribunal may consider whether the renter consented to the failure. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

**Therefore:** agreeing that an amount could be taken from the bond is not, on the documents provided, clearly the same thing as agreeing to pay a separate invoice. Your actual words, the amount agreed, the cleaning condition, the condition reports and the invoice would matter.

## What you can do or ask

You can ask the agent to provide:

1. the signed or written agreement showing exactly what amount and liability you accepted;
2. the condition report and final inspection report;
3. the cleaning invoice, receipt or other evidence of the actual cost; and
4. an explanation why the full bond was returned and why a separate invoice was issued later.

You can dispute the invoice in writing and say that you agreed only to a bond deduction—not necessarily to a separate payment—and that the full bond was later repaid. Ask them to identify the legal or contractual basis for the invoice and to show that the cost is reasonable and relates to cleaning required under the Act. The retrieved documents do not state a specific deadline for this type of separate invoice.

The current related document is **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, version 009**, in force from **30 June 2026** (Author: Lavina Mandy). It provides that professional cleaning can only be required in the specified circumstances—such as restoring the premises to their starting condition, having regard to the condition report and fair wear and tear. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes (pass). The first point is hedged but its direction is clear: the answer says agreeing to a bond deduction is 'not... clearly the same thing as agreeing to pay a separate invoice' and that 'you agreed only to a bond deduction—not necessarily to a separate payment.' It also links bond claims to Authority-approved forms and bond claim evidence. The second point is covered by 'the reasonable cost of cleaning if the premises were not left reasonably clean, having regard to their condition at the start of the tenancy,' together with the reference to the Tribunal's compensation power.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. Neither failing claim is made: the answer says agreeing to a bond deduction is 'not, on the documents provided, clearly the same thing as agreeing to pay a separate invoice,' and it notes the Act does not 'expressly say that receiving the full bond prevents a later claim for cleaning' rather than saying the landlord can never claim more.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the required document with its version, "Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115" (as at 13 October 2026, link 97-109aa115). The only other document it relies on is the in-force "Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, version 009" (30 June 2026, link 21-3sra009), and it uses no out-of-force version.

question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. I've called them twice today. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
### What the law says

A failure or breakdown of the **water supply** to rented premises is an **urgent repair** under the current **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115**, in force from **13 October 2026**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

You do **not necessarily have to wait** for the owner’s preferred tradespeople. You may arrange the urgent repair yourself if you have taken reasonable steps to get the rental provider or agent to repair it immediately and you are unable to get them to do so. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Calling the emergency contact twice today may satisfy that requirement, but the documents do not say exactly how many attempts are enough. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Only a **suitably qualified person** may carry out the repair. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

### What you can do or ask

- Tell the emergency contact **in writing** that, because the water is shut off and their tradespeople are unavailable, you will arrange a suitably qualified plumber unless they can arrange an immediate repair. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- If you arrange the repair, keep the invoice and give the rental provider **7 days’ written notice** of the repair and its cost. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- The rental provider must reimburse the **reasonable cost**, up to **$2,500**, and must reimburse you within **7 days** after receiving written notice of the repair and cost. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- If you cannot afford the repair, it costs more than **$2,500**, or the rental provider refuses to pay, you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring the rental provider or agent to carry out the repair; VCAT must hear that application within **2 business days**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved documents do not state whether this particular broken tap itself, as distinct from the resulting loss of water supply, is urgent; they do establish that the **failure or breakdown of the water supply** is urgent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered: the answer says the 'failure or breakdown of the water supply' is an urgent repair, and it says that after reasonable steps the renter may arrange the repair and must be reimbursed the reasonable cost up to $2,500 within 7 days of written notice. The hardest point, the preferred-tradesperson policy, is covered by 'You do not necessarily have to wait for the owner's preferred tradespeople. You may arrange the urgent repair yourself if you have taken reasonable steps…', which makes clear the policy cannot stop the urgent repair, though the answer does not cite the prohibited-term regulation.

must-not-say.reason: Yes — the answer says neither prohibited thing: it states 'You do not necessarily have to wait for the owner's preferred tradespeople' and that 'The rental provider must reimburse the reasonable cost, up to $2,500', which contradicts both fail conditions.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Act as "Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115" (link 97-109aa115) and identifies the Regulations by the link "21-3sra009" (version 009); both are the versions in force on that date, and no rule is taken from any other version.

question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. I haven't moved any of my things in or stayed there yet. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
## What the law says

The current documents are:

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115, in force from 13 October 2026, Author: Barbara Hargreaves** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009, in force from 30 June 2026, Author: Lavina Mandy** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

The premises must be **structurally sound and weatherproof**, and every room must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) The rental provider must also maintain the premises in good repair and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Rotting timber, damp and structural mould may therefore indicate breaches of the rental provider’s duties, depending on the facts and extent of the damage. The documents do not specifically classify rotting timber as an urgent repair. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

1. **Notify the rental provider in writing immediately.**  
   Describe each problem, attach dated photographs or reports, and ask the provider to confirm whether the premises comply with the minimum standards and when qualified tradespeople will repair them. The prescribed condition-report form says defects and needed repairs should be recorded and reported to the provider. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

2. **Ask for repairs before moving in.**  
   For non-urgent repairs, if the provider does not repair the premises within **14 days** after receiving written notice, you may apply to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria to investigate. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) You may also apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring specified repairs; the Tribunal must hear that application within **7 days**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The Tribunal may order repairs by a suitably qualified person and compensation. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

3. **Do not arrange major repairs yourself without advice.**  
   The Act allows a renter to arrange urgent repairs only after taking reasonable steps to have the provider arrange them immediately and being unable to get the provider to do so. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The documents do not establish that these particular problems are urgent repairs, so the safer documented route is written notice and an application for orders.

4. **Ask to end the agreement by mutual agreement.**  
   You can ask the provider to agree in writing to cancel the agreement and refund any bond or rent paid. The documents do not state a general right to cancel merely because the renter discovers damp, mould or rotting timber before moving in. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

5. **Consider statutory termination only if the premises are unfit for habitation.**  
   The prescribed agreement refers to a renter giving notice under section 91ZD where the premises are “destroyed or unfit for habitation”; in that situation the provider is not entitled to compensation for rent foregone under the agreement. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) The retrieved documents do not provide the full test or procedure for deciding whether this house is legally unfit for habitation, so they do not establish that you can use that provision on these facts.

6. **Ask for a lower rent, but it is not an automatic entitlement shown here.**  
   You may negotiate a rent reduction, particularly until the repairs are completed. The documents do not provide a general right to unilaterally reduce the rent because of these defects. Instead, after giving repair notice and if the provider fails to comply, you may apply to the Tribunal for an order allowing rent to be paid into the **Rent Special Account**, subject to the statutory conditions; this is not the same as simply withholding or reducing rent. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

**Practical bottom line:** document everything, notify the provider in writing, request either prompt repairs or written agreement to end the lease, and do not simply stop paying rent. On the retrieved documents alone, there is no confirmed automatic cancellation or rent-reduction right solely because you have not yet moved your belongings in.

must-mention.reason: No. The answer omits that the minimum standards, including the mould and damp standard, must be met by the day the renter moves in (s 65A). It also says the documents do not state a right to cancel, which misses the s 91L right to end the agreement by notice before taking possession. The good-repair route is covered.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer never says the renter must move in and pay rent first (it advises written notice and Tribunal applications now), and it denies any automatic rent reduction, stating "it is not an automatic entitlement shown here" and "The documents do not provide a general right to unilaterally reduce the rent because of these defects."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names both required documents with their in-force versions, 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115, in force from 13 October 2026' (link 97-109aa115) and 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009, in force from 30 June 2026' (link 21-3sra009), and every rule it applies is cited only to those versions.

question: Our rental was broken into several times while we were moving out, and there are about three weeks left on our fixed-term lease. The burglars damaged the plumbing and wiring, so we can't even clean properly. What are our options before the lease ends?
answer:
## What the law says

The current **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115, in force from 13 October 2026** (Author: Barbara Hargreaves) applies. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The current **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009, in force from 30 June 2026** (Author: Lavina Mandy) also applies. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

- A renter must notify the rental provider **in writing, as soon as practicable**, about damage to the premises and the nature of the damage. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- The rental provider must maintain the premises in good repair and in a fit condition for occupation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- Plumbing or electrical damage may require **urgent repairs**. The regulations expressly refer to urgent repairs involving a burst water service or flood damage, and say urgent repairs include failure or breakdown of an essential service supplied by the rental provider. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- If the premises are **unfit for human habitation** or have been destroyed or rendered unsafe, you may give a notice of intention to vacate that takes effect **on the date it is given or a later date**, even though the lease is fixed-term. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- The ordinary notice to vacate does not generally end a fixed-term agreement early: it is ineffective if it specifies a date before the fixed term ends. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- At the end of the agreement, you must leave the premises reasonably clean **“as far as practicable”**, and in the same condition as at the start, allowing for fair wear and tear. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The prescribed agreement also says the renter is not required to arrange professional cleaning unless the specified statutory conditions apply. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

1. **Immediately send written notice** to the rental provider or agent describing the break-ins and each plumbing, wiring, security and safety problem. Keep copies, photographs and any repair reports. The Act permits electronic notice in accordance with the Electronic Transactions (Victoria) Act 2000. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

2. **Demand immediate urgent repairs**, particularly where the plumbing or wiring affects safety or an essential service. If the provider does not act after you have taken reasonable steps to arrange the repairs, you may arrange urgent repairs yourself. The regulations state that reimbursement may be available for reasonable urgent-repair costs up to **$2,500**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

3. If you cannot pay, the repairs cost more than **$2,500**, or the provider refuses to reimburse you, apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring the provider to carry out the urgent repairs; the Act says that application must be heard within **2 business days**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The regulations say only a suitably qualified person may perform repairs. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

4. If the damage means the premises are genuinely **unfit for habitation or unsafe**, give a written notice of intention to vacate under **section 91ZD**, specifying immediate termination or a later date. The prescribed agreement states that, in this situation, the rental provider is not entitled to rent-foregone compensation for ending the agreement early. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

5. If the premises are not legally unfit or unsafe, ask the provider to agree in writing to an early end date. The retrieved documents do not state that burglary alone automatically ends a fixed-term lease or automatically cancels rent, so do not assume that it does. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

6. Explain in writing that you cannot properly clean while the provider’s damage remains unrepaired, and request written confirmation that cleaning will be assessed after repairs. Your statutory obligation is to leave the premises reasonably clean **as far as practicable**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The Act also allows a Tribunal application for compensation where the other party’s failure to comply with the Act or agreement caused loss or damage, but the retrieved documents do not determine whether your particular losses would be compensable. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. (1) It says to notify the rental provider 'in writing, as soon as practicable' about the damage. (2) It tells the renter to 'Demand immediate urgent repairs' for the plumbing and wiring, and says that 'If the provider does not act... you may arrange urgent repairs yourself' with reimbursement up to $2,500. The 'may require' wording is not hedged so far that the direction is unclear. (3) It says that if the premises are unfit or unsafe, the renter can give a notice of intention to vacate under s 91ZD that takes effect 'on the date it is given... even though the lease is fixed-term.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer says neither: it places the repair duty on the landlord ('The rental provider must maintain the premises in good repair'), presents self-arranged urgent repairs only as a reimbursable option when the provider fails to act, and says the renter may leave early if the premises are 'unfit for human habitation' via a notice 'that takes effect on the date it is given or a later date, even though the lease is fixed-term.'

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115, in force from 13 October 2026' (link 97-109aa115), and the only other document it relies on is the in-force 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009' (link 21-3sra009), with no rule drawn from a non-in-force version.

question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. The app is run by a payments company my agent uses, and it's that company that charges the card fee. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
## What the law says

Today’s applicable documents are:

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115**, in force from 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009**, in force from 30 June 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

The rental provider or agent must ensure that you have a **reasonably available rent-payment method with no additional cost**, apart from bank or account fees payable on your own bank account. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Therefore, if the manual bank-transfer option is reasonably available and genuinely fee-free, the app should not be the only way to pay rent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The Act expressly prohibits a person from charging for the **establishment or use of a direct-debit facility or any other electronic payment facility for paying rent**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The Regulations also prescribe “rent payment” as a prohibited fee, except for payment-surcharge fees permitted under another Act. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The documents do **not** say whether a particular card surcharge is permitted under that “other Act.” They therefore do not provide enough information to conclude that this specific card fee is lawful.

It does not necessarily matter that the money goes to the payments company rather than the agent. The Act’s payment-method duties apply to the residential rental provider **or that person’s agent**, and the prohibition is expressed to apply to **“a person.”** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) However, the documents do not expressly decide whether an independent payments company is liable in these circumstances, or whether it is an “ADI” for the separate prohibition in section 51A. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The provider or agent must also tell you about costs—including **third-party transaction fees** and other electronic-payment-facility fees—before you consent to use that payment method. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

Ask the agent, in writing:

1. To confirm that the bank-transfer option is an available **fee-free rent-payment method**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
2. To identify the legal basis for the card surcharge and explain whether it is a payment surcharge permitted under another Act. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
3. To confirm who receives the fee and whether the payments company is acting as the agent’s payment provider.
4. To provide the required information about all third-party and electronic-payment fees before you use the card option. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The Regulations also prohibit a rental-agreement term that requires you to pay rent through a method involving additional costs, and a term requiring you to use a third-party service provider nominated by the rental provider, subject to the stated embedded-network exception. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: No. The second point is hedged too far: the answer says it "does not necessarily matter" who collects the fee, then says the documents "do not expressly decide whether an independent payments company is liable," and calls s 51A a "separate prohibition" instead of the ban that, with reg 21C, applies to anyone but an ADI. A reader therefore can't tell that the app company is equally barred from charging the fee.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer does not say the fee is allowed merely because a fee-free option exists or that the landlord or agent is exempt; it states the documents 'do not provide enough information to conclude that this specific card fee is lawful' and that 'the prohibition is expressed to apply to "a person"', with payment-method duties applying to the 'residential rental provider or that person's agent.'

version-cited.reason: Yes: the answer names both required documents with their in-force versions, 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115' (link 97-109aa115) and 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009' (link 21-3sra009), and relies on no other version.

question: My lease is on the standard form and started in 2024. It has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. I cleaned them myself and they're back to how they were when I moved in, but the agent wants a receipt from a professional cleaner. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?
answer:
## What the law says

Under the current **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version v009 (30 June 2026)**, the standard-form professional-cleaning term does **not** require professional cleaning merely because a pet lived there. Professional cleaning may be required only if:

- professional cleaning was done immediately before the tenancy and you were told this; **or**
- professional cleaning is needed to restore the premises to the condition they were in immediately before the tenancy, based on the condition report and allowing for fair wear and tear. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The standard-form clause correspondingly says that you must have the premises professionally cleaned—or pay that cost—**only if professional cleaning becomes required to restore that original condition**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

Therefore, if your carpets are reasonably clean and restored to their starting condition, allowing for fair wear and tear, the documents do **not** establish that you must pay for professional cleaning or provide a professional cleaner’s receipt. The documents also do not specifically say that an agent may require a receipt simply because the clause mentions professional cleaning. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The current **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version v115 (13 October 2026)** says a term requiring professional cleaning is prohibited unless it is in the standard form, but confirms that a standard-form agreement may include the prescribed, limited professional-cleaning term. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) A rental provider may claim reasonable cleaning costs from the bond only if the premises were not left reasonably clean, having regard to their condition at the start of the tenancy. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

- Send the agent the signed condition report and explain that you cleaned the carpets yourself and believe they are restored to their starting condition, allowing for fair wear and tear. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- Provide dated, labelled photographs or video of each carpeted area, showing the room/location and the overall condition. The prescribed condition report specifically recommends beginning-and-end photos, including close-up and distance views. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- Ask the agent to identify the specific difference from the commencement condition that allegedly requires professional cleaning, rather than merely requesting a receipt. The final condition report must record whether items are clean and must allow for fair wear and tear. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- Attend or request the final inspection. The agent must give you a reasonable opportunity to be present, and must complete the condition report within **10 days after the agreement ends**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- If the agent makes a bond claim, ask for the supporting **bond claim evidence**. At least **3 days before** claiming bond repayment to the rental provider, the provider or agent must give you evidence supporting the claim, and that evidence must not conflict with the condition report. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The documents do not state what particular evidence VCAT would ultimately accept beyond the condition report, photographs and supporting bond-claim evidence described above.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. The hardest one, the renter's s 63 duty, is conveyed by 'A rental provider may claim reasonable cleaning costs from the bond only if the premises were not left reasonably clean, having regard to their condition at the start of the tenancy,' together with the repeated 'restored to their starting condition, allowing for fair wear and tear.' Reg 12's two conditions are stated explicitly, and the condition report is identified as the baseline evidence ('based on the condition report', 'Send the agent the signed condition report').

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the renter must pay for professional cleaning simply because the clause exists or because they had a pet; it rejects that idea, stating the term "does **not** require professional cleaning merely because a pet lived there" and that the documents "do **not** establish that you must pay for professional cleaning or provide a professional cleaner's receipt."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names both required documents with their in-force versions, "Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version v009 (30 June 2026)" and "Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version v115 (13 October 2026)", and every rule it applies is cited to those versions (links 21-3sra009 and 97-109aa115), with no reliance on any other version.

question: When I moved out I agreed the agent could take an amount for cleaning out of my bond, but I never signed a bond claim form for it. Then my full bond came back to me, and a month later the agent sent a separate invoice for the cleaning. Do I have to pay it? Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?
answer:
## What the law says

The current document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115**, incorporating amendments as at **13 October 2026**. Its author is listed as **Barbara Hargreaves**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

A renter must leave the premises reasonably clean, allowing for fair wear and tear. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The provider may claim from the bond the **reasonable cost of cleaning** if the premises were not left reasonably clean, having regard to their condition at the start of the tenancy. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

A bond claim must be made in an Authority-approved form. If the provider claims repayment of bond, they must give the renter supporting bond-claim evidence at least **3 days beforehand**; an invoice is listed as one type of bond-claim evidence. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The Act also provides for claims made by the renter, provider, or jointly, and for notice to other parties where the claim is not consented to. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The Act does **not** say in the retrieved provisions that an agreement to deduct cleaning from the bond is automatically an agreement to pay a separate invoice. Nor do the documents say that the absence of your signature on a bond claim form, or the later repayment of the full bond, automatically decides whether you owe the cleaning cost.

The Act does, however, say that recovering compensation from a bond does not prevent a person from bringing proceedings for an **additional** amount of compensation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) That provision concerns additional compensation; it does not itself establish that every unpaid or separately invoiced cleaning amount is payable.

## What you can do or ask

You can ask the agent to identify the legal and factual basis for the invoice, including:

- what cleaning was allegedly required;
- why it was more than fair wear and tear;
- the condition report evidence;
- the cleaning invoice or receipt; and
- whether they are claiming the amount as compensation rather than as a bond deduction.

question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. I've called them twice today. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
## What the law says

A failure or breakdown of the **water supply to rented premises** is an urgent repair. A malfunctioning water-using fixture that causes substantial water wastage is also an urgent repair. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) Turning off the water to the whole house because of the broken tap appears to fall within those categories, although the documents do not decide the facts of your particular tap. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

You do **not necessarily have to wait for the owner’s preferred tradespeople**. Under section 72 of the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, a renter may arrange urgent repairs if they have taken reasonable steps to get the rental provider or agent to arrange them immediately, but cannot get them to do so. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The regulations’ standard agreement also says that only a **suitably qualified person** may carry out repairs. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do

You can arrange the repair yourself now, provided you use a suitably qualified tradesperson and keep evidence of your two calls and the repair cost. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The Act requires you to give the rental provider **7 days’ written notice** of the repair and its cost. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The rental provider must reimburse the **reasonable cost**, up to **$2,500**, and must pay within **7 days** after receiving your written notice of the repair and cost. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

If you cannot pay upfront, the repair costs more than **$2,500**, or the rental provider refuses to pay, you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring the repair; VCAT must hear that application within **2 business days**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

**Current documents:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version **v115**, dated **13 October 2026**, Author **Barbara Hargreaves** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf); and *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised Version **v009**, dated **30 June 2026**, Author **Lavina Mandy** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

(2) It cites s 72: after reasonable steps the renter may arrange the repair, and the provider must reimburse the reasonable cost up to $2,500 within 7 days after receiving written notice. (3) The hardest point is covered by 'You do not necessarily have to wait for the owner's preferred tradespeople… You can arrange the repair yourself now,' which shows the preferred-tradesperson policy cannot stop an urgent repair. It does not cite reg 11(e), but the rubric accepts this equivalent.

It does not say the renter must wait for the landlord's tradesperson or that the renter cannot recover the cost.

question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. I haven't moved any of my things in or stayed there yet. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
## What the law says

Today’s retrieved Act is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026**. The retrieved Regulations are **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, version 009, in force from 30 June 2026**. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

- The rental provider must provide and maintain the premises **in good repair and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation**, even if the renter knew about the disrepair before entering occupation. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- The premises must be **structurally sound and weatherproof**, and every room must be free from mould and damp caused by, or related to, the building structure. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- Mould or damp related to the building structure, and any fault or damage making the premises unsafe or insecure, are defined as **urgent repairs**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- The renter is not required to move into premises that are not vacant and reasonably clean on the agreed occupation day, and is not required to pay rent for the period before actually entering occupation in that situation. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) This provision does not expressly address all consequences of discovering structural defects before moving in.

## What you can do or ask

1. **Do not move your belongings in or stay there while the condition is unresolved.** Give the rental provider or agent written notice immediately, describing the damp, mould and rotting timber, and attach dated photographs or reports. A condition report can also record defects and constitutes notice of repairs stated in it. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

2. **Ask for urgent repairs and a written plan and timeframe.** The provider must use a suitably qualified person for repairs, and the Act allows a renter to seek urgent repairs where the provider does not act after reasonable steps have been taken. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The documents do not expressly say whether every urgent-repair remedy can be used before the renter has entered occupation, so that specific point cannot be confirmed from the retrieved text.

3. **If the repairs are treated as non-urgent**, give written notice and, if they are not completed within 14 days, apply to the Director for an investigation or to the Tribunal for an order requiring the repairs. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The Tribunal may order specified repairs, use of a suitably qualified person and compensation. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

4. **If the premises are unfit for human habitation or unsafe**, section 91ZD allows a renter to give a notice of intention to vacate with termination on the date of the notice or a later date. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Whether the particular mould and rotting timber meet that threshold is fact-dependent; the retrieved documents do not decide that question.

5. **Ask the provider to agree in writing to cancel the agreement and refund any bond or rent paid.** The retrieved documents do not contain the text of section 91L, headed “Termination by renter before possession,” so they do not establish whether you can unilaterally cancel on these facts. Do not simply stop complying without written agreement or a Tribunal order, because the standard agreement says early termination may expose a renter to compensation for the provider’s actual rent loss, subject to the stated exceptions. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

6. **Ask for lower rent**, but the retrieved documents do not provide a general automatic right to a rent reduction merely because defects are discovered before moving in. You may negotiate a reduced rent, but record any agreement in writing. Do not withhold rent or reduce it unilaterally unless authorised by the Act, an agreement or a Tribunal order; the documents instead identify a Tribunal process for authorising payment into the Rent Special Account after a repair notice and failure to repair. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: No. The answer fails two required points. It never says the minimum standards, including the mould and damp standard, must be met by the day the renter moves in (s 65A). It also does not say a renter who has not taken possession can end the agreement by notice under s 91L; instead it says the documents 'do not establish whether you can unilaterally cancel on these facts'. The repair route is covered.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer says neither forbidden thing: it advises "Do not move your belongings in or stay there while the condition is unresolved" rather than requiring move-in and rent first, and it states "the retrieved documents do not provide a general automatic right to a rent reduction," saying a reduction would need agreement or a Tribunal order.

question: Our rental was broken into several times while we were moving out, and there are about three weeks left on our fixed-term lease. The burglars damaged the plumbing and wiring, so we can't even clean properly. What are our options before the lease ends?
answer:
## What the law says

The applicable document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115**, in force from **13 October 2026**; its metadata names **Barbara Hargreaves** as Author. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The retrieved regulations are **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009**, in force from **30 June 2026**; their metadata names **Lavina Mandy** as Author. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The plumbing and wiring problems may be **urgent repairs**: urgent repairs include a broken water service, blocked or broken lavatory system, dangerous electrical fault, failure of electricity or water supply, and damage making the premises unsafe or insecure. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

You must notify the rental provider **in writing as soon as practicable** about the damage and its nature. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The rental provider must maintain the premises in good repair and fit for occupation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

If the premises are **unfit for human habitation**, or have been destroyed totally or to an extent that makes them unsafe, you may end the fixed-term agreement by giving a notice of intention to vacate. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) That notice may specify termination **on the date it is given or a later date**, so the ordinary fixed-term end date does not prevent this option. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

You still must leave the premises, as far as practicable, reasonably clean and in their original condition, allowing for fair wear and tear; however, the cleaning duty does not apply to the extent that the rental provider is responsible for keeping the premises clean. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The standard agreement also says professional cleaning cannot generally be required beyond restoring the premises to their starting condition, taking fair wear and tear into account. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

1. **Send an immediate written notice** to the rental provider or agent describing the break-ins, plumbing damage, wiring damage, safety risks, and why cleaning is currently impossible. Keep photographs, messages, invoices and any other evidence. The Act requires written reporting of damage as soon as practicable. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

2. **Demand immediate urgent repairs**, using the provider’s emergency contact details if your agreement lists them. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) Only a suitably qualified person may perform the repairs. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

3. If the provider does not act after you have taken reasonable steps to arrange the repairs, you may arrange urgent repairs yourself. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within **7 days** after receiving written notice of the repairs and their cost. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The prescribed reimbursement limit stated in the retrieved agreement material is **$2,500**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

4. If you cannot afford the repairs, they cost more than **$2,500**, or the provider refuses to pay, you may apply to **VCAT** for an order requiring the urgent repairs. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The Tribunal must hear that application within **2 business days**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

5. If the damage makes the premises unfit for habitation or unsafe, give a **section 91ZD notice of intention to vacate**, specifying immediate termination or a later date. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Do not simply abandon the property without giving the notice or obtaining an agreed termination, because the retrieved documents do not state that ordinary abandonment ends a fixed-term agreement without further liability. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved documents **do not state whether rent is automatically reduced or suspended while these repairs are outstanding**, nor do they state a specific compensation entitlement for burglary damage.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. The answer says to notify the rental provider 'in writing as soon as practicable'. It treats the plumbing and wiring damage as urgent repairs (broken water service, dangerous electrical fault), tells the renter to 'demand immediate urgent repairs', and says the renter can arrange the repairs and be reimbursed within 7 days if the provider does not act. The 'may be urgent repairs' wording is a mild hedge that does not obscure which way the point falls. The hardest point is covered by the statement that the notice of intention to vacate 'may specify termination on the date it is given or a later date, so the ordinary fixed-term end date does not prevent this option', applying where the premises are unfit for habitation or unsafe.

question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. The app is run by a payments company my agent uses, and it's that company that charges the card fee. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997** (version 115, in force today) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), here is how the law applies to your situation:

### What the law says about rent payment fees
Under section 42 of the Act, your rental provider or their agent has two main legal obligations regarding how you pay rent:

1. **A fee-free option must be available:** The law states that *"a residential rental provider or that person's agent must ensure that a rent payment method that incurs no additional costs (other than bank fees or account fees payable on the renter's bank account) is reasonably available to the renter"* [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
2. **You must be informed of costs upfront:** The law requires that *"the residential rental provider or that person's agent must give the renter information about any costs (including third party transaction fees, direct debit dishonour fees and any other electronic payment facility fees) that the renter may incur by using a particular payment method before the renter consents to use the payment method"* [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### 1. Can the app charge you the card fee?
**Yes, but only if your fee-free bank transfer option remains available.** 
The law does not ban third-party transaction fees outright. However, because your agent is legally required to keep a no-cost payment method reasonably available [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), they cannot force you to use the card-paying app. As long as the manual bank transfer option remains open and accessible, the app's card fee is permissible.

### 2. Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or the agent?
**No, it does not matter who receives the money.** 
The law focuses entirely on **the cost to you**, not who pockets the surcharge [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Whether the payments company keeps the card fee or passes it on to your agent is irrelevant under tenancy law. The only legal requirements are that a genuinely fee-free alternative exists for you and that you are transparently informed of any third-party transaction fees before you agree to use them [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do or ask
* **Stick to the free method:** You are fully within your rights to continue using the manual bank transfer option. 
* **Ask for transparency:** If you ever choose to use the card app, ask your agent to confirm in writing that they will disclose any third-party transaction fees before you consent to the payment [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* **Report non-compliance:** If your agent removes the fee-free bank transfer option or pressures you into using a paid method, they are breaching section 42(4) of the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You can raise this with Consumer Affairs Victoria.

must-mention.reason: No — the second point is missing: the answer says the card fee is permissible ('As long as the manual bank transfer option remains open and accessible, the app's card fee is permissible'), but under s 51A with reg 21C rent payment fees are banned for anyone other than a bank, so its 'it does not matter who receives the money' conclusion rests on the opposite legal position. The other two points, the fee-free method requirement and the next steps (bank transfer, Consumer Affairs Victoria), are covered.

must-not-say.reason: No: the answer says the fee is allowed simply because a fee-free option exists, stating "As long as the manual bank transfer option remains open and accessible, the app's card fee is permissible."
