question: My lease is on the standard form and started in 2024. It has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. I cleaned them myself and they're back to how they were when I moved in, but the agent wants a receipt from a professional cleaner. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?
answer:
Based on the Victorian residential tenancy laws currently in force today, here is how your situation is handled:

**Applicable Documents & Versions**
* `Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021`, v009 (in force from 30 June 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
* `Residential Tenancies Act 1997`, v115 (in force from 13 October 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

### What the law says about your situation
**Do you have to pay for a professional cleaner?**
No. Under Clause 11 of the standard form lease, a rental provider **must not require** you to arrange professional cleaning or pay for it unless one of two specific conditions is met:
1. Professional cleaning was carried out immediately before you moved in *and* you were advised of this; or
2. Professional cleaning is strictly required to restore the premises to the same condition they were in immediately before you started, taking into account fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

The law focuses entirely on the **condition** of the carpets at the end of your tenancy, not the *method* used to clean them [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Since you have cleaned them yourself and restored them to their original state (accounting for fair wear and tear), you do not need to provide a professional cleaning receipt or pay for one. A blanket clause demanding professional cleaning regardless of the actual condition is unenforceable under these rules.

**What would help show the carpets' condition?**
To prove you have met your legal obligation, you should rely on:
* **The signed Condition Report:** This form records the state of the premises when you moved in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). You were required to sign and return your copy within 5 business days of moving in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
* **Photos:** The standard condition report explicitly advises renters to "take photos that show the condition of items, fixtures and fittings" at both the beginning and end of the tenancy [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). You are permitted to attach these photos directly to your copy of the condition report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
* **The Final Inspection Report:** When you leave, the agent must complete a final inspection on the condition report within 10 days and give you an opportunity to attend [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do or ask for
1. **Politely decline the receipt request.** Explain that under Victorian law, your obligation is to leave the carpets in the same condition they were when you moved in (accounting for fair wear and tear), not to use a specific cleaning method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
2. **Provide evidence.** Send the agent your signed start-of-tenancy condition report alongside clear end-of-tenancy photos of the carpets as proof that they have been restored to their original state.
3. **Attend the final inspection.** If possible, be present when the agent completes the final condition report so you can verify they note the carpets are clean and undamaged [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
4. **Dispute any bond claim.** If the agent tries to deduct money from your bond for professional cleaning despite the carpets being in good condition, you can object to the claim through the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority (RTBA) or apply to VCAT to resolve the dispute [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. (1) The answer says professional cleaning can only be required if it 'was carried out immediately before you moved in and you were advised of this' or is 'strictly required to restore the premises to the same condition... taking into account fair wear and tear.' (2) The hardest point is covered by 'your obligation is to leave the carpets in the same condition they were when you moved in (accounting for fair wear and tear)'; it omits the words 'reasonably clean', but returning to the move-in state already implies that cleanliness. question: When I moved out I agreed the agent could take an amount for cleaning out of my bond, but I never signed a bond claim form for it. Then my full bond came back to me, and a month later the agent sent a separate invoice for the cleaning. Do I have to pay it? Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (v115)** and the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (v009)**, which are in force today, here is how the law applies to your situation:

### 🔹 The Law on Bond Claims & Cleaning
Under Victorian law, a rental provider can only access money from a bond by lodging a formal claim with the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority (RTBA) using an approved form [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). While a provider is entitled to claim the reasonable cost of cleaning if the premises were not left reasonably clean (accounting for fair wear and tear), this must be done through the official bond claim process while the money is still held by the RTBA [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 

Once the RTBA has repaid your full bond to you, their statutory role in that tenancy ends. The law explicitly states that no further claims can be made against the Authority or the Residential Bonds Account once a bond has been paid out in good faith [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Because you never signed a bond claim form and received your full refund, the agent cannot retroactively deduct money from the bond.

### 🔹 Is Agreeing to a Bond Deduction the Same as Agreeing to Pay an Invoice?
**No.** They are legally distinct mechanisms:
* **A bond deduction** is a specific statutory process for accessing funds already held by the RTBA [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
* **An invoice** is a commercial request for payment outside of the bond scheme.

Agreeing to have money taken from your bond does not automatically mean you agreed to pay a separate invoice later. Unless your tenancy agreement or a separate written contract explicitly states that any cleaning costs will be invoiced separately if they are not covered by the bond, agreeing to a bond deduction does not create an obligation to pay a later invoice. 

Additionally, under the regulations, a provider can only require you to pay for professional cleaning if it was carried out at the start of your tenancy or is strictly necessary to restore the premises to their original condition (accounting for fair wear and tear) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### 🔹 What You Can Do
1. **Review your paperwork:** Check your original tenancy agreement and any written correspondence to see if you explicitly agreed to pay a separate invoice for cleaning costs. 
2. **Respond in writing:** If you did not agree to an invoice, reply to the agent stating that you only agreed to a bond deduction (which was never processed) and that you do not accept liability for a separate invoice.
3. **Check the condition report:** If the agent claims the cleaning was necessary, they must prove the premises were left unreasonably dirty compared to the initial condition report [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). 
4. **Dispute if necessary:** If the agent continues to demand payment or threatens legal action, you can seek free advice from the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) or a community legal centre regarding contract and tenancy law.

*Note: This information is based on the current statutory framework. It does not constitute formal legal advice.*

The answer says a bond deduction is 'a specific statutory process for accessing funds already held by the RTBA' and that agreeing to it 'does not automatically mean you agreed to pay a separate invoice later'. For the hardest point, the reasonable-cleanliness test, it says the provider can claim cleaning costs only 'if the premises were not left reasonably clean (accounting for fair wear and tear)' and 'must prove the premises were left unreasonably dirty compared to the initial condition report'. question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. I've called them twice today. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Authorised Version 115)** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) and the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (Authorised Version 009)** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf), which are in force today, here is how the law applies to your situation:

### What the Law Says
A broken tap that forces you to turn off the water to the entire house qualifies as an **urgent repair** (specifically, a burst water service or failure of a water appliance) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 

The owner's restriction to only using their own tradespeople does not override your statutory rights. The law states that you may arrange for urgent repairs yourself if:
1. You have taken reasonable steps to get the rental provider or agent to carry out the repairs immediately; and
2. You are unable to get them to do so [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 

The regulations also clarify that only a suitably qualified person may perform these repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### What You Can Do
* **Get it fixed immediately:** Since you have already called twice today, you have taken reasonable steps. You are legally entitled to hire a licensed plumber to fix the tap without waiting for the owner's preferred tradespeople [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* **Claim reimbursement:** The owner must reimburse you for the reasonable cost of these urgent repairs, up to a maximum of **$2,500** (including GST) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). 
* **Provide written notice:** You must give the owner written notice detailing the repairs carried out and the cost within 7 days of them being completed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The owner is legally required to reimburse you within 7 days of receiving this notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* **Escalate if necessary:** If the repair costs more than $2,500, or if you cannot afford to pay upfront, you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring the owner to carry out the repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

You do not have to wait. You can proceed with getting a qualified plumber to fix the tap now and submit your invoice to the owner within 7 days.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered: the tap failure is called an urgent repair ('a burst water service'); the answer says reasonable steps let the renter arrange repairs, with reasonable costs up to $2,500 reimbursed 'within 7 days of receiving this notice'; and the hardest point is covered by 'The owner's restriction to only using their own tradespeople does not override your statutory rights.'

question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. I haven't moved any of my things in or stayed there yet. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
Based on the Victorian residential tenancy laws currently in force today (9 November 2026), here is how your situation is addressed:

**Applicable Documents & Versions:**
*   *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version v115 (in force from 13 October 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
*   *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised Version v009 (in force from 30 June 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### 🔍 The Law on Property Condition
Under the current regulations, your landlord has strict legal obligations regarding the condition of the premises at the start of a tenancy:
*   **Rental Minimum Standards:** Every room must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure, and the premises must be structurally sound and weatherproof [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Rotting timber and structural mould/damp are direct breaches of these standards.
*   **Landlord's Duty:** The rental provider must ensure the premises comply with these minimum standards, remain vacant and reasonably clean when you move in, and maintain the property in good repair and a fit condition for occupation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### 📋 Your Options

**1. Can you cancel the lease before moving in?**
The provided documents do not explicitly state a statutory right to unilaterally cancel a residential rental agreement *before* you have moved in due to disrepair. However, because the landlord is legally required to provide premises that are structurally sound and free from structural mould/damp at commencement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf), you may be able to negotiate an early termination or seek remedies under general contract/consumer law (which the regulations acknowledge applies) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). You should formally notify the agent/landlord in writing of the defects immediately.

**2. Can you ask for repairs?**
Yes. Once the tenancy begins, damp and mould caused by the building structure are legally classified as **urgent repairs** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
*   **Urgent Repairs:** You must notify the landlord in writing. They are required to carry out these repairs immediately [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If they fail to do so after you have taken reasonable steps to contact them, you may arrange the repairs yourself and claim reimbursement for reasonable costs (up to $2,500) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf), or apply to VCAT for an order requiring the landlord to fix it [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
*   **Non-Urgent Repairs:** For other structural issues (like rotting timber not deemed immediately urgent), you must give written notice. The landlord has 14 days to complete the repairs. If they do not, you can apply to the Director or VCAT for a compliance order [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**3. Can you ask for lower rent?**
The provided documents do not allow you to unilaterally reduce your rent. However, if you have given written notice requiring repairs, you can apply to VCAT to pay your rent into a **Rent Special Account** while the repair dispute is being resolved [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Additionally, if VCAT finds the landlord breached their duty to maintain the premises in good repair, the Tribunal can order the landlord to pay you compensation [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### ✅ Recommended Immediate Steps
1.  Take dated photos of the damp, mould, and rotting timber.
2.  Send a written notice (email or letter) to the agent/landlord immediately stating that the premises do not meet the rental minimum standards for structural soundness and are free from structural mould/damp [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3.  Clearly state whether you wish to negotiate an early termination of the lease before moving in, or if you intend to proceed with the tenancy and require urgent repairs under section 72 of the Act [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

question: Our rental was broken into several times while we were moving out, and there are about three weeks left on our fixed-term lease. The burglars damaged the plumbing and wiring, so we can't even clean properly. What are our options before the lease ends?
answer:
**Applicable Law**: *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, v115 (in force from 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

Based on this legislation, here are your options regarding the burglary damage and the remaining three weeks of your fixed-term lease:

1. **Report the damage immediately**
You must give written notice to your rental provider as soon as practicable about both the fact that the damage occurred and its nature [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This also applies to any breakdown of facilities or fixtures they provided [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

2. **Request urgent repairs**
Damaged plumbing and wiring likely qualify as urgent repairs (faults that make premises unsafe, unsecure, or uninhabitable) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You can ask your provider to fix them immediately [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If you cannot reach them and must arrange the repairs yourself, give written notice of the cost within 7 days; they are legally required to reimburse reasonable costs within 7 days of receiving that notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If the cost is too high or you cannot pay upfront, apply to VCAT for an order requiring them to do it (heard within 2 business days) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

3. **End the lease early due to uninhabitability**
If the damage makes the premises "unfit for human habitation" or "destroyed totally or to such an extent as to be rendered unsafe," you can give a notice of intention to vacate specifying a termination date that is the same day or later [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This lets you leave before your 3-week term ends.

4. **Apply to VCAT for termination due to hardship**
If the premises are still technically habitable but the situation causes you severe hardship due to this unforeseen event, you can apply to VCAT under section 91U to have the fixed-term agreement reduced or terminated [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Tribunal will compare the hardship you would suffer staying versus the hardship your provider would suffer if you leave early.

5. **Cleaning and bond obligations**
You are generally required to leave the premises reasonably clean [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). However, because the damage was caused by burglars (not you or your visitors), you are not responsible for it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The condition report will record the state of the property at the start, and you are only liable for damage you cause, taking fair wear and tear into account [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Yes: all three required points are covered. (1) The answer says to give the rental provider written notice of the damage 'as soon as practicable' (s 72AA). (2) It says damaged plumbing and wiring 'likely qualify as urgent repairs', that the renter can ask the provider to fix them immediately, and that if the renter arranges the repairs the provider is 'legally required to reimburse reasonable costs' (s 72); 'likely' does not hedge enough to leave the point unclear. (3) The hardest point is covered by 'you can give a notice of intention to vacate specifying a termination date that is the same day or later... This lets you leave before your 3-week term ends' (s 91ZD).

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer says neither prohibited claim. It states that "because the damage was caused by burglars (not you or your visitors), you are not responsible for it" and that the provider must "reimburse reasonable costs". It also offers early exit options, such as a "notice of intention to vacate" and a VCAT application "to have the fixed-term agreement reduced or terminated", so it never says the renter must stay until the lease ends.

question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. The app is run by a payments company my agent uses, and it's that company that charges the card fee. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
Based on the current Victorian residential tenancy laws, here is how your situation is regulated:

### 🔍 What the Law Says
* **A fee-free method must be available:** The rental provider or their agent must ensure that a rent payment method with no additional costs (other than your own bank's standard account fees) is reasonably available to you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Because your agent offers a manual bank transfer with zero fees, this legal requirement is already satisfied.
* **Third-party fees are legally recognized:** The law explicitly accounts for `"third party transaction fees"` [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This means external payment apps or processors can charge you, provided the fee complies with other applicable laws (such as credit card surcharging regulations).
* **Upfront disclosure is mandatory:** Before you agree to use a specific payment method, the provider or agent must give you clear information about any costs you will incur, including third-party transaction fees [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
* **You cannot be forced into a paid option:** The tenancy agreement cannot contain a term that requires you to pay rent via a method that incurs additional costs (other than your own bank fees) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Furthermore, general `"rent payment"` fees are prohibited unless they qualify as legitimate surcharge fees permitted under another Act [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### 🛠 What You Can Do or Ask
1. **Confirm the fee is a legitimate surcharge:** Ensure the charge is a standard credit/debit card processing fee allowed under financial regulations, rather than an illegal administrative `"rent payment"` fee [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask for proof of disclosure:** Request confirmation from your agent that they provided you with clear information about this third-party transaction fee *before* you consented to use the app [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If they cannot prove this was done, they are legally required to provide it now.
3. **Continue using the free option:** You are fully within your rights to stick with the manual bank transfer. The law guarantees that a fee-free method must remain reasonably available to you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Who receives the fee is irrelevant:** It does not matter whether the money goes to the payments app company or the agent. The law treats `"third party transaction fees"` [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) and agent-collected fees under the exact same disclosure rules, as long as a fee-free alternative exists and you are informed upfront.

**Documents referenced:**
* *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (v115, in force from 2026-10-13) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
* *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (v009, in force from 2026-06-30) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The answer briefly mentions that rent payment fees are prohibited unless permitted as a surcharge, but it then says 'external payment apps or processors can charge you' and that who receives the fee is irrelevant because the law treats both 'under the exact same disclosure rules, as long as a fee-free alternative exists and you are informed upfront', which presents the fee as allowed if disclosed rather than banned. The first point (a fee-free method must be reasonably available) and the third point (a next step, such as continuing to use the free bank transfer) are covered.

The law treats "third party transaction fees" and agent-collected fees under the exact same disclosure rules, as long as a fee-free alternative exists and you are informed upfront."

question: My lease is on the standard form and started in 2024. It has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. I cleaned them myself and they're back to how they were when I moved in, but the agent wants a receipt from a professional cleaner. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?
answer:
Based on the laws in force today (11 November 2026), the relevant documents are:
* *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. v115 (in force from 13 October 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
* *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised Version No. v009 (in force from 30 June 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

### What the Law Says About Your Situation
Under Victorian law, a rental provider **cannot** require you to arrange or pay for professional cleaning unless it is strictly necessary to restore the premises to the condition they were in immediately before the start of your tenancy, taking into account fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Because you have already cleaned the carpets yourself and restored them to their original state, you have legally fulfilled your obligation. Any lease clause that demands a professional cleaning receipt beyond this threshold is void and unenforceable [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Furthermore, a bond claim for cleaning is only valid if the premises were not left reasonably clean compared to the condition at the commencement of the agreement [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What Would Help Show the Carpets' Condition
To prove you met the required standard, you should rely on:
* **The Condition Report:** You were given two copies (or one emailed) of a condition report when you moved in and had 5 business days to fill it out and note any disagreements with the agent's assessment [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). This document is the primary record used to resolve disputes over cleaning or damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
* **Dated Photos:** The official condition report form explicitly advises renters to take photos showing the condition of items like floor coverings at both the beginning and end of the tenancy, and to attach them to the report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). 
* **The Final Inspection Record:** The agent must complete the "End of Rental Agreement" section of the condition report within 10 days after your tenancy ends, and you have the right to a reasonable opportunity to attend this inspection [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### What You Can Do or Ask For
* **Decline the receipt demand:** Politely inform the agent that because you have already restored the carpets to their original condition (minus fair wear and tear), no professional cleaning is legally required.

question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. I've called them twice today. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?

The law explicitly states that if you have taken reasonable steps to get the owner or agent to immediately carry out urgent repairs, and they fail to do so, you are legally entitled to arrange for those repairs yourself [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). An owner's internal policy restricting repairs to their own tradespeople does not override this statutory right when they are unresponsive [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Additionally, only a suitably qualified person (such as a licensed plumber) may perform the repair [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**What You Can Do or Ask For**
You do not have to wait. Here is exactly what you should do next:
1. **Hire a Licensed Plumber:** Contact a qualified tradesperson immediately to fix the tap. 
2. **Send Written Notice:** Within 7 days of the repair, send the owner a written notice (email is legally valid) detailing the repairs carried out and the cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
3. **Claim Reimbursement:** The owner is legally required to reimburse you for the reasonable cost of the repairs within 7 days of receiving your notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Under current regulations, this reimbursement is capped at **$2,500** (including GST) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
4. **If Costs Exceed $2,500 or You Cannot Pay Upfront:** If the repair costs more than the cap or you cannot afford it, you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring the owner to carry out the repairs directly [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

If the owner refuses to reimburse you after you follow these steps, you can apply to VCAT for a compliance order [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. I haven't moved any of my things in or stayed there yet. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
Based on the Victorian residential tenancy laws in force today (11 November 2026):
- ***Residential Tenancies Act 1997***, v115 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- ***Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021***, v009 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

### What the law says about your situation
Your landlord has strict legal obligations regarding the condition of the property before you move in. Under the rental minimum standards, each room in the premises must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The premises must also be structurally sound and weatherproof [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Rotting timber likely breaches this structural standard. Your landlord is legally required to ensure the premises comply with these minimum standards and are in a fit condition for occupation when you move in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do or ask
**1. Ask for repairs: Yes.**
Damp or mould caused by the building structure is legally classified as an "urgent repair" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You should notify your landlord in writing immediately. If they fail to act, you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring them to carry out the urgent repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). For non-urgent structural issues (like rotting timber that isn't making the property unsafe), you must give written notice and wait 14 days before applying to VCAT for a compliance order [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If VCAT finds your landlord in breach, they can order the repairs to be done by a qualified person and may also order compensation under section 212(2) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**2. Ask for lower rent: Not directly, but you can control payments.**
The provided documents do not explicitly grant a right to unilaterally "lower" or reduce your rent. However, if you have given written notice requiring repairs, you can apply to VCAT for an order authorising you to pay your rent into a Rent Special Account instead of paying your landlord directly [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This effectively pauses rent payments to the landlord while the repair dispute is resolved.

**3. Cancel the lease: The documents do not cover this.**
The provided documents do not contain specific provisions regarding cancelling a residential tenancy agreement *before* moving in due to property condition issues. The retrieved laws focus on remedies, obligations, and dispute resolution processes once the tenancy has commenced. 

*(Note: While you can't cancel based on these specific documents, you should complete and return the condition report within 5 business days of receiving it, noting the damp, mould, and rotting timber to create a formal written record of the property's state before occupation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).)*

The law lets a renter who has not taken possession end the agreement by notice where the premises do not meet the minimum standards, are not in good repair, or are unfit to live in. The other two points are covered: the minimum standards must be met when the renter moves in, and urgent repairs are available for building-related damp and mould.

question: Our rental was broken into several times while we were moving out, and there are about three weeks left on our fixed-term lease. The burglars damaged the plumbing and wiring, so we can't even clean properly. What are our options before the lease ends?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (v115)**, which is in force today [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), here is how the law applies to your situation and what you can do:

### What the law says about your situation
Under Victorian tenancy law, a rental provider has a duty to ensure rented premises are maintained in good repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If burglary damage to plumbing and wiring makes the property unsafe or impossible to live in, the Act provides specific legal pathways for early lease termination and emergency repairs. 

### What you can do or ask for

**1. Report the damage immediately**
The law requires you to give written notice to your rental provider as soon as practicable after becoming aware of any damage to the premises or breakdown of facilities [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Your notice must clearly state both the fact that the damage occurred and its nature (e.g., broken plumbing and wiring) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**2. Arrange urgent repairs yourself (or apply to the Tribunal)**
If the damaged plumbing or wiring constitutes an "urgent repair" (such as a serious fault making the premises unsafe, unsecure, or uninhabitable), you can arrange for the repairs to be done if your provider won't do it immediately [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
* If you pay for these urgent repairs yourself, you must give your provider written notice of the work and costs within 7 days, and they are legally required to reimburse you for the reasonable costs within 7 days of receiving that notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* If you cannot afford the repairs or the cost exceeds the prescribed limit, you can apply directly to the Tribunal for an order requiring the provider to do the work. The Tribunal must hear this application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**3. Give a Notice of Intention to Vacate (if the property is unsafe/uninhabitable)**
If the burglary damage has rendered the premises "unfit for human habitation" or destroyed them "to such an extent as to be rendered unsafe," you are entitled to give your provider a notice of intention to vacate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
* You can specify a termination date that is **the same day you give the notice** or a later date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This allows you to end the fixed-term lease early without penalty if the property is genuinely uninhabitable.

**4. Apply to the Tribunal for termination due to severe hardship**
If the situation does not quite meet the threshold for being "unfit for habitation" but still causes you significant distress, you can apply to the Tribunal under the "hardship" provisions [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
* The Tribunal may order to reduce your fixed-term lease or terminate it entirely if they are satisfied that an unforeseen change in your circumstances would cause you **severe hardship** that is greater than the hardship your provider would suffer by ending the lease early [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### Recommended next steps
1. Send a written notice to your agent/provider detailing the burglary damage and requesting urgent repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
2. If they do not act immediately, get quotes for urgent repairs and proceed if necessary, keeping all receipts for reimbursement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
3. If the home is truly uninhabitable, serve a formal Notice of Intention to Vacate under section 91ZD [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 

*(Note: All citations refer to the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (v115), in force from 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).*

All three points are covered: (1) written notice of the damage 'as soon as practicable'; (2) urgent repairs the renter can arrange and be reimbursed for 'within 7 days'; (3) a notice of intention to vacate with a termination date 'the same day you give the notice', even on a fixed-term lease. The hardest point is the second, which is phrased conditionally ('If the damaged plumbing or wiring constitutes an "urgent repair"'). It still counts because the next steps treat the damage as urgent repairs to request and, if the provider does not act immediately, to arrange for reimbursement.

question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. The app is run by a payments company my agent uses, and it's that company that charges the card fee. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
Based on the current Victorian residential tenancy laws in force today, here is how your situation is regulated:

### 📜 What the Law Says
Under the ***Residential Tenancies Act 1997*** (Authorised Version No. 115, in force from 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) and the ***Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*** (Authorised Version No. 009, in force from 30 June 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf):
* **A fee-free option must be available:** The rental provider or their agent must ensure that a rent payment method with no additional costs (other than your own bank fees) is reasonably available to you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* **Costs must be disclosed upfront:** Before you consent to use a payment method, the provider or agent must give you information about any costs you may incur, including third-party transaction fees [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* **You cannot be forced into a costly method:** Your tenancy agreement cannot include a term that requires you to pay rent via a method that incurs additional costs (other than your own bank fees) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
* **Rent payment fees are generally prohibited:** The regulations explicitly list "rent payment" fees as prohibited, with a specific carve-out for *"payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act"* [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### 💳 Can the app charge you the card fee?
**Yes, but only if strict legal conditions are met.** Because the regulations allow an exception for *"payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act"* [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf), a third-party payments company may legally charge a card processing surcharge *if* that surcharge is permitted by relevant payment laws. However, this is entirely conditional on:
1. The provider/agent offering you a genuinely fee-free alternative (like the manual bank transfer you mentioned) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. The provider/agent clearly disclosing the exact cost of using the card option **before** you agree to it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### 💰 Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or the agent?
**No, it does not matter who ultimately receives the money.** The legal obligation sits squarely with the **residential rental provider or their agent** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). They are responsible for ensuring that:
* A compliant, fee-free payment method is available.
* You are fully informed of any third-party transaction fees before consenting to use them.

Whether the fee is passed on to a payments processor or kept by the agency does not change their responsibility to provide you with a free alternative and full transparency [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### ✅ What You Can Do or Ask
* **Ask for written confirmation:** Request that your agent confirms in writing that they are providing a compliant, fee-free payment method as required by law [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* **Check the disclosure timeline:** Ensure you received clear information about the card fee *before* you consented to use the app. If you were not informed beforehand, the provider has breached their disclosure obligations [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* **Use the free option:** You are entitled to use the manual bank transfer (or other fee-free method) without penalty [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* **Report non-compliance:** If no fee-free alternative is offered, or if you were forced into a costly payment method, you can report this to Consumer Affairs Victoria or apply to VCAT.

question: My lease is on the standard form and started in 2024. It has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. I cleaned them myself and they're back to how they were when I moved in, but the agent wants a receipt from a professional cleaner. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?
answer:
**What the Law Says**
Under Victorian residential tenancy law, a rental provider cannot force you to hire a professional cleaner unless one of two specific conditions is met: (1) professional cleaning was carried out immediately before your tenancy started and you were advised of this; or (2) professional cleaning is strictly required to restore the carpets to the same condition they were in at the start of your tenancy, accounting for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). 

Because you have cleaned the carpets yourself and they are back to their original condition (minus fair wear and tear), you do not have to pay for a professional cleaner. The law requires you to leave the premises "reasonably clean" and "in the same condition as when the renter entered into possession," but it does not mandate a specific cleaning method if your DIY work successfully achieves that result [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Any lease clause demanding professional cleaning regardless of the actual condition is likely unenforceable under these regulations.

**What You Can Do or Ask For**
*   **Stand your ground politely:** Inform the agent that you have fulfilled your legal obligation to leave the premises reasonably clean and in their original condition, which you have achieved through your own cleaning [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
*   **Request a joint final inspection:** Ask to be present during the final inspection so you can point out that the carpets match their condition at move-in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
*   **Reference the Condition Report:** Direct the agent to the signed Condition Report from when you moved in. question: When I moved out I agreed the agent could take an amount for cleaning out of my bond, but I never signed a bond claim form for it. Then my full bond came back to me, and a month later the agent sent a separate invoice for the cleaning. Do I have to pay it? Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Authorised Version v115)** and the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (Authorised Version v009)**, which are both in force today, here is how the law applies to your situation:

### Direct Answer
**No, you do not automatically have to pay the invoice, and agreeing to a bond deduction is not the same as agreeing to pay an invoice.** Under Victorian tenancy law, these are two entirely separate legal mechanisms. 

### Why They Are Different
1. **The Bond Process:** A bond is held by the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority (RTBA), not the agent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). To access any part of it, the agent must follow a strict statutory process and submit a claim using an approved form to the RTBA [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Because your full bond was returned to you, the agent failed to successfully lodge or sign the required bond claim form in time. Once the bond is paid out, those funds are gone, and the agent cannot retroactively deduct money from it.
2. **The Invoice (Debt) Process:** An invoice is a request for you to pay a debt under your tenancy agreement. A verbal agreement to *deduct* cleaning costs from a bond does not legally bind you to *pay* an invoice later. While the agent may still pursue the cleaning cost as a separate debt if they believe you breached your tenancy agreement, they cannot force payment of an invoice simply because you verbally agreed to a bond deduction.

### What the Law Says About Cleaning & Bonds
* **Cleaning Costs from Bonds:** Under the Act, an agent is only entitled to claim the reasonable cost of cleaning from a bond if the premises were not left reasonably clean, taking into account fair wear and tear and the condition at the start of the tenancy [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
* **Professional Cleaning Rules:** The Regulations state that an agent cannot require professional cleaning unless it was carried out immediately before you moved in, or it is strictly necessary to restore the premises to their original condition based on the condition report [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
* **Claim Requirements:** Any claim for bond repayment must be made in a form approved by the RTBA and must specify the exact amount being refunded or apportioned [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 

### What You Can Do
* **Do not feel pressured to pay the invoice immediately.** Since the bond was returned, the agent missed their statutory window to access those funds through the RTBA. 
* **Assess your obligation:** If you genuinely left the premises reasonably clean (considering fair wear and tear), you do not owe the money at all. You can politely decline the invoice and state that the tenancy has been concluded and the bond returned.
* **If you do owe the money but just didn't want it taken from the bond:** You are not legally forced to pay a retroactive invoice for a service you agreed to have deducted from a bond. If the agent insists, they would need to take you to VCAT to prove you owe the debt under your tenancy agreement. 
* **Keep records:** Save all emails, texts, and photos of the property's condition when you moved out. This protects you if the agent tries to dispute the matter later.

*Note: This information is based on Victorian residential tenancy law as it stands today. For personalised legal advice, you may contact VCAT or a community legal centre.*

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both required points are covered. On point 1, the answer says "agreeing to a bond deduction is not the same as agreeing to pay an invoice" and that a bond claim must use an RTBA-approved form specifying the amount. On point 2, the hardest one, it says cleaning costs are claimable only "if the premises were not left reasonably clean, taking into account fair wear and tear and the condition at the start of the tenancy", and that the agent "would need to take you to VCAT to prove you owe the debt". Some extra claims are questionable, such as the agent having "missed their statutory window", but they do not change the meaning of either required point.

question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. I've called them twice today. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
### What the law says about your situation
Under Victorian tenancy law, a broken tap that is leaking or cutting off your water supply qualifies as an **urgent repair**. The law defines urgent repairs to include *"any fault or damage that... results or will result in a substantial amount of water being wasted"* and *"a failure or breakdown of any essential service or appliance provided for... water"* [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 

The owner cannot legally force you to wait, nor can they restrict you to only their own tradespeople if they are failing to respond. The law requires the rental provider to carry out urgent repairs immediately after being notified [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Because your contact has stated that none of their tradespeople can come yet, you have been unable to get them to carry out the repairs, which triggers your legal right to step in.

### What you can do right now
Because you have already called twice today (which satisfies the requirement of taking *"reasonable steps"* to get the provider to act), **you do not have to wait**. You are legally allowed to arrange for a qualified tradesperson to fix the tap yourself. Here is exactly how the process works:

1. **Arrange the repair:** Hire a suitably qualified person to carry out the urgent repair [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
2. **Get reimbursed:** The owner must reimburse you for the reasonable cost of the repairs, up to a maximum of **$2,500** (including GST) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). 
3. **Provide written notice:** After the repair is completed, you must give the owner written notice within 7 days detailing the repairs carried out and the cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The owner then has exactly 7 days to reimburse you once they receive this notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**If the cost exceeds $2,500 or the owner refuses to pay:**
If the repair costs more than $2,500, or if you cannot afford to pay upfront and get reimbursed later, you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring the owner to carry out the repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The Tribunal is legally required to hear your application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

---
**Documents applied (in force today):**
* *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version v115 (in force from 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
* *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised Version v009 (in force from 30 June 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered: the tap fault is called an urgent repair (failure of an essential water service and substantial water wasted). The answer says that after reasonable steps (calling twice) the renter can arrange the repair and be reimbursed reasonable costs up to $2,500 within 7 days of written notice. The hardest point is met by 'nor can they restrict you to only their own tradespeople if they are failing to respond', which conveys that the preferred-tradesperson policy cannot stop an urgent repair.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer asserts neither failure condition, stating that "you do not have to wait" and that "The owner must reimburse you for the reasonable cost of the repairs, up to a maximum of $2,500".

question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. I haven't moved any of my things in or stayed there yet. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
Based on the law in force today (9 November 2026), your rights are governed by:
- ***Residential Tenancies Act 1997***, Authorised Version **v115** (in force from 13 October 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- ***Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021***, Authorised Version **v009** (in force from 30 June 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

---

### What the Law Says About Your Situation
Under Victorian law, your landlord has strict duties regarding the condition of the property:
- **Minimum Standards:** Every room must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure. The premises must also be structurally sound and weatherproof [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). 
- **Fit for Occupation:** The landlord must ensure the premises comply with these minimum standards, are vacant and reasonably clean when you move in, and are maintained in good repair and a fit condition for occupation .
- **Urgent Repairs:** Damp or mould caused by building structure is legally classified as an *urgent repair* [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Rotting timber that affects structural soundness also breaches the minimum standards [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

---

### Your Options

**1. Can you cancel the lease?**
The provided documents do not explicitly contain provisions for cancelling a residential tenancy agreement *before* moving in due to property defects. However, because the landlord is legally required to provide premises that meet minimum standards and are fit for occupation , these defects constitute a breach of their duties. You should document this immediately (see below) as it strengthens your position if you need to negotiate an exit or apply to VCAT.

**2. Can you ask for repairs?**
Yes, and the law provides clear pathways depending on severity:
- **Urgent Repairs:** Because mould/damp from building structure is an urgent repair [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), the landlord must carry it out immediately upon being notified . 
  - If they refuse or fail to act, you can arrange the repairs yourself and claim reimbursement for reasonable costs up to **$2,500** (or a prescribed amount if higher) . 
  - Alternatively, you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring them to do the work .
- **Non-Urgent Repairs:** If the issue is deemed non-urgent, you must give the landlord written notice. If they do not carry out the repairs within **14 days**, you can apply to VCAT for a compliance order .

**3. Can you ask for lower rent?**
The provided documents do not contain specific provisions allowing you to directly negotiate or demand a lower rent due to these defects. 
- The only related option mentioned is that if the landlord breaches their duty to maintain the premises, you may apply to VCAT for an order authorising you to pay your rent into a **Rent Special Account** .

---

### Immediate Steps You Should Take
Since you have picked up the keys but haven't moved in yet, you must act quickly to protect your rights:
1. **Complete the Condition Report:** Before moving anything in, fill out and sign the condition report provided by the landlord. Explicitly note the damp, mould, and rotting timber on it . This creates a legal record that the defects existed before you took possession .
2. **Send Written Notice:** Formally notify your rental provider or agent in writing (email is acceptable) about the defects and request urgent repairs . Keep a copy of this notice.
3. **Take Photos:** Document the damp, mould, and rotting timber with dated photos to support your condition report and repair requests .

*Note: If the landlord fails to address these breaches, you may also apply to VCAT to amend an inaccurate condition report or seek further remedies under the Act .*

It should have said that a renter who has not yet taken possession can end the agreement by notice if the premises fail the minimum standards or are unfit. The minimum-standards point and the repair route are adequately covered.

The answer never says the renter must move in and pay rent first, and it denies any direct right to lower rent, stating "The provided documents do not contain specific provisions allowing you to directly negotiate or demand a lower rent due to these defects" and pointing only to a VCAT order for a Rent Special Account.

question: Our rental was broken into several times while we were moving out, and there are about three weeks left on our fixed-term lease. The burglars damaged the plumbing and wiring, so we can't even clean properly. What are our options before the lease ends?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997**, Authorised Version No. 115 (in force today) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), here is what the law says and what your options are:

### What the Law Says About Damaged Premises
* If rented premises become **"unfit for human habitation"** or are destroyed to such an extent that they are **"rendered unsafe,"** a renter has the right to terminate the agreement early [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* Renters must notify their landlord/agent in writing **"as soon as practicable"** after becoming aware of any damage, including both the fact and nature of that damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This reporting duty also covers any breakdown of facilities, fixtures, or equipment provided by the landlord [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* The landlord is responsible for urgent repairs. If they fail to act, the law allows renters to either arrange the repairs themselves or apply to the Tribunal for an order forcing the landlord to do it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What You Can Do Before Your Lease Ends
1. **Report the damage immediately**: Send written notice to your residential rental provider "as soon as practicable" detailing the break-ins and the specific damage to the plumbing, wiring, and any broken fixtures [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Terminate the lease early (if the property is unsafe)**: If the damaged plumbing and wiring make the home "unfit for human habitation" or "unsafe," you can give your landlord a notice of intention to vacate under section 91ZD [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You can set the termination date as the day you hand over the notice or a later date, effectively ending your fixed-term lease early without penalty [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Arrange urgent repairs yourself**: If the damage qualifies as an "urgent repair" (e.g., serious water leaks or electrical faults) and you have tried to get your landlord/agent to fix it immediately but cannot, you may hire a professional to do it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You must give the provider 7 days' written notice of the work and cost afterward; they are legally required to reimburse your reasonable costs within 7 days of receiving that notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Apply to VCAT for urgent repairs**: If you cannot afford the repairs or the cost exceeds the prescribed amount, you can apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring the provider to carry out the work. The Tribunal must hear this application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

*Note: Because you are still on a fixed-term lease with three weeks remaining, your primary leverage is the landlord's legal duty to maintain the premises in good repair and ensure they remain safe and habitable during that term.*

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered: (1) written notice to the provider 'as soon as practicable'; (2) the landlord must fix urgent repairs, and the renter may 'hire a professional' and be reimbursed 'within 7 days', with 'serious water leaks or electrical faults' given as examples, which is the hardest point because it is somewhat hedged; and (3) a s 91ZD notice of intention to vacate may set 'the termination date as the day you hand over the notice... effectively ending your fixed-term lease early' if the premises are unfit or unsafe.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer asserts neither failing claim: it says 'The landlord is responsible for urgent repairs', frames renter-arranged repairs as optional and reimbursable ('they are legally required to reimburse your reasonable costs'), and says the renter can end the lease early ('effectively ending your fixed-term lease early without penalty').

question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. The app is run by a payments company my agent uses, and it's that company that charges the card fee. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
## What the law says

I relied on two documents that are in force today (9 November 2026):
- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997**, file *rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf*, version 115, in force from 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021**, file *rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf*, version 009, in force from 30 June 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

The version numbers come from the files' metadata. The excerpts I retrieved don't print an "Authorised Version No." line.

**1. A fee-free option must be reasonably available.** The provider or their agent must ensure that a rent payment method with no additional costs, other than your own bank or account fees, is reasonably available to you. The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person and 400 for a body corporate (s 42(4)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Your free bank transfer is the kind of method this refers to. The Act doesn't say whether a slower method is still "reasonably available", and I found nothing in the documents that defines the term.

**2. Fee disclosure.** Before you consent to a payment method, the provider or agent must tell you about any costs you may incur. This expressly includes third party transaction fees and other electronic payment facility fees (s 42(7)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**3. Charges for electronic payment facilities.** A person must not demand or receive a charge for "the establishment or use of direct debit facilities or any other electronic payment facility for payment of rent" (s 51(3)(b)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**4. Rent payment fees.** A person, other than an ADI, must not demand or receive a fee for any prescribed matter relating to the payment of rent (s 51A) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person and 400 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The regulations apply from 31 March 2026 and prescribe "rent payment (other than payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act)". They also prescribe "failed payments" and "administrative costs" (reg 21C) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- So a card fee for paying rent is prohibited unless it is a surcharge permitted under another Act.
- The documents don't say which other Act that might be. They also don't say whether your payments company is an ADI.

**Can the app charge you the card fee?** On these documents, probably not, unless the fee is a surcharge permitted by another law. I can't confirm that either way from the documents.

## Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or the agent?

On the text, no. Sections 51(3) and 51A apply to "a person", not only to the agent or provider [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A fee kept by the payments company is therefore not automatically outside them. The disclosure and fee-free-method duties in s 42(4) and (7) apply to the provider and agent, so your agent is responsible for those even though the app is a third party's [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

- **Use the free bank transfer.** It avoids the fee. Electronic funds transfer is the prescribed payment method that the provider or agent must permit (s 42(5), reg 19) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Ask your agent for written details.** Ask for the fee amount and for which law permits it as a "payment surcharge". Check that you were told about the fee before you agreed to use the card option (s 42(7)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Check your agreement.** A term requiring you to pay rent in advance by a method with additional costs is a prescribed prohibited term (reg 11(d)) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The standard-form notes also say the provider must permit a fee-free payment method [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Raise it with the agent if the free option isn't practical.** You could point to s 42(4) and s 51A [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't cover where to complain or how to enforce these rules, so I can't advise on that.

For the hardest point, it says 's 51A apply to "a person"', that 'a person, other than an ADI, must not demand or receive a fee' for rent payment under reg 21C, and that 'On the text, no' it doesn't matter who collects, 'unless the fee is a surcharge permitted by another law'. It also gives the next step 'Use the free bank transfer.'
