question: My lease is on the standard form and started in 2024. It has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. I cleaned them myself and they're back to how they were when I moved in, but the agent wants a receipt from a professional cleaner. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?
answer:
**Short answer:** On the documents retrieved, you probably don't have to pay for a professional cleaner. Two caveats are below. I haven't seen your actual lease wording or condition report.

**Documents used**
- *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026 (file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf") [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, version 009, in force from 30 June 2026 (file "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf") [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The excerpt I retrieved doesn't print an "Authorised Version No." on its face. The 009 comes from the file name and metadata.
- These are the latest versions I found. I did not retrieve the 2024 versions, so I haven't checked what they said when your lease started.

## What the law says

- **Professional cleaning terms are prohibited unless they are in the standard form.** A lease must not include a term requiring the premises to be professionally cleaned at the end of the tenancy, or requiring the renter to pay for it, unless that term is in the standard form (s 27B(1)(d)–(e)) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A prohibited term is void and unenforceable (s 26A(2)) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Your pet clause is probably void.** The standard form's pet clause only deals with consent to keep a pet. It says nothing about carpet cleaning [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). A carpet-cleaning requirement in an added pet clause is an extra term, so it likely falls within the prohibition. This assumes the clause is an additional term and not part of the standard form text.
- **What the standard form allows.** The standard-form clause (clause 11 of Form 1) says the rental provider must not require professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy unless one of two things applies [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf):
  1. The premises were professionally cleaned immediately before the tenancy started, **and** you were told so.
  2. Professional cleaning is needed to restore the premises to their condition at the start of the tenancy, having regard to the condition report and taking fair wear and tear into account.
- **Your general duty.** You must leave the premises reasonably clean and in the same condition as when you moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear (s 63) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The same standard appears in the regulation and the standard form [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## Your two caveats

- If the carpets were professionally cleaned before you moved in and you were told, the agent can require professional cleaning [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Check your condition report and move-in paperwork.
- If the carpets are genuinely not back to their starting condition, professional cleaning may be required under the second exception [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What helps show the carpets' condition

The condition report is the key document. The form says it helps resolve disputes over cleaning and damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Start-of-tenancy report.** You should have filled in, signed and dated it within 5 business days of moving in. Your comments and photos on floor coverings are the baseline [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Photos.** The form says to take photos at the start and the end of the tenancy. They should be dated, labelled, show the location or room, and include close-up and distance shots [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **End-of-tenancy report.** The agent must complete the final inspection and condition report within 10 days after the agreement ends. They must give you a chance to attend, and they must allow for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). For each item, they must note whether it is clean, undamaged and working. If an item has changed, they are advised to comment and take pictures [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Your own cleaning evidence.** Your own dated photos and any record of the cleaning you did are useful. The documents don't say anything about receipts for self-cleaning.

## What you can ask the agent

- Ask them to point to the lease term that makes the pet clause enforceable. Say you understand that professional cleaning terms outside the standard form are prohibited (s 27B) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Ask them to show, from the condition report, either that the carpets were professionally cleaned before your tenancy or that professional cleaning is needed to restore them [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- Ask to attend the final inspection [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- A renter can apply to the Tribunal to have a term declared invalid or varied if it is harsh or unconscionable (s 28) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

The documents I retrieved don't cover how a bond or compensation dispute proceeds once the agent claims against you. I haven't covered that process here.

Its substance is still stated correctly: the agent may not require professional cleaning unless 'the premises were professionally cleaned immediately before the tenancy started, and you were told so' or it 'is needed to restore the premises to their condition at the start of the tenancy... taking fair wear and tear into account'. The answer also gives the s 63 duty to leave the premises reasonably clean, and says the start-of-tenancy report is 'the baseline'.

question: When I moved out I agreed the agent could take an amount for cleaning out of my bond, but I never signed a bond claim form for it. Then my full bond came back to me, and a month later the agent sent a separate invoice for the cleaning. Do I have to pay it? Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?
answer:
**Document used:** *rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf*, the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, **Authorised Version No. 115**, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). It is the most recent version in the retrieved documents, so I've treated it as the version in force today.

## What the law says

- **Cleaning duty and bond claims:** A renter must leave the premises "reasonably clean" at the end of the agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A provider (which includes an agent) may claim from the bond the reasonable cost of cleaning, if the premises weren't left reasonably clean, having regard to their condition at the start [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Bond claim form:** A bond claim goes to the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority and must be in a form the Authority approves [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A provider must not request or obtain your signature on a claim form that doesn't state the amount of bond to be refunded and how it is apportioned [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Evidence:** At least 3 days before claiming bond for the provider, the provider or agent must give you "bond claim evidence". This means an invoice, receipt, quote, photograph or other prescribed evidence, and it must not conflict with the condition report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Where the full bond is refunded:** If the provider or agent claims repayment of the bond *to the renter*, the Authority must repay it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Act makes no mention of this closing off later claims.
- **Claims after the bond:** If a person has recovered compensation from a bond, they can still take proceedings to recover an additional amount [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). That section speaks of someone who *has recovered* from the bond. Here nothing was taken from it, so the documents don't squarely answer your situation.
- **Tribunal route:** The cleaning duty is a "duty provision" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The agent would give a breach of duty notice, which must be in writing, give details of the loss and be signed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If it isn't complied with, the agent may apply to the Tribunal for compensation or a compliance order [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Tribunal can order compensation as specified [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). It may consider whether money has been recovered from the bond, any offer of compensation, and whether the applicant took steps to mitigate the loss [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?

**The documents don't say.** Nothing in the Act treats a verbal or informal agreement to a bond deduction as an agreement to pay a separate invoice. I can't tell you whether your agreement is legally binding as a contract, because the documents don't cover that.

What the Act does show is that the bond mechanism is formal. It requires an approved form with specified amounts, supporting evidence and your signature [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You never signed a claim form, and the bond was refunded in full.

## What you can do

1. **Ask for the evidence.** Request the invoice, photos and quote showing the premises weren't reasonably clean, and compare them with the condition report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Check the cost is reasonable.** The Act only allows the *reasonable* cost of cleaning, taking the starting condition into account [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Don't assume you must pay.** If you dispute it, the agent's route under the Act is a breach of duty notice and then an application to the Tribunal [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Check the agreement for a professional cleaning term.** A term requiring professional cleaning, or requiring you to pay for it, is prohibited unless it is in the standard form [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. **For a definitive answer,** contact Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy advice service. The retrieved documents don't settle whether your informal agreement binds you.

must-mention.reason: Yes: both points are covered, though the first is borderline because it is framed as the documents being silent. Point 1 is covered by "Nothing in the Act treats a verbal or informal agreement to a bond deduction as an agreement to pay a separate invoice," together with the explanation that a bond claim needs an approved form, stated amounts and evidence. The rubric accepts saying the documents do not say something, and the answer still leans clearly that the two are different. Point 2 is covered by "reasonably clean" and "the reasonable cost of cleaning... having regard to their condition at the start," which is tied to the duty provision and the Tribunal route.

must-not-say.reason: Yes, neither failure condition is asserted: the answer says the documents "don't say" whether agreeing to a bond deduction means agreeing to pay the invoice and advises "Don't assume you must pay"; on the full refund, it says "The Act makes no mention of this closing off later claims" and describes the agent's remaining Tribunal route.

question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. I've called them twice today. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
## What the law says

I relied on two documents: the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997** (file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", version 115, in force from 13 October 2026) and the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021** (file "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf", version 009, in force from 30 June 2026). Both are the latest versions I retrieved before today, 9 November 2026. The text I retrieved doesn't print an "Authorised Version No." line, so the version numbers come from the documents' metadata.

- **You don't have to wait indefinitely.** A renter may arrange urgent repairs if (a) they have taken reasonable steps to arrange for the provider or agent to carry out the repairs immediately, and (b) they are unable to get the provider or agent to do so [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **A broken tap with the water off is likely to count as "urgent".** The Act's definition of urgent repairs includes a burst water service, a failure or breakdown of the water supply, and a water-using fitting or fixture malfunctioning so that a substantial amount of water is wasted [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Act doesn't mention taps specifically, so how it applies to yours is a judgment call.
- **The owner's "own tradespeople only" position.** The documents say nothing about a provider being allowed to limit repairs to their own tradespeople. The legal test is whether the provider or agent actually gets the repair done immediately [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Whether two calls today count as "reasonable steps" isn't defined in the documents.
- **Who can do the work.** The standard rental agreement form says only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, urgent or non-urgent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The Act says a suitably qualified person includes a registered or licensed tradesperson where the work requires it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). In practice, use a licensed plumber rather than fixing it yourself.

## What you can do or ask

1. **Give written notice now.** The form says to notify the provider in writing of an urgent repair [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The Act requires written notice as soon as practicable of damage or a breakdown [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Say that you've phoned twice, that the water is off to the whole house, and that you will arrange a plumber if the repair isn't done immediately. This also records your "reasonable steps".
2. **Arrange the repair** if they still don't act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Send a second written notice.** You must give the provider 7 days' written notice of the repairs carried out and their cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Claim the cost back.**
   - The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days of receiving that notice. The Act caps this at the reasonable cost or a higher prescribed amount if one applies, whichever is less [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
   - The standard form states the figure as up to **$2,500** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
5. **If they don't pay within 7 days**, you can apply to the Tribunal (VCAT) for a compensation or compliance order [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
6. **If you can't afford the repair, or it costs more than the prescribed amount, or they refuse to pay**, you can apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring the urgent repairs to be done. The Tribunal must hear that application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

The Tribunal must also consider whether you gave the required written notice when it decides compensation claims [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered, though the third only by implication. Point 1: the answer says urgent repairs include 'a burst water service, a failure or breakdown of the water supply.' Point 2: it says the renter may arrange the repair after reasonable steps and the provider 'must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days', capped at the prescribed amount ($2,500). Point 3 is the hardest: the answer never cites reg 11(e) and wrongly implies the documents are silent on nominated tradespeople, but it does cover the alternative by stating 'The documents say nothing about a provider being allowed to limit repairs to their own tradespeople. The legal test is whether the provider or agent actually gets the repair done immediately,' then telling the renter to arrange the repair if they still don't act.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer says neither failing claim; it states "You don't have to wait indefinitely" and "The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days of receiving that notice," which reject waiting for the owner's tradespeople and confirm the renter can recover costs.

version-cited.reason: Yes: the answer names both required documents with their in-force versions, "Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (file \"rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf\", version 115, in force from 13 October 2026)" and "Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (file \"rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf\", version 009, in force from 30 June 2026)". Every rule it applies is cited to the links 97-109aa115 or 21-3sra009, and it relies on no other version.

question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. I haven't moved any of my things in or stayed there yet. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
## Sources
- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997** (file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf"), **Authorised Version No. 115**, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This is the latest version in the documents, so I treat it as the one in force today (9 November 2026).
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021** (file "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf", dated 30 June 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The text I retrieved doesn't print an "Authorised Version" number. Only the file metadata says version "009".

## What the law says

- **Condition on moving in.** The rental provider must make sure the premises comply with the prescribed rental minimum standards on or before the day you move in (s 65A(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Mould, damp and structure.** The minimum standards say each room must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure (Sch 4, item 8). The premises must also be structurally sound and weatherproof (item 7) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Duty to repair.** The provider must maintain the premises in good repair and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs.** The definition includes a failure to comply with the rental minimum standards. It also includes any fault or damage that makes the premises unsafe or insecure, including mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do

**1. Cancel the lease before moving in (s 91L)**
- The agreement terminates if you have not entered into possession and you give the provider a notice of termination on one of these grounds. The ones relevant to you are that the premises are not in good repair, are unfit for human habitation, or do not meet the rental minimum standards [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Caveat 1:** the retrieved text does not define "entered into possession". You have the keys but haven't moved in, so check how that applies to you.
- **Caveat 2:** the retrieved text does not set out the form of a s 91L notice or a notice period. Put it in writing and say which ground you rely on.
- **Alternative:** s 91ZD lets a renter give a notice of intention to vacate if the premises are unfit for human habitation. The termination date can be the date of the notice [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The standard-form agreement also says the provider can't claim lease-break compensation where this section is used (clause 16.3 of Form 2) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). That clause appears in the more-than-5-years form, so check your own agreement.

**2. Ask for repairs**
- **Urgent repairs.** Mould or damp tied to the building structure is listed as an urgent repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
  - If the premises don't meet the standards when you take occupation, you can issue an urgent repair request (s 65A(2)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
  - If the provider won't act, you may arrange the repairs yourself after taking reasonable steps to get the provider to do them. The provider must reimburse reasonable costs within 7 days of written notice, up to the prescribed amount [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The standard form states that amount as $2500 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
  - You can apply to VCAT if you can't meet the cost, the cost is over the prescribed amount, or the provider refuses to pay. VCAT must hear it within 2 business days [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Rotting timber.** It isn't named as urgent. It may fall under "unsafe or insecure" or the structural-soundness standard, depending on the facts [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). If it's non-urgent:
  - Give written notice. If the provider hasn't done the repairs within 14 days, you can apply to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria to investigate (s 74) or to VCAT (s 75) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
  - VCAT must hear a non-urgent application within 7 days. It can order specified repairs by a suitably qualified person and award compensation under s 212(2) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Rent into the Rent Special Account.** After you give notice and the provider fails to repair, you can apply to VCAT to pay rent into the Rent Special Account for a set period (s 77) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**3. Lower rent**
- I found **no provision in these documents that lets you simply reduce the rent** for this problem.
- Rent only accrues day to day (s 39) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If the premises aren't vacant and reasonably clean on the agreed entry day, you don't owe rent until you actually move in (s 65(3)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Mould is not expressly mentioned in that section, so it may not apply to your situation.
- Withholding rent into the Rent Special Account (above) and compensation under s 76(1)(c) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) are the closest remedies the documents give. The text of s 212, which governs compensation, was not in what I retrieved.

## Practical points
- Document everything with photos and written notices. A condition report you give the provider is treated as notice of the defects in it (s 36(1A)) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You must return it within 5 business days after entering occupation (s 35(2)) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Under the Regulations, a provider must disclose a repair notice about structural mould or damp received in the last 3 years [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

This is general information from the documents, not legal advice. Consumer Affairs Victoria or a community legal centre can confirm how s 91L applies once you have the keys.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three required points are present. First, the answer states that the provider 'must make sure the premises comply with the prescribed rental minimum standards on or before the day you move in (s 65A(1)),' and that this includes being free from 'mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure (Sch 4, item 8).' Second, it explains that under s 91L the agreement 'terminates if you have not entered into possession and you give the provider a notice of termination' on the grounds that the premises are 'not in good repair, are unfit for human habitation, or do not meet the rental minimum standards.' Its caveat that 'entered into possession' is undefined is a reasonable flag, not a hedge that hides the rule. Third, it covers the repair route, saying 'you can issue an urgent repair request (s 65A(2))' and explaining the duty to maintain the premises in good repair.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. Neither prohibited claim appears: the answer explicitly says "I found no provision in these documents that lets you simply reduce the rent" and points only to Tribunal-ordered remedies (Rent Special Account, compensation), and it offers pre-move-in options such as cancelling under s 91L because "you have not entered into possession", so it never says the renter must move in and pay rent first.

question: Our rental was broken into several times while we were moving out, and there are about three weeks left on our fixed-term lease. The burglars damaged the plumbing and wiring, so we can't even clean properly. What are our options before the lease ends?
answer:
**Sources:** I used the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", version 115, in force from 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I also used the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (file "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf", version 009, in force from 30 June 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). These are the latest versions I found, so I've treated them as current today (9 Nov 2026). The retrieved text doesn't print an "Authorised Version No." The numbers above come from the file names and metadata.

## What the law says

- **Leaving early because the premises are unfit.** A renter may give a notice of intention to vacate if the premises are unfit for human habitation, or have been destroyed or damaged enough to be unsafe [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The termination date can be the day you give the notice or any later date. The notice must be in writing and signed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Why an ordinary notice won't help.** A normal notice needs at least 28 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). In a fixed-term agreement it has no effect if its termination date is before the end of the term [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). With about three weeks left, it wouldn't shorten anything.
- **Urgent repairs.** "Urgent repairs" include a burst water service, a dangerous electrical fault, and any fault or damage that makes the premises unsafe or insecure [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The plumbing and wiring damage may fall within these.
- **Your duties.** You must give the provider written notice of damage as soon as practicable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). At the end of the agreement you must leave the premises reasonably clean and in the same condition as when you moved in, but only "as far as practicable" and allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask for

1. **Notify the provider in writing now.** Describe the break-ins and the plumbing and wiring damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Keep photos and any police report. The documents don't say anything about police reports or insurance.
2. **Ask for urgent repairs.** The provider must carry out urgent repairs after being notified [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
   - If the provider won't act immediately, you can arrange the repairs yourself [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
   - You must give 7 days' written notice of the repairs and their cost. The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days of that notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations put the direct reimbursement limit at $2,500 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Apply to VCAT.** You can apply for an order requiring urgent repairs if you can't meet the cost, the cost is above the prescribed amount ($2,500), or the provider refuses to pay [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). VCAT must hear the application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Consider ending the lease under s 91ZD.** This depends on the premises actually being unfit for human habitation or unsafe. The documents don't define those terms or say whether burglary damage qualifies, so this is a factual question.
   - In the more-than-5-year standard form agreement, the provider can't claim "rent foregone" if the renter ends the agreement under s 91ZD [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The documents don't show the equivalent term for shorter standard-form leases.
5. **Cleaning.** Because you can only clean "as far as practicable" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), tell the provider in writing that the damage prevents proper cleaning. Keep photos of the state you left it in.

## What the documents don't answer

- They don't say who is liable for burglary damage or how it affects your bond. The Act's damage duty applies to the renter and their "visitors", meaning people on the premises with the renter's permission [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Burglars wouldn't seem to fit that definition, but the documents don't address burglary directly.
- They don't say whether the provider must fix the locks after repeated break-ins. The standard form only says the provider must ensure the premises have working locks that meet the rental minimum standards [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

Consumer Affairs Victoria or a community legal centre can advise on your specific facts.

must-mention.reason: Yes: all three points are covered. (1) The answer says "You must give the provider written notice of damage as soon as practicable." (2) It lists burst water services and dangerous electrical faults as urgent repairs. It says the provider must carry them out and that, if the provider "won't act immediately, you can arrange the repairs yourself" and be reimbursed. Its "may fall within these" is a mild hedge, not one that leaves the point unclear. (3) The hardest point is covered by "A renter may give a notice of intention to vacate if the premises are unfit for human habitation, or have been destroyed or damaged enough to be unsafe... The termination date can be the day you give the notice." The answer presents this, unlike an ordinary notice, as available within their fixed term.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never makes the renter liable for the burglary damage or bound to stay regardless: it notes that 'Burglars wouldn't seem to fit that definition' of visitors, presents self-arranged repairs only as an option with reimbursement ('The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost'), and says a renter 'may give a notice of intention to vacate if the premises are unfit for human habitation' with a termination date that 'can be the day you give the notice'.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 with its version three ways: 'version 115, in force from 13 October 2026', the file 'rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf', and the link 97-109aa115. This matches Authorised Version No. 115, the version in force. The only other document it relies on is the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, cited as 'version 009, in force from 30 June 2026' (link 21-3sra009), which is also the in-force version. No rule comes from an earlier or later version.

question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. The app is run by a payments company my agent uses, and it's that company that charges the card fee. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
## What the law says

I used the Act and Regulations in force today (9 November 2026).

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997**, file *rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf*, dated 13 October 2026. Its metadata gives the version as 115 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The excerpts don't print an "Authorised Version" label, so I'm relying on that metadata.
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021**, file *rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf*, dated 30 June 2026, version 009 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**1. A fee-free payment method must be available.**
- The provider or their agent must ensure a rent payment method with no additional costs, other than the renter's own bank or account fees, is reasonably available to the renter [1, s 42(4)].
- The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person and 400 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Your free bank transfer fits this. Electronic funds transfer is also the prescribed payment method that must be permitted [2, reg 19; 1, s 42(5)].
- The documents don't say whether a "slower" free option is still "reasonably available".

**2. The agent must disclose costs first.**
- Before you consent to a payment method, the provider or agent must tell you about any costs you may incur. These expressly include third party transaction fees and other electronic payment facility fees [1, s 42(7)].

**3. Fees on rent payments are restricted, whoever gets the money.**
- A person must not demand or receive from a renter a charge for establishing or using direct debit or "any other electronic payment facility for payment of rent" [1, s 51(3)(b)]. The penalty is 60 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Separately, a person other than an ADI must not demand or receive a fee for any prescribed matter relating to the payment of rent [1, s 51A]. The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person and 400 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The prescribed matters include "rent payment (other than payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act)". Regulation 21C has applied since 31 March 2026 [2, reg 21C(2)(i)].

## Does it matter if the fee goes to the app company or the agent?

**Mostly no.** Sections 51(3) and 51A apply to "a person", not just the agent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A fee kept by the payments company is therefore not automatically outside them.

There are two limits:
- The duties in s 42(4) and s 42(7) bind the provider and agent specifically [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Your agent remains responsible for having a free method available and for disclosing the card fee.
- Section 51A excludes an "ADI" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and reg 21C excludes surcharges "permitted under any other Act" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The retrieved documents don't define "ADI" or say which other Act permits surcharges. I can't tell you whether your payments company falls into either exception.

## Can the app charge you the card fee?

On these documents, a card fee on rent is likely prohibited unless one of those two exceptions applies. I can't confirm that either does. The documents also don't say whether a card fee counts as an "electronic payment facility" charge under s 51(3).

## What you can do

- **Use the free bank transfer.** That avoids the fee [1, s 42(4)].
- **Ask your agent in writing** to confirm which fee-free method is available and what the card fee is. They must give you this cost information before you consent [1, s 42(7)].
- **Ask for the legal basis of the surcharge.** Ask whether they rely on the ADI exception or on a surcharge permitted under another Act [1; 2].
- **If you've already paid the fee,** the documents don't cover refunds, complaints or VCAT steps, so I can't advise on those from them.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are present. Point 1 is stated directly: a no-extra-cost method must be 'reasonably available to the renter' (s 42(4)). Point 3 is covered by 'Use the free bank transfer.' The hardest point, point 2, is covered without being hedged into ambiguity: 'Mostly no. Sections 51(3) and 51A apply to "a person", not just the agent' and 'a card fee on rent is likely prohibited unless one of those two exceptions applies' (the ADI exception and surcharges 'permitted under any other Act').

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer makes neither forbidden claim. It never treats the free bank transfer as permitting the fee, and instead says "a card fee on rent is likely prohibited unless one of those two exceptions applies." It also never exempts the landlord or agent, stating that "Sections 51(3) and 51A apply to 'a person', not just the agent" and that the only exclusions are for an ADI and surcharges "permitted under any other Act."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as 'version 115' (file rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf, link 97-109aa115) and the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 as 'version 009' (file rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf, link 21-3sra009); both are the versions in force on 9 November 2026, and it relies on no other version.

question: My lease is on the standard form and started in 2024. It has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. I cleaned them myself and they're back to how they were when I moved in, but the agent wants a receipt from a professional cleaner. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?
answer:
## Short answer

On the retrieved text, you probably don't have to pay for a professional cleaner just because the pet clause says so. A term requiring professional carpet cleaning that isn't in the standard form is prohibited. What matters is whether the carpets are back to their move-in condition, allowing for fair wear and tear.

**Which documents:** I used the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", version 115, in force from 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I also used the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, file "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf", version 009, in force from 30 June 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). These version numbers come from the documents' metadata. The retrieved text doesn't show an "Authorised Version No." label, so I can't confirm that wording. I also don't have the versions that applied when your lease started in 2024, so this is the law as it stands today.

## What the law says

- **Prohibited terms.** A residential rental agreement must not include a term requiring all or part of the premises to be professionally cleaned at the end of the tenancy, unless that term is in the standard form. The same applies to a term making the renter pay for professional cleaning [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Effect.** A prohibited term is void and unenforceable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). An additional term is also invalid if it is a prohibited term [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **What the standard form allows.** Standard form clause 11 says the rental provider must not require professional cleaning unless one of two things applies [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf):
  - Professional cleaning was done immediately before the tenancy started and you were told so; or
  - Professional cleaning is needed to restore the premises to their condition at the start of the tenancy, "having regard to the condition report and taking into account fair wear and tear".
- **Your general duty.** You must leave the premises reasonably clean and, as far as practicable, in the same condition as when you moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The standard form pet clause.** It only covers asking for consent to keep a pet [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). A professional carpet-cleaning requirement in your pet clause would be an additional term. I haven't seen your clause's exact wording, so this assumes it requires professional cleaning outright.

## What you can do and ask

1. **Ask the agent for the legal basis.** If the carpets are in their move-in condition, professional cleaning isn't "required to restore" them under clause 11 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). You can ask the agent to point to the provision they rely on.
2. **Check the "cleaned before you moved in" exception.** Professional cleaning can only be required if it was done before your tenancy and you were told [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Look at your move-in paperwork for that.
3. **Challenge the term if needed.** A renter can apply to the Tribunal for an order declaring a term invalid or varying it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Act also notes the Tribunal may declare terms invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Evidence of the carpets' condition

The prescribed condition report (Form 4) is the key document [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf):

- **Move-in condition report.** It lists floor coverings and records whether each item is clean, undamaged and working. It is meant to help resolve disputes over cleaning and damage [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Keep your signed copy [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Your own comments and photos.** The form invites you to comment and attach photos [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Photos at both ends of the tenancy.** Take them at the beginning and end. They should be dated and labelled, show the location or room, and include close-ups and wider shots [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **The final inspection.** The agent must complete the end-of-tenancy part of the report within 10 days after the agreement ends. They must give you a reasonable opportunity to be present, and they must allow for fair wear and tear [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## Gaps

The retrieved documents don't cover how a bond claim would proceed. They also don't say whether any 2024 wording differed from today's. I haven't stated anything on those points.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. The hardest is the professional-cleaning limit, which the answer states as allowed only if 'Professional cleaning was done immediately before the tenancy started and you were told so; or Professional cleaning is needed to restore the premises to their condition at the start of the tenancy... taking into account fair wear and tear'. It cites this as standard form clause 11 rather than reg 12, which does not change the meaning. The renter's duty is also covered: 'leave the premises reasonably clean and... in the same condition as when you moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear'. So is the evidence point: the move-in condition report 'records whether each item is clean' and is 'meant to help resolve disputes'.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer says the opposite of the failure condition, stating "you probably don't have to pay for a professional cleaner just because the pet clause says so" and that "A term requiring professional carpet cleaning that isn't in the standard form is prohibited."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as "version 115, in force from 13 October 2026" (file rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf, link 97-109aa115) and the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 as "version 009, in force from 30 June 2026" (file rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf, link 21-3sra009). Every rule it applies is cited to those in-force versions, and its mention of the 2024 versions only notes they are unavailable rather than relying on them.

question: When I moved out I agreed the agent could take an amount for cleaning out of my bond, but I never signed a bond claim form for it. Then my full bond came back to me, and a month later the agent sent a separate invoice for the cleaning. Do I have to pay it? Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents I retrieved don't say that agreeing to a bond deduction is the same as agreeing to pay a later invoice. They also don't say you must pay this invoice just because it was sent. They do set out how an agent can recover cleaning costs, and your facts don't fit the bond route.

**Source:** *rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf* (Residential Tenancies Act 1997), Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I also drew on *rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf* (Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021), dated 30 June 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). I can't confirm from the documents that nothing newer exists, but these are the versions retrieved, and both are dated before today.

## What the law says

- **Cleaning can be claimed from a bond.** A residential rental provider (including its agent) may claim bond for "the reasonable cost of cleaning any part of the premises, if the premises were not left reasonably clean", having regard to the condition at the start of the agreement (s 411AB(1)(c)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **A bond claim must be in an approved form.** The claim must be "in a form approved by the Authority" (s 411(2)(a)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Your agreement alone isn't a claim.** A claim on the bond is a form lodged with the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority. An informal agreement that the agent could "take an amount" isn't that. Your full bond was repaid, so no cleaning claim appears to have been made on it.
- **Cleaning duties.** At the end of the agreement you must leave the premises "as far as practicable" reasonably clean, and in the same condition as when you moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear (s 63(2)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **A later invoice isn't barred.** Someone who has recovered compensation from a bond "is not precluded from taking proceedings under this Part to recover an additional amount by way of compensation" (s 214(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). So the agent may still pursue you, but the route is a Tribunal application for compensation, not simply an invoice. The retrieved text includes only the headings for sections 209 and 210, not their wording, so I can't set out the exact requirements or any time limit [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Tribunal considerations.** When hearing such an application the Tribunal may consider whether money has been recovered from the bond, whether the applicant took action to mitigate the loss, and any offer of compensation (s 211(c), (e), (f)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Professional cleaning.** Under reg 12, the agent can't require professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy unless either of these applies [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf):
  - professional cleaning was done before the tenancy started and you were told so; or
  - it is needed to restore the premises to their starting condition, judged against the condition report and allowing for fair wear and tear.

## What you can do

1. **Ask the agent in writing** for the basis of the invoice. Useful evidence includes an invoice, receipt, quote or photographs, which the Act lists as "bond claim evidence" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Ask for a comparison with the start-of-tenancy condition report.
2. **Check whether the amount is reasonable.** It should reflect the reasonable cost of cleaning, the starting condition and fair wear and tear. If the agent demands professional cleaning, check it meets reg 12 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Dispute any excess in writing.** If you disagree with the amount or the need for cleaning, say so. If the agent applies to the Tribunal, you can raise the points above.
4. **Mention what you agreed.** If you really did agree to an amount for cleaning, that may matter, but the documents don't say whether it binds you beyond the bond. That is a contract-law question they don't cover.

I can't say from these documents whether you must pay. That depends on whether the premises weren't left reasonably clean and on what the agent can prove.

must-mention.reason: No. The first point is missing because the answer hedges it. It says only that the documents "don't say that agreeing to a bond deduction is the same as agreeing to pay a later invoice" and calls the effect of the agreement "a contract-law question they don't cover". It never states that agreeing to a deduction is agreement to a claim on the bond (a claim form or bond claim evidence) rather than to a separate invoice. The second point is covered: the answer cites s 411AB(1)(c) and s 63(2) and says the outcome depends on whether the premises were left reasonably clean compared with their starting condition.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer says neither forbidden thing: it states the documents "don't say that agreeing to a bond deduction is the same as agreeing to pay a later invoice" and "I can't say from these documents whether you must pay", and rather than claiming the bond repayment bars further claims, it says "A later invoice isn't barred" because the provider "is not precluded from taking proceedings... to recover an additional amount" (s 214(1)).

question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. I've called them twice today. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
**Short answer:** You don't have to wait indefinitely. If the owner or agent won't or can't get the repair done immediately, the law lets you arrange it yourself, but only once you've taken reasonable steps and failed to get it done. I'd also suggest sending written notice now.

*Sources: the* Residential Tenancies Act 1997 *(file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", Version 115, in force from 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). That is the version in force today, 9 November 2026. I also used the* Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 *(file "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf", Version 009, 30 June 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The retrieved files show version numbers in their file names and metadata. I didn't see the words "Authorised Version No." in the extracts.*

## What the law says

- **This is likely an "urgent repair".** The Act's definition includes a burst water service, a failure or breakdown of the water supply to the premises, and a water-using fitting that is malfunctioning so that a substantial amount of water is or will be wasted [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A broken tap that forced you to shut off water to the whole house probably fits one of these. The documents don't say which category applies to your tap.
- **You may arrange urgent repairs yourself if both of these are true** (s 72(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf):
  1. You've taken reasonable steps to arrange for the rental provider or their agent to carry out the repairs immediately.
  2. You're unable to get them to carry out the repairs.
- **The repair must be done by a suitably qualified person.** The standard rental agreement says only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, urgent or non-urgent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The Act says this includes a registered or licensed tradesperson where the work requires it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). So use a licensed plumber.
- **The documents don't address the owner's "own tradespeople only" rule.** Nothing in them says a provider can require that only their chosen tradespeople do urgent repairs, or that this stops you using s 72. The test in s 72 is whether you've taken reasonable steps and can't get the repair done. The documents also don't say whether two calls count as "reasonable steps". That is a judgement on the facts.

## What you can do

1. **Give written notice of the breakdown.** The Act requires a renter to give written notice as soon as practicable after becoming aware of damage or a breakdown of provided facilities or fixtures (s 72AA) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The standard agreement also says to notify the rental provider in writing of an urgent repair [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Email counts, because the Act allows notices to be given by electronic communication [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Keep a record of both phone calls.
2. **Ask for a firm, immediate time.** If the owner's tradesperson still can't come immediately, you can arrange the repair under s 72(1) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **After a repair you've arranged** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf):
   - Give the rental provider 7 days' written notice of the repairs done and the cost.
   - The provider is liable to reimburse the reasonable cost, or a prescribed greater amount if there is one, whichever is less. This includes GST.
   - They must reimburse you within 7 days after receiving that written notice.
4. **Reimbursement limit.** The standard rental agreement summary says a renter may be reimbursed the reasonable cost of repairs up to **$2500** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Keep your invoice. I didn't retrieve the regulation that sets the prescribed amount itself, so check that if the cost may be near that figure.
5. **If you can't pay, or the owner won't reimburse you,** you can apply to VCAT (the Tribunal) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf):
   - You can apply for an order that the provider carry out specified urgent repairs if you can't meet the cost, the cost exceeds the prescribed amount, or the provider refuses to pay (s 73). The Tribunal must hear that application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
   - If you've paid, given written notice, and weren't reimbursed within 7 days, you can apply for a compensation or compliance order (s 209AAB) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**Also check your paperwork.** If an agent manages the property, the provider must have given you a written statement saying whether the agent can authorise urgent repairs, up to what amount, and the number to call [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). That may help you work out who to press.

This is based only on the retrieved documents, not legal advice. For a specific dispute, Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy advice service can confirm the details.

question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. I haven't moved any of my things in or stayed there yet. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
**Sources:** *rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf* (Residential Tenancies Act 1997, version 115 per its metadata, in force from 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). *rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf* (Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, version 009, in force from 30 June 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). These are the latest versions I retrieved, and they cover today's date. The files do not use the words "Authorised Version No.", so the version numbers come from the metadata.

## What the law says

- **Minimum standards:** The rental provider must ensure the premises meet the prescribed rental minimum standards on or before the day you move in. The penalty is 60 penalty units for a natural person and 300 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Damp and structure:** Under the standards, the premises must be "structurally sound and weatherproof" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Each room must be "free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs:** The definition includes a failure to comply with any rental minimum standards. It also includes faults that make the premises unsafe, such as "the presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Your options

**1. Cancel the lease**
- A lease ends if you have not entered into possession and you give the provider a notice of termination on one of these grounds [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf):
  - the premises are not in good repair;
  - the premises are unfit for human habitation;
  - the premises do not meet any rental minimum standards; or
  - the premises are for any other reason unavailable for occupation.
- Damp, mould and rotting timber could fit the first three grounds, but whether they do is a question of fact.
- Collecting the keys may or may not count as "entered into possession". The retrieved text does not define the term. Do not move in or store belongings until you have settled this.
- The retrieved text gives no required form or notice period for this notice. Put it in writing and keep a copy.

**2. Ask for repairs**
- You can issue a request for urgent repairs to bring the premises up to the standards [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Give written notice of damage as soon as practicable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- If the provider does not act immediately, you can arrange urgent repairs yourself. You must first have taken reasonable steps to get the provider to do them [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- You must then give 7 days' written notice of the repairs and their cost. The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days of that notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The standard-form agreement summary states the reimbursement cap as $2,500 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- You can apply to VCAT for an urgent repairs order if you cannot meet the cost, the cost is over the prescribed amount, or the provider refuses to pay. VCAT must hear the application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- For non-urgent repairs, give written notice. If the provider has not acted within 14 days, you can ask the Director to investigate or apply to VCAT, which must hear the application within 7 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- VCAT can order specified repairs by a suitably qualified person, within a set time [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Once you have given repair notice, you can ask VCAT to let you pay rent into the Rent Special Account. VCAT must make the order if the provider has not done the repairs and has not shown financial hardship [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**3. Lower rent**
- I found no provision in the retrieved documents that lets you simply reduce the rent for damp or mould.
- The rent-free rule in section 65(3) applies only where premises are not vacant or not reasonably clean. It runs from the agreed move-in day until you actually move in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The retrieved text does not extend it to damp or mould.
- Rent accrues from day to day [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- VCAT can order compensation under section 212(2) when the provider breaches the repair duty [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The text of section 212 was not retrieved, so I cannot say how it works.
- The Rent Special Account holds your rent while repairs are outstanding. It is not a reduction [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**Also useful:** The provider must give you a condition report before you move in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Within 30 days of the agreement starting, you can ask VCAT to amend a condition report that is inaccurate or incomplete [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A condition report given to the provider counts as notice of the defects it records [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Not covered in the retrieved documents
- Whether collecting the keys counts as "entered into possession".
- The form and timing of a notice under the cancellation provision.
- A general right to a rent reduction.

Photograph the defects and put everything in writing.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. The answer says the provider "must ensure the premises meet the prescribed rental minimum standards on or before the day you move in," including that rooms be "free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure." It says a lease ends if you "have not entered into possession and you give the provider a notice of termination" because the premises are not in good repair, are unfit for human habitation, or do not meet the minimum standards. It also says "You can issue a request for urgent repairs to bring the premises up to the standards."

It also denies a statutory rent reduction: 'I found no provision in the retrieved documents that lets you simply reduce the rent for damp or mould,' and notes the Rent Special Account 'is not a reduction.'
