question: Our rental was broken into several times while we were moving out, and there are about three weeks left on our fixed-term lease. The burglars damaged the plumbing and wiring, so we can't even clean properly. What are our options before the lease ends?
answer:
**Documents used:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", version 115, in force from 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). It is the version in force today (9 November 2026). I also used the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, file "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf", version 009, in force from 30 June 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The files give these as version numbers in their metadata. I did not see the phrase "Authorised Version No." in the text I retrieved.

## What the law says

- **Leaving early because the premises are unusable.** A renter may give a notice of intention to vacate if the premises are unfit for human habitation, or have been destroyed totally or to such an extent as to be rendered unsafe. The termination date can be the day you give the notice or a later date (s 91ZD) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Ordinary early exit.** A normal notice of intention to vacate needs at least 28 days' notice (s 91Z) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). For a fixed-term lease, a notice with a termination date before the end of the term is of no effect in the ordinary case (s 91ZA(1)(b)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). With about three weeks left, this route doesn't give you anything.
- **Urgent repairs.** The definition covers a burst water service, a dangerous electrical fault, and any fault or damage that makes the premises unsafe or insecure [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Burglary damage to plumbing and wiring may fall within these, but that depends on the facts.
- **Reporting damage.** A renter must give written notice of damage to the rental provider as soon as practicable (ss 62, 72AA) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Tribunal can take into account whether you gave that notice when it decides compensation claims (s 211(h)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Cleaning.** At the end of the agreement you must leave the premises reasonably clean "as far as practicable", and in the same condition as when you moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear (s 63(2)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Damage duty.** A renter must not intentionally or negligently damage the premises (s 61) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do

1. **Give written notice of the break-ins and damage now.** Email counts [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Keep a copy.
2. **Ask the rental provider (or agent) to carry out urgent repairs immediately.**
   - If they don't, you may arrange the urgent repairs yourself, provided you took reasonable steps to get them done and couldn't (s 72) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
   - Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
   - You must give the provider 7 days' written notice of the repairs and the cost. The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days of receiving that notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
   - The regulations' standard rental agreement summary states the reimbursement limit as $2,500 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Apply to VCAT for an urgent repairs order.** You can do this if you can't meet the cost, the repairs cost more than the prescribed amount, or the provider refuses to pay. VCAT must hear the application within 2 business days (s 73) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If the provider doesn't reimburse you within 7 days of written notice, you can apply for a compliance or compensation order (s 209AAB, s 212(1B)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Give notice of intention to vacate under s 91ZD**, but only if the damage really makes the premises unfit for human habitation or unsafe. You can set the termination date as today or later [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say what counts as "unfit" or "unsafe", so you would be judging that yourself. A dispute would be for VCAT.
5. **Explain the cleaning problem in writing.** Say you can't clean properly because of the damage. That supports your position under the "as far as practicable" wording [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't cover

- They don't say who bears the cost of burglar damage, or how the bond would be treated. Section 61 only refers to damage a renter causes intentionally or negligently [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- They don't say whether this particular damage meets the "unfit" or "unsafe" test.
- They don't address insurance or police reports.

For a firm answer on those points, get advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria or a community legal centre. The Act's urgent-repairs and VCAT provisions are time-sensitive, so act quickly.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. (1) The answer tells the renter to give written notice of the damage to the rental provider 'as soon as practicable (ss 62, 72AA)'. (2) It lists a burst water service and a dangerous electrical fault as urgent repairs, tells the renter to 'Ask the rental provider (or agent) to carry out urgent repairs immediately', and explains the renter may arrange the repairs and be reimbursed if the provider does not act (s 72). (3) It says a renter may give notice of intention to vacate under s 91ZD if the premises are unfit for habitation or unsafe, with a termination date that 'can be the day you give the notice', and presents this as the route available despite the fixed term. The hardest point is (2), because the answer says the damage 'may fall within these, but that depends on the facts'. That hedge is mild and the answer still clearly treats the damage as urgent repairs.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer says the renter 'may give a notice of intention to vacate if the premises are unfit for human habitation' (s 91ZD), so they are not bound to stay, and it says the renter may arrange urgent repairs only if the provider doesn't, with the provider required to 'reimburse the reasonable cost,' which is not liability for the burglary damage.

version-cited.reason: Yes: the answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as "version 115, in force from 13 October 2026" (file rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf, link 97-109aa115), and the only other document it relies on is the in-force Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 "version 009" (link 21-3sra009), with no rule taken from any other version.

question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. The app is run by a payments company my agent uses, and it's that company that charges the card fee. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents don't give a clear yes or no. Several provisions point against the fee, but there is a carve-out for card surcharges "permitted under any other Act", and the documents don't say whether it applies here. It also doesn't turn on whether the fee goes to the app company or the agent.

**Documents applied (the versions in force today, 9 Nov 2026)**
- *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", Version 115, in force from 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The excerpts I retrieved don't show the printed "Authorised Version No." cover page, so I'm taking "115" from the file's version metadata.
- *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, file "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf", Version 009, in force from 30 June 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Fee-free option:** The rental provider or their agent must make sure a rent payment method with no additional costs, other than your own bank or account fees, is reasonably available to you (s 42(4)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Your free bank transfer may meet this. The documents don't say whether "slower" still counts as "reasonably available".
- **Electronic payment charges:** A person must not demand or receive a charge from a renter for "the establishment or use of direct debit facilities or any other electronic payment facility for payment of rent" (s 51(3)(b)). The penalty is 60 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This wording covers any "person", not just the provider or agent. A card-payment fee plausibly falls within it, but the documents don't define "electronic payment facility".
- **Rent payment fees:** A person, other than an ADI, must not demand or receive a fee for any prescribed matter relating to the payment of rent (s 51A) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
  - The prescribed matters include "rent payment (other than payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act)". This has applied from 31 March 2026 (reg 21C) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
  - So a card surcharge that another Act permits is carved out. The documents don't identify any such Act.
  - They also don't define "ADI" or say whether your payments company is one.
- **Disclosure:** Before you consent to a payment method, the provider or agent must tell you about any costs you may incur, expressly including "third party transaction fees" and "other electronic payment facility fees" (s 42(7)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This is a disclosure duty. It doesn't say such fees are allowed.

## Does it matter who gets the fee?

- **Sections 51(3)(b) and 51A:** Both say "a person", so on their wording it doesn't matter whether the app company or the agent receives the fee [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The only exceptions in these provisions are ADIs (s 51A) and surcharges permitted under another Act (reg 21C) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Sections 42(4) and 42(7):** These bind only the provider and their agent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). So the agent still has to ensure a free method is available and to disclose the fees, even though a third-party company runs the app.

## What you can do

- **Use the free bank transfer.** The Regulations prescribe electronic funds transfer as a payment method the provider or agent must permit (reg 19) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The standard form agreement also says the provider must permit a fee-free payment method [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Ask your agent in writing** to disclose all fees for each payment method (s 42(7)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Ask the agent to identify** which "other Act" they say permits the card surcharge, and whether the payments company is an ADI. If they can't, the fee may fall within ss 51(3)(b) and 51A [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

The documents I retrieved don't cover complaint or enforcement steps, or whether card surcharges are permitted under another Act, so I can't answer those. For a definite answer on the surcharge, check that other legislation.

(2) The hardest point is covered by 'A person, other than an ADI, must not demand or receive a fee for any prescribed matter relating to the payment of rent (s 51A)', the reg 21C carve-out for 'payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act', and 'Both say "a person", so on their wording it doesn't matter whether the app company or the agent receives the fee'. (3) It gives a next step: 'Use the free bank transfer.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as "Version 115, in force from 13 October 2026" (file rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf, link 97-109aa115) and the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 as "Version 009, in force from 30 June 2026" (file rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf, link 21-3sra009), both the in-force versions, and it relies on no other version.

question: My lease is on the standard form and started in 2024. It has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. I cleaned them myself and they're back to how they were when I moved in, but the agent wants a receipt from a professional cleaner. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?
answer:
## What the law says

**Sources used:** Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (S.R. No. 3/2021), **Authorised Version No. 009**, incorporating amendments as at 30 June 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). I also used the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, file *rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf* (version 115, in force from 13 October 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Act extracts I retrieved don't show an "Authorised Version No." heading, so I'm taking "115" from the file name and metadata. I applied these versions because they are current today. The documents don't include the versions in force when your 2024 lease started.

- **Professional cleaning terms are generally banned.** A lease must not require professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy, or require the renter to pay for it, unless that term is in the standard form [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The standard form allows it only in two cases.** The rental provider must not require professional cleaning unless one of these applies [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf):
  1. Professional cleaning was done immediately before your tenancy started and you were told so.
  2. Professional cleaning is needed to restore the premises to their condition at the start of the tenancy. This is judged by the condition report, allowing for fair wear and tear.
- **Prohibited terms are void.** A prohibited term in a lease is void and unenforceable [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Your general duty is lighter.** At the end of the lease you must leave the premises reasonably clean and in the same condition as when you moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**Applied to you:** The pet clause is an extra term. On my reading, it can only be enforced to the extent it matches the two standard-form cases above. If your carpets are back to their move-in condition, professional cleaning isn't "required to restore" them, so case 2 shouldn't apply. The documents don't address pet-specific cleaning clauses or receipts, so that is my reading of the general rules rather than something they state directly. The pet provisions I retrieved (ss 71A–71E) say nothing about cleaning conditions [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**One thing to check:** Case 1 could apply if the carpets were professionally cleaned before you moved in and you were told so [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Look at your condition report and the move-in paperwork.

## What you can do

1. **Ask the agent which standard-form ground they rely on.** They need either pre-tenancy professional cleaning that you were told about, or a condition-report basis showing it's needed to restore the carpets [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
2. **Rely on the condition report.** It is the reference point [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The form says the report "will help to resolve disputes over cleaning" and lists "floor coverings" among the items to be recorded [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). You should have signed and returned your copy within 5 business days of moving in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Use photos.** The form says to take photos at the beginning and end of the tenancy [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). They should be dated, labelled and show the location, both close-up and from a distance [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Photos of the carpets now, set against your move-in photos and comments, are your best evidence.
4. **Attend the final inspection.** The agent must complete the end-of-tenancy report within 10 days after the agreement ends. They must give you a chance to attend if possible and must allow for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
5. **Challenge the term if needed.** You can apply to the Tribunal to have a term declared invalid or varied if it is harsh or unconscionable [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

The documents I retrieved don't say how a bond dispute over this would play out, so I haven't covered that.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered: the two standard-form cases for professional cleaning (pre-tenancy cleaning the renter was told about, or cleaning needed to restore the start condition allowing for fair wear and tear); the duty to leave the premises 'reasonably clean and in the same condition as when you moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear'; and the condition report as evidence ('Rely on the condition report. It is the reference point', backed by the advice to use move-in photos).

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the renter must pay simply because of the clause or the pet. It says professional cleaning terms are "generally banned", that "Prohibited terms are void", and that the pet clause "can only be enforced to the extent it matches the two standard-form cases above", noting that if the carpets are back to move-in condition then "case 2 shouldn't apply."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 as "Authorised Version No. 009" (link 21-3sra009) and the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as "version 115" (file rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf, link 97-109aa115), both in-force versions, and every rule it applies comes from those versions.

question: When I moved out I agreed the agent could take an amount for cleaning out of my bond, but I never signed a bond claim form for it. Then my full bond came back to me, and a month later the agent sent a separate invoice for the cleaning. Do I have to pay it? Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?
answer:
**Source:** *rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf*, the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). It is the version in force today (9 November 2026). I found no other version of the Act in the documents. If your tenancy ended long before this version took effect, an earlier version might apply, and the documents don't cover that.

## What the law says

- **Bond claims have a set process.** A claim to the Bond Authority "must be in a form approved by the Authority" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A provider can't request or obtain a renter's signature on a claim form unless it states the amount of bond to be refunded and how it is apportioned [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Cleaning is a valid bond claim.** A provider may claim "the reasonable cost of cleaning any part of the premises, if the premises were not left reasonably clean by the renter, having regard to the condition of the premises at the commencement" of the agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). At the end of the tenancy you must leave the premises "reasonably clean" and in the same condition as at the start, allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Evidence for bond claims.** At least 3 days before a claim to the bond is made, the provider or agent must give you "bond claim evidence". That means an invoice, receipt, quote, photograph or other prescribed evidence, and it must not conflict with the condition report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **A bond claim doesn't stop a further claim.** Someone who has recovered compensation from a bond "is not precluded" from taking Tribunal proceedings to recover an additional amount [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The agent can therefore still pursue you, but the route the Act describes is the Tribunal. Under s 212(2) the Tribunal can order compensation if it is satisfied it should be paid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). When it assesses compensation it considers whether money has already been recovered from the bond and whether the applicant mitigated its loss [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **A signed condition report is strong evidence.** If both parties signed it, it is conclusive evidence of the premises' condition on the day it states. This doesn't apply to statements you disagreed with in writing [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?

The retrieved text doesn't say so. It doesn't make an informal agreement to a bond deduction into an agreement to pay a separate invoice, and it doesn't make an invoice enforceable on its own. It only provides a formal bond claim (on the approved form) and Tribunal applications [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents say nothing on whether your verbal or informal agreement creates a separate debt under general contract law, so I can't answer that part.

## Do you have to pay?

Not automatically, on what the documents show. Whether you owe anything depends on whether the premises were left reasonably clean compared with the start of the tenancy, and whether the amount is a reasonable cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). An invoice alone isn't a Tribunal order.

## What you can do

1. **Ask in writing** for the agent's evidence: itemised invoice, photos and the condition report. Compare these with the condition report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Dispute the amount in writing** if the premises were reasonably clean or the cost seems unreasonable.
3. **Keep your records**, including the condition reports, any messages where the deduction was discussed, and your bond refund confirmation.
4. **If the agent applies to the Tribunal**, raise the points above, including that the full bond was returned [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't give any time limit for the agent to pursue you after the bond is refunded, so I can't say whether one applies.

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered. On the hardest one, the answer says the Act "doesn't make an informal agreement to a bond deduction into an agreement to pay a separate invoice" and "only provides a formal bond claim (on the approved form)". It leaves only general contract law open, so a reader can still tell the point falls on the 'not the same' side. On the cleaning test, it states that what you owe depends on whether the premises were left "reasonably clean compared with the start of the tenancy" and on whether the cost is reasonable, assessed by the Tribunal.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: neither failure condition is asserted, since the answer says 'Not automatically, on what the documents show' and that the text 'doesn't make an informal agreement to a bond deduction into an agreement to pay a separate invoice,' and it rejects the second claim by saying 'The agent can therefore still pursue you, but the route the Act describes is the Tribunal.'

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the only required document with its in-force version, 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026' (file rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf, link 97-109aa115), and every rule it applies is cited to that version alone.

question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. I've called them twice today. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
**Short answer:** You don't have to wait indefinitely, but you can't fix it yourself as a DIY job. The Act allows you to arrange an urgent repair, and the repairer must be suitably qualified. The documents don't say whether two calls in one day is enough to trigger that right.

**Sources:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", version 115, in force from 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I also used the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, file "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf", version 009, dated 30 June 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Both are the latest versions I retrieved, so they apply today (9 November 2026). The excerpts don't print an "Authorised Version No." label, so the numbers come from the file metadata.

## What the law says

- **Urgent repairs include water problems.** The definition covers a burst water service, a failure or breakdown of the water supply to rented premises, and a water fitting or fixture malfunctioning so that a substantial amount of water is or will be wasted [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A broken tap isn't named, so whether yours qualifies depends on these categories. Having to shut off water to the whole house suggests it does, but that is my reading.
- **When you may arrange the repair.** You may arrange urgent repairs if both of these apply [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf):
  - You have taken reasonable steps to get the rental provider or agent to carry out the repairs immediately.
  - You are unable to get them to do so.
- **Gap in the documents.** They don't define "reasonable steps" or say whether a provider's "own tradespeople only" policy counts as being "unable to get" them to act. Two calls with no repair date is a strong position, but it isn't guaranteed.
- **The repairer must be qualified.** The standard rental agreement says only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, urgent or not [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). "Suitably qualified person" includes a registered or licensed tradesperson where the work requires it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). So hire a licensed plumber rather than doing it yourself.
- **Reimbursement.**
  - The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost, or the prescribed amount if that is less. They must pay within 7 days of receiving your written notice of the repairs and their cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
  - The standard agreement summary gives the figure as up to $2500 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do

1. **Put it in writing now.** Send the provider or agent written notice of the broken tap. You must report damage or breakdowns in writing as soon as practicable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Email is allowed if electronic service is valid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Say you've called twice today, that the water is off, and that you'll arrange a licensed plumber if no one can attend immediately. Phone calls alone won't meet the written-notice requirement.
2. **Allow a short, reasonable window** for a response, because the right depends on you having taken reasonable steps first [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **If there's no workable response, engage a licensed plumber.** Keep the invoice.
4. **Give the provider written notice of the repair and its cost** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The provider must reimburse you within 7 days of getting that notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. **If you're not reimbursed within 7 days,** you can apply to VCAT for a compensation or compliance order [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
6. **If you can't afford the repair, it costs more than the prescribed amount, or the provider refuses to pay,** you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring the provider to carry out the urgent repairs. VCAT must hear that application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

This is general information based only on the retrieved documents. It isn't legal advice for your situation.

must-mention.reason: No: the third point is missing. The answer never says a nominated-tradesperson term is prohibited (reg 11(e)) or that the 'own tradespeople only' policy cannot stop an urgent repair; it says the documents don't address whether the policy counts as being 'unable to get' the provider to act, which leaves that point unresolved. The urgent-repair definition and the s 72 reimbursement point are both covered.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer says neither forbidden claim: it states "You don't have to wait indefinitely" and "The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost, or the prescribed amount if that is less", so it does not require waiting for the landlord's tradesperson or deny cost recovery.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as "version 115" (file rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf, link 97-109aa115) and the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 as "version 009" (file rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf, link 21-3sra009), both the versions in force on the date, and every rule it applies comes from these versions.

question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. I haven't moved any of my things in or stayed there yet. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
**Documents used**
- *rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf*, the Residential Tenancies Act 1997. It is dated 13 October 2026, and its metadata gives version 115. This is the version in force today (9 Nov 2026). The text I retrieved doesn't print an "Authorised Version No." label, so "115" comes from the file metadata. I can't confirm from the documents that no later version exists.
- *rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf*, the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021. It is dated 30 June 2026, version 009.

## What the law says

- **Minimum standards.** Premises must be structurally sound and weatherproof, and each room must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Timing.** The rental provider must make sure the premises meet these standards on or before the day the renter moves in [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Duty to maintain.** The provider must keep the premises in good repair and reasonably fit for occupation. This applies even if the renter knew of disrepair before moving in [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Unoccupied premises.** A renter isn't required to enter premises that aren't vacant and reasonably clean. If the premises don't meet that standard, no rent is payable from the agreed move-in day until the renter actually moves in [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Damp, mould and rot are not clearly covered by "reasonably clean", so this may not apply to you.

## Your options

**1. Cancel (you haven't moved in)**
- If you haven't entered into possession, the agreement ends once you give the provider a notice of termination. The permitted grounds include that the premises:
  - are not in good repair;
  - are unfit for human habitation;
  - don't meet rental minimum standards [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Your facts (damp, mould, rotting timber) point to these grounds. Whether they are made out is a factual question.
- The retrieved text sets no notice period for this type of notice.
- The documents don't say whether collecting the keys counts as "entering into possession". Avoid moving in or staying until this is settled.
- If you did take possession, a different route applies. You could give notice of intention to vacate if the premises are unfit for human habitation, with a termination date of the notice date or later [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**2. Ask for repairs**
- A failure to comply with rental minimum standards counts as an urgent repair. So does mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure that makes the premises unsafe [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Where premises don't meet the standards when you move in, you may request urgent repairs [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- If the provider doesn't act, you can arrange urgent repairs yourself after taking reasonable steps to get the provider to do them. Give 7 days' written notice of the repairs and their cost [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
  - The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days of that notice [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
  - The Form 1 summary states the reimbursement limit as $2500 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- You can apply to VCAT for an urgent repairs order if you can't meet the cost, the cost is over the prescribed amount, or the provider refuses to pay. VCAT must hear it within 2 business days [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- For non-urgent repairs, give written notice. If the provider hasn't acted within 14 days, you can apply to the Director to investigate or to VCAT for an order [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- VCAT can order specified repairs by a suitably qualified person, with a deadline, and can order compensation [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**3. Lower rent**
- I found no provision giving a general right to reduce rent for these defects.
- Related remedies exist:
  - If the provider has been given notice of the repairs and hasn't done them, VCAT can authorise you to pay rent into the Rent Special Account. It must do so unless the provider shows financial hardship [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
  - VCAT can order compensation [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
  - If premises aren't vacant and reasonably clean, rent isn't payable until you move in (see above) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Practical step
Put everything in writing to the provider or agent, with photos. A condition report you give the provider is taken to be notice of the defects it lists [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If you weren't given one, you can complete and return your own [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

This is a summary of the retrieved text, not legal advice. Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy advice service can help with your specific facts.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three required points are stated. The answer gives the mould and damp standard ('free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure') and says the provider must meet the standards 'on or before the day the renter moves in'. It states that a renter who hasn't entered into possession can end the agreement by notice because the premises are not in good repair, are unfit for human habitation, or don't meet rental minimum standards; its uncertainty about whether collecting keys counts as possession concerns the facts, not the rule. It covers the repair route: 'Where premises don't meet the standards when you move in, you may request urgent repairs.'

question: Our rental was broken into several times while we were moving out, and there are about three weeks left on our fixed-term lease. The burglars damaged the plumbing and wiring, so we can't even clean properly. What are our options before the lease ends?
answer:
# Options for a rental broken into with three weeks left on a fixed term

I used the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I also used the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (file "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf", dated 30 June 2026, version 009 per its file name and metadata) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). These are the latest versions in the documents I retrieved. The documents don't confirm that nothing newer exists.

## What the law says

- **Early exit for unfit premises:** A renter may give a notice of intention to vacate if the premises are unfit for human habitation, or have been destroyed totally or enough to be unsafe (s 91ZD). The notice can give a termination date that is the date of the notice or later [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Normal exit rules don't suit you:** An ordinary notice of intention to vacate needs a termination date at least 28 days after the notice is given (s 91Z) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A notice on a fixed-term agreement is also of no effect if its termination date is earlier than the end of the term (s 91ZA(1)(b)). So the ordinary route doesn't help with three weeks left [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs:** "Urgent repairs" include a burst water service, a dangerous electrical fault, and any fault or damage that makes the premises unsafe or insecure [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Cleaning:** At the end of the agreement, a renter must leave the premises reasonably clean "as far as practicable" (s 63(2)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Maintenance:** The rental provider must maintain the premises in good repair and in a fit condition for occupation [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

1. **Report the damage in writing now.** Renters must give written notice of damage as soon as practicable (s 72AA) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask for urgent repairs.** If the provider or agent won't carry out the repairs, you may arrange them yourselves, but only after taking reasonable steps to get the provider to do them immediately (s 72). You must then give 7 days' written notice of the repairs and their cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The provider must reimburse you within 7 days of that notice, up to $2,500 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Apply to VCAT if needed.** You can apply for an order requiring urgent repairs if you can't meet the cost, the cost is over $2,500, or the provider refuses to pay. VCAT must hear the application within 2 business days (s 73) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
4. **Consider ending the lease early under s 91ZD.** This depends on whether the premises are actually unfit for habitation or unsafe. That is a factual question the documents don't decide for your property. The notice must be in writing and signed (s 91ZZN) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The agreement ends when you vacate on or after the termination date in the notice (s 91E) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. **Lease-break costs.** One prescribed form of agreement in the regulations says the provider isn't entitled to "rent foregone" if the renter ends the agreement under s 91ZD [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). I can't tell from the excerpt which form applies to your lease, so check your own agreement.
6. **Hardship.** VCAT can reduce or terminate a fixed term for severe hardship caused by an unforeseen change in circumstances (s 91U) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). That seems a weaker fit here than s 91ZD.

## What the documents don't answer

- They don't say who bears the cost of burglary damage, or how your bond or any compensation claim would be treated.
- They don't define "unfit for human habitation".
- They don't cover insurance or police reporting.

You may want to get advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy legal service.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. Point 1 is in step 1: 'Renters must give written notice of damage as soon as practicable (s 72AA).' Point 2 is covered because urgent repairs are defined to include 'a burst water service, a dangerous electrical fault', and step 2 lets renters arrange repairs after 'taking reasonable steps to get the provider to do them immediately', with reimbursement up to $2,500. The hardest point, 3, is covered by 'A renter may give a notice of intention to vacate if the premises are unfit for human habitation, or have been destroyed totally or enough to be unsafe (s 91ZD). The notice can give a termination date that is the date of the notice or later', which is offered as the way to end the fixed term early.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer never makes the renter liable for the repairs; it says 'The provider must reimburse you within 7 days of that notice, up to $2,500', and instead of binding them to stay it says 'A renter may give a notice of intention to vacate if the premises are unfit for human habitation... (s 91ZD)'.

The answer names the Act as "Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026" (link 97-109aa115), and the only other source it relies on is the in-force Regulations version 009 dated 30 June 2026 (link 21-3sra009), so no rule comes from a version not in force on that date.
